event_model_payload.headline: LocalSend: Like AirDrop, but for Every Device, Free and Open Source
event_model_payload.summary:
LocalSend is a free open source app that sends files, photos, and messages between any of your devices over your local network. It works like AirDrop, but it covers Android, iPhone, Windows, Mac, and Linux, and it never touches the internet.

What LocalSend Is: AirDrop Without the Walled Garden

LocalSend is a free, open source app for sharing files and messages with nearby devices over your local network, and it needs no internet connection to do it. It is the cross-platform answer to AirDrop: send a photo from an Android phone to an iPhone, a document from a Windows laptop to a Mac, or a video from a Linux desktop to a tablet, all without a cable, an account, or a cloud service in the middle. It has 98,900 stars on GitHub, it is licensed under Apache 2.0, and it runs on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, Linux, and Fire OS. The pitch is simple. Every phone already knows how to share with its own kind, and almost none of them know how to share with the other kind. LocalSend fills that gap with one app on every device, and it does it without asking you to trust a server you have never heard of, because there is no server at all.

How It Works: Your Wi-Fi Is the Only Infrastructure

LocalSend devices find each other on the same local network and talk directly, using a REST API over HTTPS. Every device generates its own TLS certificate on the fly, so the transfer is encrypted end to end even though nothing ever leaves your network. There are no third-party servers, no upload step, and no account to create. The app listens on port 53317 for TCP and UDP traffic, which is the one detail worth knowing before you use it: if a device does not show up, your firewall is the usual suspect. On Linux, allow the port with your firewall tool, for example sudo ufw allow 53317, and check that AP isolation is off on your router, since some routers, especially on guest networks, block devices from seeing each other. A VPN can also hide local devices, so allow local traffic or pause it while you send. If discovery still fails, LocalSend lets you send to a device by its exact address instead, and the command line client can target an IP Check result directly. When devices on the same network cannot see each other at all, a DNS Lookup can help confirm whether the network itself is resolving names the way it should.

What You Can Send: Files, Folders, and Messages

LocalSend moves more than files. You can send photos, videos, documents, and whole folders, and directories are collected recursively with their folder names and nested paths preserved on the receiving side. You can also send a short text message, a link, or a snippet of text, which is handy when you want to move a URL or a code from your phone to your computer without emailing it to yourself. Text longer than 64 KB is sent as a .txt file instead, and you can read text from standard input on the command line. Sharing works from other apps too: use the system share sheet on your phone to send a photo or a file straight into LocalSend, and it appears on the destination device as a normal download. There is no file size limit in the app itself, so the only real constraint is your Wi-Fi. The README is upfront about one speed quirk on Android and recommends 5 GHz Wi-Fi, with encryption off on both devices if a transfer feels slow.

Every Platform, Every Store

LocalSend is on every major platform, and it is in the stores and package managers people already use. Windows users can install it from Winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, or the Microsoft Store, or grab the EXE installer or a portable ZIP from the releases page. On macOS it is in the App Store and Homebrew, with a DMG installer as well. Linux users get Flathub, Snap, Nixpkgs, the AUR, DEB packages, AppImages, and TAR archives. Android has the Play Store, F-Droid, and a direct APK, and iOS has the App Store. There is even a Fire OS build for Amazon tablets. The README recommends installing from a store or a package manager rather than a manual download, because the app has no auto-update. Minimum versions are reasonable: Android 7, iOS 15, macOS 12 Monterey, and Windows 10, with older releases still available for older systems. That breadth is the point. AirDrop works because Apple controls both ends, and LocalSend works because it refuses to care which ends you have.

The Command Line Client: LocalSend in a Terminal

There is also a terminal client, localsend-cli, built on LocalSend Protocol v2. On macOS and Linux you install it with Homebrew, then send files with a single command: localsend-cli send report.pdf photo.jpg ./project-backup. The command opens the discovered-device list so you can pick a destination interactively, or you can skip the list and target a device by its exact alias or IP address, for example localsend-cli send --to "Cute Tomato" report.pdf. To send text instead of a file, add --text, and pass a dash to read the text from standard input. That makes the CLI useful in scripts: pipe a command's output into a file on another machine, or move a build artifact to a phone without touching a GUI. The same 64 KB text rule applies, and standard input must be UTF-8 and no larger than 16 MB. The CLI is a separate small install from the app, and it speaks the same protocol, so a terminal on one machine and the app on another work together without any extra setup.

Portable Mode, Hidden Starts, and Staying Out of the Way

LocalSend has a few quiet features for people who run it all day. Portable mode, added in version 1.13.0, stores settings next to the executable instead of in the system settings folder: create an empty file called settings.json beside the app and it keeps everything there, which makes it easy to carry on a USB stick. You can also start the app hidden, so it sits in the system tray without opening a window, using the --hidden flag, and an autostart option does the same at login. Windows binaries are signed, and the signing policy is published in the repo, which is a small detail that matters for an app that opens a network port on your machine. The project is actively maintained, with CI, translations through Weblate, and a Discord community, and it is also mirrored on Codeberg for anyone who prefers it. None of this changes the core idea, which is that moving a file between your own devices should not require the internet, an account, or a subscription.

Getting Started in Two Minutes

Install LocalSend on the two devices you want to move files between, then open it on both. Each device shows its own name and the devices it can see on the network. Pick the destination, choose the files, and the transfer starts over HTTPS with a progress bar on both ends. If a device does not appear, check the three usual causes in order: the firewall on port 53317, AP isolation on the router, and an active VPN blocking local traffic. The receiver can save files to a chosen folder or let LocalSend pick the default download location. That is the whole setup. There is no account to make, no QR code to scan, no cable to find, and nothing to upload first. For anyone who regularly moves files between an Android phone and a Windows PC, or an iPhone and a Linux desktop, LocalSend removes a daily friction that most people have quietly accepted as normal.

FAQs

What is LocalSend?

LocalSend is a free open source app that shares files, photos, folders, and messages between nearby devices over a local network. It works across Android, iPhone, Windows, Mac, Linux, and Fire OS, like AirDrop but for every device, and it needs no internet connection, no account, and no outside servers.

Is LocalSend free?

Yes. LocalSend is free and open source under the Apache 2.0 license. There is no paid tier, no account, and no subscription. It is available in the Play Store, App Store, Flathub, Homebrew, Winget, and other package managers at no cost.

Does LocalSend need an internet connection?

No. LocalSend works entirely over your local network. Devices discover each other on the same Wi-Fi and transfer files directly over HTTPS, with a TLS certificate generated on the fly on each device. Nothing is uploaded to the internet and no outside server is involved.

Is LocalSend secure?

Transfers are encrypted with HTTPS, and each device generates its own TLS certificate on the fly, so traffic is encrypted even though no central server exists. Your files never pass through a third-party server. The app listens on port 53317, so if a device does not show up, check your firewall, router AP isolation, and VPN settings.

Which devices does LocalSend work on?

Android 7 and newer, iOS 15 and newer, macOS 12 Monterey and newer, Windows 10 and newer, Linux, and Fire OS. It is available from the Play Store, App Store, F-Droid, Flathub, Snap, Homebrew, Winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, and direct downloads from the releases page.

Can I use LocalSend from the command line?

Yes. The localsend-cli terminal client is available through Homebrew on macOS and Linux. Run localsend-cli send followed by files or folders, pick a device from the list or target one by alias or IP address, and use --text to send a message instead of a file.

Originally published at devpik.com/open-source/localsend. Repo: localsend/localsend.

event_model_payload.headline: I Built a Claude Code Plugin Because I Was Becoming a Rubber-Stamp Reviewer
event_model_payload.summary:
My development team has two members: me and AI. And lately, I've been feeling like I'm becoming the less useful member of the team.

I've been using AI coding agents for years. Claude Code, and plenty of other tools. They're incredible at what they do, but somewhere along the way, my development process started looking like this:

Me: "Implement this feature."

AI: "Done! Changed 27 files, added 3,400 lines, refactored two modules. All tests passed."

Me: "LGTM."

Narrator: He did not, in fact, look.

The code gets written. Features get shipped. Productivity looks great. But here's what bothers me: Am I actually reviewing the code anymore, or am I just approving whatever the AI tells me?

And if I'm not making the technical decisions, what exactly is my role as a developer?

The problem isn't that AI writes code

I don't think developers need to manually write every line of code. That's not the point. The problem is that we're slowly outsourcing something much more important than typing: our judgment.

Think about how often this happens. The AI makes an architectural decision without asking you. It assumes a requirement that was never specified. It changes something outside the original scope. Then it confidently reports that all tests passed, and you trust the summary because reviewing everything yourself would take too long.

None of this necessarily means the AI is bad at coding. It means our development workflow hasn't caught up with how much code AI can produce.

I wanted a workflow where AI could do most of the implementation without quietly taking ownership of the decisions. I also didn't want to become an unpaid project manager, manually breaking everything into tiny tasks and supervising every step.

So I built human-rights.


GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

human-rights is an open-source Claude Code plugin built around a simple idea: Don't make humans review every line. Make sure they understand and approve the decisions that matter.

The requirements. The architecture. The risks. The acceptance criteria. And the evidence that the implementation actually works.

But there's an obvious problem with this approach. If every tiny change requires a design document, three approvals, and a meeting with yourself, nobody is going to use it.

So the workflow adapts to the task.

  1. Not every change deserves the same process

human-rights classifies development requests into four levels, from simple edits to high-risk changes.

Level

Example

Workflow

L0 — Direct

Center a login card

Make the change and check it

L1 — Focused

Add input validation hints

Short plan and targeted tests

L2 — Planned

Add Google authentication

Investigate, design, and review

L3 — Governed

Modify safety-critical control logic

Human approvals, integration tests, and final verification

The classification considers ambiguity, scope, architectural impact, risk, verification difficulty, and dependencies. A small UI change shouldn't require the same process as modifying authentication or controlling physical hardware.

For larger changes, the agent investigates the existing code, asks questions that could change the design, and creates a testable implementation plan. If the request is too large, it first breaks the work into smaller features that can be reviewed and verified independently.

The human decides what should happen. The AI figures out how to implement it.

  1. The AI cannot simply approve its own work

This was one of the most important design decisions. I didn't want to rely entirely on instructions like "Always ask the user for approval." An AI agent following a prompt is not the same thing as an enforced workflow.

So human-rights has two parts: a Claude Code skill that decides what process a task needs, and a deterministic Python runtime that enforces state transitions, approvals, test evidence, and failure handling.

Design approvals are tied to the approved plan, while final approvals are tied to the code being verified. If the plan changes, the previous design approval becomes invalid. If the code changes, the final approval becomes invalid too.

A test result is not accepted just because the agent says it passed. The runtime records the execution result and associates it with the relevant code version.

The goal is simple: stop trusting the AI's description of what happened and start requiring evidence of what actually happened.

  1. Then I realized something worse: humans can still blindly approve everything

Even with all those safeguards, there's a fundamental weakness in the system.

The human.

You can build the most carefully controlled approval system in the world, and I can still click "Approve" without reading anything.

So I added a feature called Red Pill Mode.

Here's how it works. When enabled, the system occasionally introduces a deliberately incorrect item into the review material. The developer is supposed to notice it before approving the work.

For example, suppose the original requirement says:

The system must support four simultaneous drone connections.

But the review table contains:

TEST-010: Verify that two simultaneous drone connections work correctly.

Would you notice the difference? Or would you just approve?

If you catch the incorrect item, the system records the catch and explains why it was wrong. If you blindly approve, the approval is blocked.

And yes, it makes fun of you:

You didn't really review this, did you, human? Keep approving like that and the AI really will take your job. lol.

It's intentionally a little ridiculous, but the underlying problem is serious. An approval button means nothing if the person clicking it isn't paying attention.

The planted mistakes never modify the actual implementation plan or executable code. They exist only in the review material, so they cannot accidentally become part of the software being built.

Red Pill Mode is optional and off by default. It also supports adaptive difficulty, so the review exercises can become harder as you successfully identify mistakes.

I find this particularly interesting because we're entering a world where developers may spend more time reviewing AI-generated work than writing code themselves. If that's where we're heading, shouldn't we be actively improving our review skills instead of letting them deteriorate?

  1. Bigger requests are split before implementation

Another issue I kept encountering was asking an agent to implement something too large. It would produce an enormous plan, and I'd be expected to approve the whole thing.

That's not meaningful review. That's just outsourcing a massive amount of work and hoping the result is correct.

So compound requests are split into independently verifiable features. The human approves the feature list before implementation starts, and each feature gets its own workflow, decisions, and verification.

After those features are implemented, the system checks that they work together. Independent tasks can also run in parallel using isolated Git worktrees, while conflicting tasks are kept sequential.

The idea isn't to slow down AI development. It's to gain the speed of AI agents without giving up control of the overall design.

  1. You can try it

The project is currently at v0.5.0 and is open source under the MIT license. It runs as a Claude Code plugin with a Python 3.8+ standard-library runtime.

Install it in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add kiduki77/human-rights

/plugin install hrs@human-rights

Initialize it in your project:

/hrs:init

Then start a task:

/hrs:new add Google authentication

Or, if you want to see whether you're actually paying attention during reviews, try:

/hrs:redpill on 5 adaptive

The repository includes an automated test suite, but this is still an early-stage project. Some integrations, including live GitHub adapter operation and real concurrent sub-agent execution, still need field validation.

GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

Where this could go

Right now, human-rights focuses on individual development workflows, but I think the underlying problem could become much more important for engineering teams.

As AI generates more code, how do we know that code was meaningfully reviewed? How do we distinguish a real technical decision from a rubber-stamp approval? And how do we help developers improve at finding problems instead of gradually losing that skill?

Imagine an engineering team where AI generates most of the code. A developer approves a pull request without noticing that an important requirement was missed. Another developer catches the same issue immediately.

Today, we can track who approved a pull request, but that doesn't necessarily tell us how thoroughly it was reviewed. What if we could help developers identify the types of mistakes they tend to miss, practice reviewing realistic changes, and improve over time?

I think there's an opportunity to build something that doesn't just manage AI-generated code, but helps humans become better reviewers of it.

That's a longer-term idea, not something I'm claiming the current plugin already solves.

For now, I'm starting with the problem I experience every day: making sure I still understand and control the software I'm building.

I'd love to hear what other developers think

I'm especially curious whether other developers have noticed themselves reviewing AI-generated code less carefully over time. Would enforced approval gates help, or would they just become another form of bureaucracy? And would you actually enable something like Red Pill Mode in your own development workflow?

I don't have all the answers, and I'm sure there are things I've overlooked. That's why I'm releasing this as open source and looking for feedback from developers who are experiencing the same problems.

I built this because I don't want to stop using AI.

I just don't want to stop being a developer while using it.

human-rights — AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

event_model_payload.headline: Lively Wallpaper: Bring Your Windows Desktop to Life With Animated Wallpapers
event_model_payload.summary:
Lively Wallpaper is a free open source app that brings your Windows desktop to life with animated wallpapers. Drag in any video, GIF, or webpage and it becomes your background, run a Unity or Godot game behind your icons, or use any wallpaper as a screensaver. No paywall, no hidden features.

What Lively Wallpaper Is: Your Desktop, Alive

Lively Wallpaper is free and open source software that lets you set animated desktop wallpapers and screensavers on Windows, and it has 20,151 stars on GitHub. It is a native Windows app built with WinUI 3 and the Windows App SDK, it is licensed under GPL-3.0, and every feature is free: no paywall, no hidden features, no black magic. It runs on Windows 10 and 11, and it is also listed on the Microsoft Store. If your desktop has looked the same for years, Lively is the fastest way to make it feel new again.

Three Kinds of Wallpaper: Video, Webpage, and Games

Lively supports three kinds of wallpaper. Video and GIF wallpapers play a clip behind your desktop at a fixed resolution, with hardware accelerated playback through mpv or VLC and customizable video filters. Webpage wallpapers are live web pages as your background, interactive and variable in resolution, rendered by a minimal Chromium based renderer. Application and game wallpapers run real Unity or Godot games behind your icons, also interactive. You can even paste a Shadertoy.com URL and use it as a wallpaper. Setting one is as simple as dragging media or a webpage into Lively.

Screensavers and Automation: Any Wallpaper, on a Schedule

Any wallpaper in Lively can also be used as a screensaver, with multiple monitor support, so your whole setup can stay animated even when you step away. Automation is built in: Lively can be controlled with command line arguments from a terminal, which means you can drive it from Python scripts or AutoHotKey, and there is a full API for developers who want to build interactive wallpapers that read hardware sensors, audio graphs, and music information. There is even machine learning support for creating dynamic depth wallpapers. It is a small app with a surprising amount of depth once you start digging.

Make Your Own Webpage Wallpaper

The most creative part of Lively is the webpage wallpaper, because it is just a web page running behind your desktop. If you have a page you love, drag it in and it is your wallpaper. If you want to build one, start simple: a Text to HTML pass turns plain text into a page you can drop straight into Lively, and then you can style it from there. When you are tuning the layout, sizes in CSS often come in em units, and an Em to Px Converter gives you the exact pixel value so your text lands where you expect it on screen. Interactive wallpapers can react to your music, your system stats, or your mouse, so a page you build can feel alive in a way a still image never will.

Performance: It Pauses When You Play

The obvious worry with an animated wallpaper is that it will slow your PC down, and Lively is built to avoid exactly that. Wallpaper playback pauses automatically when a fullscreen application or game runs, dropping to around zero percent CPU and GPU usage, and you can set playback rules based on which application is in the foreground. It pauses on battery power on laptops, and it pauses during a remote desktop session too. Video playback is hardware accelerated, and the app itself is native, so when you are working, Lively mostly gets out of the way. The animation is there when you look at your desktop, and gone when you need the power.

Installing Lively: Microsoft Store or the Installer

The easiest install is the Microsoft Store, which needs Windows 10 version 1809 or above. If you prefer the classic route, download the installer from the releases page on GitHub, which needs Windows 10 version 1903 or above. The project wiki explains the differences between the distributions if you are unsure which one to pick. Once installed, drag a video, a GIF, or a webpage into the window and it becomes your wallpaper immediately. There is an active Reddit community and a GitHub discussions page if you want ideas, and translations are handled on Crowdin if you want to help the project reach more people.

FAQs

What is Lively Wallpaper?

Lively Wallpaper is a free open source app for Windows that sets animated desktop wallpapers and screensavers. You can use videos, GIFs, webpages, or even Unity and Godot games as your background, and any wallpaper can also be used as a screensaver.

Is Lively Wallpaper really free?

Yes. Lively Wallpaper is completely free and open source under the GPL-3.0 license. There is no paywall and no feature hidden behind a payment. It is also available on the Microsoft Store at no cost.

Does Lively Wallpaper slow down my PC?

It is designed not to. Wallpaper playback pauses automatically when a fullscreen application or game is running, dropping to around zero percent CPU and GPU usage. You can also set it to pause on battery power, and video playback is hardware accelerated.

Can I use my own videos as wallpaper?

Yes. Just drag any video, GIF, or webpage into Lively and it becomes your wallpaper. You can also run Unity or Godot games as your background, use Shadertoy URLs, or build your own interactive webpage wallpaper.

Does Lively Wallpaper work on multiple monitors?

Yes. Lively supports multiple monitors, and any wallpaper can be used as a screensaver across them. You can set different wallpapers per monitor from the app.

Which Windows versions does Lively Wallpaper support?

Windows 10 and Windows 11. The Microsoft Store version needs Windows 10 version 1809 or above, and the installer needs Windows 10 version 1903 or above.

Originally published at devpik.com/open-source/lively. Repo: rocksdanister/lively.

event_model_payload.headline: Immich: A Free Google Photos Alternative You Run Yourself
event_model_payload.summary:
Immich is a free, self-hosted photo and video manager that replaces Google Photos: automatic backup from your phone, face recognition, smart search, maps and memories, with your photos staying on your own server.

What Immich Is: Google Photos, On Your Own Server

Immich is a free alternative to Google Photos that you run yourself. It does the job people actually pay Google for: it backs up every photo and video from your phone, organizes them into albums, finds faces, searches by what is in the picture, and shows your memories from years ago, except the server is yours, not Google's. It has 119,219 stars on GitHub, making it one of the most starred self-hosted projects there, and the whole thing is open source under the AGPL-3.0 license. The trade is honest and the project states it plainly: you need a computer or server to run it on. If you have an old PC, a home server, or a cheap VPS, that machine becomes your private photo cloud, and your photos never sit on someone else's servers, under someone else's scanning and storage limits.

Auto Backup: Your Photos Save Themselves

The feature that makes Immich a real replacement is automatic backup. Install the mobile app, point it at your server, and it uploads your photos and videos when the app opens, with background backup so it keeps working without you thinking about it. You can pick exactly which albums back up and which stay on the phone, and Immich skips duplicates so the same photo is never stored twice. It handles Live Photos and Motion Photos, the short video clips attached to stills on iPhone and Android, and plays them back properly. It supports raw photo formats for photographers, and the mobile app keeps working offline, so your gallery is there on a plane as well as at home. The point is that backup stops being a chore: the photos leave your phone on their own, and the copy on your server is yours to keep.

Find Any Photo: Faces, Search, and the Map

Once your photos are backed up, Immich helps you find them. Facial recognition groups photos of the same person together, so one tap shows every picture of your kid, your partner, or your dog. Search understands metadata, objects, and faces, and it uses CLIP, an AI model that matches words to what is actually in the picture, so searching for "beach" finds beach photos even when nobody tagged them. The global map plots your photos where they were taken, the metadata view shows EXIF details for every shot, and Memories resurfaces photos from years ago, the same gentle nostalgia Google Photos built its reputation on. Stacked photos group burst shots together, tags and folder views keep big libraries tidy, and the virtual scroll keeps the timeline smooth even with tens of thousands of photos. For a free tool running on your own hardware, the search is startlingly close to what the big cloud services offer.

Sharing Without Giving Your Photos Away

Immich is built for families as well as for one person. Multi-user support means everyone in the house gets their own account on the same server, partner sharing lets two people automatically share their libraries with each other, and shared albums work the way group albums should: everyone adds photos, everyone sees them. Public sharing creates a link anyone can open without an account, which is how you send a wedding album to relatives who will never install an app. Archive and Favorites keep the timeline clean, and read-only galleries let you show photos without letting anyone change them. And when a shot deserves to leave the screen, a Pixels to Inches conversion tells you how large it will print at full quality, so you know before ordering whether that favourite portrait works as a framed print or only as a small one.

Setting It Up: Docker on Your Own Machine

Installation is Docker, and the docs walk through it step by step. You need a machine that stays on, a home server, an old laptop, a Raspberry Pi for a small library, or a VPS, and the requirements page lists what each setup needs. There is a public demo at demo.immich.app, login demo@immich.app with the password demo, so you can click around the real interface before installing anything. If you open Immich to the internet so family can reach it from anywhere, an IP Check confirms the public address your server is reachable at, and the docs cover OAuth login and API keys for locking it down. One warning the README carries in bold is worth repeating: follow a 3-2-1 backup plan for your photos. Immich is your photo library, not your backup strategy, so keep a second copy somewhere else, because a single hard drive can always fail.

Why Self-Host: Your Photos Stay Yours

The reason Immich exists is privacy, and it is the same reason Google Photos makes some people uneasy. Your photos are the most personal files you own: your kids, your home, your travels, your documents. On a cloud service they sit on someone else's servers, under a privacy policy that can change, with storage limits that can shrink and prices that can rise. Immich removes that trade. Your photos live on hardware you control, the project is open source so anyone can read the code, and nothing is scanned for advertising. User management, OAuth, and API keys are built in, so you decide who gets an account and what they can see. It is free, it is yours, and the only subscription is the electricity for the machine it runs on.

FAQs

What is Immich?

Immich is a free, self-hosted photo and video management app and a Google Photos alternative. It backs up photos from your phone automatically, organizes them into albums, and adds face recognition, smart search, maps and memories, all running on your own server.

Is Immich really free?

Yes. Immich is free and open source under the AGPL-3.0 license, with no paid tier and no storage limits beyond your own hardware. You only pay for the machine it runs on, an old PC, a home server, or a VPS.

Do I need a server to run Immich?

Yes, you need a computer or server that stays on: a home server, an old laptop, a Raspberry Pi for a small library, or a VPS. Immich installs with Docker, and the docs list the requirements for each setup. Without a machine to run it on, there is nowhere for your photos to go.

Can I try Immich before installing it?

Yes, there is a public demo at demo.immich.app. Log in with demo@immich.app and the password demo, and for the mobile app use https://demo.immich.app as the server endpoint URL.

Does Immich work offline?

The mobile app supports offline viewing, so your gallery is available without a connection. Backup needs a connection to your server, and the web app needs to reach the server too.

Is Immich a good Google Photos replacement?

For most people, yes. It covers the features that matter: automatic backup, albums, face recognition, search, maps, memories, and sharing. What it does not give you is Google's cloud: you provide the storage and the machine, and in return your photos stay entirely under your control.

Originally published at devpik.com/open-source/immich. Repo: immich-app/immich.

event_model_payload.headline: Your AI tool changed this week. Would your team know?
event_model_payload.summary:
Most teams version-pin their dependencies, read changelogs and get a pull request when a library bumps. Then they hand a chunk of their daily work to an AI service that can change under them with no version bump at all.

This week the Ada Lovelace Institute published a feature called Running up that bill? (Charlie Grossman, 16 November 2026). It catalogues how AI subscriptions have changed what they deliver while the price stayed put. It's written about consumer plans, but it says organisations on business plans "remain exposed to practices like plan repricing or changes to how usage is counted."

Here's the engineering version, and a small fix.

What the feature documents

Some of the examples from the past 15 months, as the feature reports them:

  • Anthropic cut Claude Code's weekly limits by 17% after a temporary increase.
  • A new Anthropic tokeniser produced up to 35% more tokens for the same text.
  • OpenAI cut the reasoning time behind GPT-5.2 Thinking's "standard" setting and kept the name.
  • OpenAI's GPT-5 router sent some requests to less capable model variants.
  • OpenAI acknowledged an issue that applied the wrong usage limits to 40,000 accounts.

It isn't only pricing games

Two older data points matter more to engineers, because they're about quality, not allowances.

In 2023, Chen, Zaharia and Zou compared the March and June versions of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. On identifying prime numbers, GPT-4 fell from 84% accuracy to 51%. GPT-3.5 improved on the same task. Their conclusion was that the same named service can change a lot in a short time and needs continuous monitoring.

In September 2025, Anthropic published a postmortem of three infrastructure bugs that intermittently degraded Claude's output between August and early September. At the worst hour, one routing bug hit 16% of Sonnet 4 requests. Anthropic said plainly these were bugs, not demand-based cuts. The bit I'd underline is its admission that "we relied too heavily on noisy evaluations."

If the provider's own evals missed it, "the model feels off today" in Slack is not a detection strategy.

My inference: treat the AI service like a dependency you can't pin

This is my mapping onto engineering work, not something the sources prescribe.

You probably can't pin a consumer chat plan. You can still do the three things you'd do for any upstream you don't control:

  1. Record the contract. Plan, model names, stated limits, reasoning setting, price. Write it down on the day you adopt the tool.
  2. Run a canary. A fixed set of your own tasks, run on a schedule, scored the same way every time.
  3. Keep a change log. One table where canary results and provider announcements sit side by side.

Build the canary set in an afternoon

  • Pick 10 to 20 tasks from real work: a function with existing unit tests, a SQL query with a known result set, a log excerpt with a known root cause, a diff with a known bug.
  • Prefer tasks with a mechanical pass mark. Tests pass, query matches, bug found. Skip anything that needs a long debate to grade.
  • Fix the prompt, settings and context. Store them in the repo next to the expected answers.
  • Run it weekly, same day, and record pass count, wall-clock time and tokens where the API reports them. The feature notes that API responses come back with a token count, which consumer web apps don't show.
  • Expect noise. The feature cites a 2026 study where the most expensive run of the same coding task typically used around twice the tokens of the cheapest. Look for a shift that holds across two runs, not one bad Tuesday.

If you're on the API, pin a dated model version where the provider offers one, and treat a version change like a dependency upgrade: run the canary before you switch.

The artefact: an AI service change log

Copy this into your repo as ai-service-log.md. The rows are labelled examples to show the shape. They are not measurements from the sources.

| Week | Tool / plan / model | Canary pass (of 20) | Median time | Tokens (API) | Provider change seen | Our change | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EXAMPLE 2026-W45 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 18 | 41s | 212k | None | None | Baseline recorded |
| EXAMPLE 2026-W46 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 18 | 44s | 260k | Changelog: new tokeniser | None | Watch token use, check allowance |
| EXAMPLE 2026-W47 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 14 | 63s | 255k | None found | Longer system prompt | Revert prompt, rerun before blaming vendor |
| EXAMPLE 2026-W48 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 14 | 61s | 250k | None found | Prompt reverted | Raise ticket with vendor, attach W45 vs W48 |

Two columns do the real work. "Our change" stops you blaming the vendor for your own prompt edits. "Provider change seen" forces someone to actually read the changelog and status page each week.

What to ask before you renew

Take these to your next renewal:

  • How much notice do we get before models, limits, reasoning settings or usage counting change?
  • Can we export usage data per user and per request?
  • What credit applies if a bug drains our allowance?

Consumer plans give weak answers to all three, the feature argues. Business contracts are where you can get better ones.

Sources

  • Running up that bill?, Charlie Grossman, Ada Lovelace Institute, 16 November 2026.
  • How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?, Chen, Zaharia and Zou, arXiv, July 2023.
  • A postmortem of three recent issues, Anthropic, 17 September 2025.

Has your team ever caught an AI tool getting worse with actual numbers, or was it gut feel every time?
