event_model_payload.headline: Atlas for Government: The Only FedRAMP® Class D Certified Cross-Cloud Operational Database
event_model_payload.summary:
Federal, state, and local agencies are under mounting pressure to modernize legacy systems, adopt AI, and protect sensitive data, all at the same time. Many of the databases that can currently handle an agency's most sensitive, high-impact workloads are native to a single cloud and run nowhere else, leaving agencies with a limited set of authorized options and little room to change course when missions, mandates, or threats shift.

MongoDB is the intelligent data platform for the AI era, and today we're extending it to the workloads where the stakes are highest: MongoDB Atlas for Government has achieved FedRAMP® Class D Certification. Formerly known as FedRAMP High, Class D is the highest level of assessment under the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP). Atlas for Government has also added support for Azure Government, expanding its existing support for AWS GovCloud and Commercial Regions and Google Cloud Assured Workloads.

Together, these milestones make MongoDB Atlas for Government the only FedRAMP Class D (High) Certified cross-cloud operational database in the world. Public sector organizations and the independent software vendors (ISVs) that serve them can now run their most sensitive mission-critical workloads—including production AI applications built on real-time operational data—on a single platform and on the cloud provider of their choice, across AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. To learn more, visit the MongoDB Atlas for Government product page or the FedRAMP Marketplace page.

What is MongoDB Atlas for Government?

MongoDB Atlas for Government is an independent, dedicated environment of the MongoDB Atlas intelligent data platform built specifically for the U.S. public sector and the ISVs that build government solutions. It brings the core capabilities of MongoDB’s intelligent data platform to government, giving agencies a fully managed way to deploy, run, and scale mission-critical applications in the cloud, including transactional workloads, search, vector search for AI applications, and time series data, all within a single, unified data platform.

Atlas for Government is operated by MongoDB employees who are United States persons on U.S. soil, and all encryption within MongoDB-managed infrastructure is FIPS 140-3 validated. The platform maintains a 99.995% uptime SLA and has been generally available since 2021.

MongoDB Atlas for Government is already trusted across the federal government. MongoDB works with 13 U.S. Federal Cabinet-level agencies. With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification, agencies like these can bring even more sensitive, high-impact workloads to Atlas for Government. For example, a health agency could modernize benefits and eligibility systems that handle protected health information and personally identifiable information. A financial agency could run real-time fraud detection across high-volume transaction streams. And a civilian agency could build an AI application that lets analysts search policy and case records in natural language, without that data leaving a FedRAMP Class D (High) environment.

What is FedRAMP Class D (High)?

FedRAMP provides the standardized authorization framework that cloud service providers (CSPs) must successfully navigate to demonstrate compliance with federal security requirements before hosting federal agency workloads. In 2026, FedRAMP moved away from labeling these standards Low, Moderate, and High, replacing them with a four-tier Certification Class system, A through D. FedRAMP Class D (High) is the direct successor to what was previously known as FedRAMP High, and it remains the most rigorous tier a CSP can achieve within the FedRAMP program.

FedRAMP Class D (High) certification is designed for cloud services that support an agency's high-impact systems, where a security failure could have severe or catastrophic consequences for operations, assets, or people. This includes systems tied to national security, law enforcement, and emergency response, as well as high-impact modernization initiatives across civilian agencies. Achieving this certification requires meeting hundreds of stringent security controls covering everything from access management to incident response.

MongoDB Atlas for Government achieved FedRAMP Moderate authorization in 2023 and has been a trusted, fully managed data platform for federal agencies and ISVs since then. With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification, that foundation is now extended to high-impact workloads, including production AI applications. Agencies can bring those workloads to the cloud on a platform that meets the security and compliance requirements for high-impact systems, and build secure, production-grade AI applications on top of them.

Freedom to run anywhere: Now spanning AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud

With the addition of support for Azure Government, MongoDB Atlas for Government now runs across all three major cloud providers: AWS (both GovCloud and AWS commercial regions), Google Cloud (via Assured Workloads), and Azure Government. This makes MongoDB Atlas for Government the only FedRAMP Class D (High) certified, cross-cloud database in the world.

For public sector organizations, this cross-cloud support is about more than convenience. A database tied to a single cloud provider limits an agency's options if costs rise, a mission requirement changes, or a new mandate calls for a different cloud environment. MongoDB Atlas for Government gives agencies and ISVs the freedom to run their workloads on the cloud that best fits their needs today, and to change that decision later without rewriting their applications. Within FedRAMP-certified cloud environments (AWS GovCloud, Google Cloud Assured Workloads, and Azure Government), data can be distributed across providers to optimize for performance, cost, or resilience, and to strengthen disaster recovery with automatic failover across providers.

Getting started on Azure Government works the same way as it does on AWS GovCloud or Google Cloud Assured Workloads. Agencies and ISVs can create a project in Atlas for Government, designate it as a FedRAMP Class D (High) Gov Regions Only project, and select Azure as the cloud provider when creating a cluster.

Protecting data and powering AI at the highest level

FedRAMP Class D (High) sets a high bar for how a provider documents, assesses, and maintains its security program, but that is only one part of the picture. Agencies handling the country's most sensitive data also need assurance that the data itself stays protected, even if a system is compromised.

MongoDB Atlas for Government provides robust protection for sensitive data, supporting workloads that include Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Protected Health Information (PHI), and Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) data. Data at rest is protected using database encryption with Customer Managed Keys, and data in transit is protected via TLS.

For organizations that require protection beyond the authorization boundary, MongoDB Queryable Encryption performs encryption and decryption client-side, so designated fields remain encrypted throughout their lifecycle, in transit, at rest, and in use. MongoDB, cloud operators, and even the organization's own database administrators never have access to keys or unencrypted data.

This same secure foundation enables agencies to deploy production AI applications in their high-impact environments. MongoDB Atlas for Government includes MongoDB Vector Search, allowing teams to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and other AI-powered applications directly on top of their operational data. Instead of standing up a separate vector database and building a pipeline to keep it in sync, agencies can run transactional workloads, search, and vector search in a single, FedRAMP Class D-certified environment, reducing both complexity and risk.

How to get started with MongoDB Atlas for Government

With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification and support for Azure Government, MongoDB’s intelligent data platform for the AI era now reaches the public sector’s highest-stakes missions. MongoDB Atlas for Government gives public sector organizations and ISVs a secure, fully managed, and truly multi-cloud way to run their most sensitive workloads and build production AI applications.

To get started, visit the MongoDB Atlas for Government product page, view the FedRAMP Marketplace listing, or refer to the Atlas for Government documentation for setup details.

FAQ

What is MongoDB Atlas for Government?

MongoDB Atlas for Government is an independent, dedicated environment of MongoDB Atlas built for the U.S. public sector and the ISVs that build government solutions. It is a fully managed, FedRAMP Class D (High) certified operational database.

What is FedRAMP Class D (High)?

FedRAMP Class D (High) is the highest tier in FedRAMP’s four-tier Certification Class system and the direct successor to what was previously known as FedRAMP High. It is designed for cloud services that support high-impact government systems.

Which cloud providers does Atlas for Government support?

Atlas for Government runs on AWS (GovCloud and Commercial Regions), Google Cloud (via Assured Workloads), and Azure Government. Within FedRAMP-certified cloud environments, data can be distributed across providers with automatic failover.

Can agencies build AI applications on Atlas for Government?

Yes. MongoDB Vector Search enables teams to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and other AI applications directly on operational data, in a single FedRAMP Class D (High) certified environment, without a separate vector database or sync pipeline.

event_model_payload.headline: Diagnosing MongoDB Search Performance with Atlas Metrics
event_model_payload.summary:
Your MongoDB Atlas metrics show elevated disk I/O, high search CPU, increasing query latency, or a rising search max replication lag. Like when your car’s mysterious “check engine” light comes on, these signals can mean different things. To figure out the issue, you’ll want to start by identifying which process and metric is under pressure.

Scaling the database tier may provide temporary relief, but it does not separate the search and operational workloads. When mongot and mongod share nodes, search can compete with database activity for memory, disk I/O, and CPU. The right response depends on whether the index does not fit in available memory, the workloads contend during traffic spikes, or possibly even both occurring simultaneously.

This post explains how to diagnose slow search performance, decide whether dedicated search nodes are the right fix, and size them correctly if they are.

Why tackling the underlying issue matters

The default response to slow search is often to scale up the database tier. More RAM and CPU can help the database portion of the workload, but they do not create a separate resource budget for search on a co-located deployment.

Two cases can produce similar symptoms, but they call for different responses. With index-size pressure, the Search index is larger than the memory available to mongot, so queries page data from disk even when database activity is low. A larger Search tier with enough memory addresses this problem; isolation by itself does not. With resource contention, the index fits in memory, but search latency rises when database reads, writes, or replication become busy. Separate search nodes address this contention by giving mongot different CPU, memory, and disk resources.

The distinction matters when you select a tier. Dedicated search nodes remove competition with database workloads, but they still need to be sized correctly.

Search nodes explained

MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search use mongot, the search process that maintains and queries search indexes. mongod is the database process that stores application data and handles database operations. In a colocated deployment, both processes run on the same nodes.

Dedicated search nodes run mongot on separate infrastructure from the nodes running mongod. Dedicated search nodes provide workload isolation for search, similar to how Analytics Nodes isolate analytical workloads.

With dedicated search nodes, database nodes handle operational reads and writes while search nodes handle search queries and index work. Each workload gets its own memory budget, CPU capacity, and scaling lifecycle. This applies to both MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search on Atlas.

Why colocated search runs into resource constraints

When mongot and mongod share nodes, memory and CPU are common sources of resource pressure. WiredTiger, the operating system, and mongot share RAM; if the index is larger than the memory available to mongot, queries may read index pages from disk. Search queries and background indexing also compete with database reads, writes, and replication for CPU time, so latency can rise even when the index fits in memory.

Atlas metrics help show which process is under pressure and whether the issue is paging or contention. Look at these signals together rather than treating any one metric as a diagnosis:

  • Search Page Fault, which reports average page faults per second in the Search process

  • Search Process Memory and Search Index Size compared with the node's RAM

  • Search Normalized Process CPU compared with Normalized System CPU

  • Search Process Throttling, which indicates that work is arriving faster than the Search process can admit it

  • Search query latency and Search Max Replication Lag

If database CPU and memory look healthy while Search metrics are under pressure, Search is consuming the resources available to it. That does not identify the root cause by itself. Compare index size with available memory to test for paging; compare latency and Search CPU with database activity to test for contention.

If page faults and latency stay high while the database is quiet, Search needs more memory. If latency only rises when the database gets busy, the two workloads are competing.

How dedicated search nodes separate search and database workloads

Memory isolation and cache performance

On a colocated node, the memory shown in the Atlas tier specification is shared. WiredTiger uses part of it for the database cache, the operating system and runtime need additional memory, and the remainder is available to mongot. The exact amount varies with tier and workload, and there is no fixed co-located cache size for mongot.

Dedicated search nodes give mongot a separate memory budget. MongoDB documentation describes approximately 90% of search node RAM as available for index data, with the remainder used by the JVM and other process needs. MongoDB Search indexes do not need to fit entirely in memory. A single query usually touches only part of the index, and the OS keeps the frequently used pages in RAM. MongoDB Vector Search is different and works best when the index fits in memory.

When there is sufficient memory to accommodate the majority of the index data, sustained page faults should reduce and latency should become more stable. If page faults remain high after migration to search nodes, the Search tier may still be undersized, or the workload may have another bottleneck. Isolation will help, but if this is an index sizing issue at the core, you may need to combine this approach with other techniques. Those techniques could include switching from dynamic mapping to static mapping on specific fields, using alternate tokenization strategies other than nGram for autocomplete fields, leveraging vector quantization for vector search indexes, and other actions needed to reduce the size of the index.

CPU separation and parallel segment search

Search queries and index updates can consume substantial CPU. Separate search nodes prevent database traffic from taking those cores during the same interval. For $search queries, parallel segment search can search multiple Lucene segments concurrently when enabled with the query's concurrent option. For $vectorSearch queries, concurrent segment search is on by default on search nodes. The Search tier's CPU count limits the parallelism available.

MongoDB Search might fall back to single-threaded execution when too many concurrent queries are queued. Treat parallel segment search as additional capacity, not as a guarantee that every query will run in parallel. Monitor query latency, Search Normalized Process CPU, and Search Process Throttling under representative concurrency.

No competition with operational traffic

Search Max Replication Lag means index staleness: How far behind mongot is in applying changes from the mongod oplog to a MongoDB Search or MongoDB Vector Search index. This is different from replica set replication lag, which measures how far secondary mongod members are behind the primary.

Isolation removes one cause of Search Max Replication Lag: Indexing work from mongot competing with mongod for CPU on the same node. It does not remove the indexing work. mongot still reads every change from mongod and applies it to the search index on search nodes.

Isolation does not resolve issues due to write-heavy workloads. Sustained write volumes and the amount of indexing work created by each change can increase index staleness. Factors include the number of indexed fields, autocomplete fields using nGram or edgeGram tokenizers, and embeddedDocuments mappings where one document change can rewrite many Lucene documents. Indexes get updated when their associated documents and fields change; minimally, one write to a document will generate at least one corresponding write to the index(es) (where the indexed field is updated). Schema changes or sharding may be required with dedicated nodes to optimally support the workload.

Replica set replication lag is separate. Search nodes may reduce CPU contention that affects the database, but they do not guarantee lower replica set lag or lower Search Max Replication Lag when write or indexing volume remains high.

Example: From page faults to consistent search performance

Consider a co-located M30 deployment with 8 GB of RAM per node. As an illustration rather than a fixed Atlas allocation, about 2 GB may go to the WiredTiger cache and at least 1 GB to the OS, mongod, connections, and other runtime needs, leaving about 5 GB or less for mongot. If the Search index is 6 GB, sustained Search Page Fault activity is highly likely. The database may show low CPU and healthy memory metrics while Search still reads index data from disk.

Before search nodes

In this example, the co-located deployment is an M30 with 8 GB RAM per node and a 6 GB Search index. Atlas metrics show sustained non-zero Search Page Fault during normal traffic, and search query latency p95 is 650 ms. Validate the estimated 5 GB or less available to mongot against the actual metrics.

After search nodes

Assume the workload moves to an S40 Search tier with 16 GB of RAM per node. Using the documented approximate 90% allocation as a planning estimate gives about 14.4 GB for index data, leaving room for a 6 GB index and query working set. Validate the tier's available memory and observed behavior in Atlas rather than treating the estimate as a guarantee.

After the move, the dedicated S40 Search tier has about 14.4 GB of memory available for the same 6 GB index. In this example, Search Page Fault falls after the index is resident, except during warm-up or workload changes, and search query latency p95 is 120 ms.

Performance improves once Atlas finishes building the index on the search nodes and routes queries to them. During the build, queries continue to use the existing colocated indexes, and index construction adds read load to the database cluster. Plan for that transition instead of expecting a change when the Search Nodes are first deployed.

When to move to dedicated search nodes

Dedicated search nodes are not necessary for every slow query: if an index fits comfortably in available memory and latency targets are met without contention, co-location may remain the simpler choice. The example above shows why a team might move when paging indicates that the Search index does not fit the memory budget. In production, look for a pattern across several signals before choosing a dedicated tier:

  • Sustained non-zero Search Page Fault with an index that approaches or exceeds available Search memory

  • Search Process Throttling remaining above zero, indicating that work is arriving faster than the Search process can admit it

  • High Search Normalized Process CPU or a high Search-to-system CPU ratio during query traffic

  • Search latency that rises when database activity increases

  • Search Max Replication Lag that rises with indexing activity, after ruling out write volume and index-mapping causes

  • Query latency targets that require consistent performance

  • Repeated database scaling to accommodate Search growth

On a colocated node, total disk I/O combines mongod and mongot activity, so disk IOPS alone is a weak signal for Search diagnosis. Start with Search Page Fault to attribute paging to the Search process, and use total disk IOPS as corroborating evidence.

Best practices

These checks make a tier decision more reliable: they help identify whether the bottleneck is memory, CPU, or indexing work, and when to plan the migration. Use the relevant metrics together, and account for the workload and operational requirements before changing deployment architecture.

  • Check Search Process Memory, Search Index Size, and Search Page Fault together when testing for memory pressure.

  • Check Search Normalized Process CPU, Normalized System CPU, latency, and Search Process Throttling together when testing for contention or saturation.

  • Treat Search Max Replication Lag as index staleness, and investigate replica set replication lag separately.

  • Size Search Nodes for both index memory and query or indexing CPU; plan for index growth and concurrency.

  • Confirm prerequisites before migration. Dedicated search nodes require an M10 or higher cluster, so upgrade a Flex cluster before attempting to use them.

  • Expect an index-building period before query routing changes, then monitor the search nodes after the cutover.

What workload isolation enables

Analytics nodes separate analytical workloads from operational database traffic. Dedicated search nodes apply the same workload-isolation model to MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search, allowing each infrastructure tier to be sized for its own workload.

The result is easier diagnosis and more predictable behavior. Page faults can be addressed with sufficient Search memory, CPU contention can be addressed with isolation, and indexing lag can be investigated using write volume and index-mapping details rather than treated as a generic replication problem. Views for search indexes, quantization for vector indexes, sharding, and other techniques can also be used with isolation to further improve performance. Search index partitioning can also extend the capacity of supported deployments beyond a single index or node's limits; consult the current MongoDB documentation for those limits.

Next steps

Use the metrics to identify whether memory pressure, workload contention, or indexing volume is limiting performance. Then use the deployment guidance to assess the appropriate Search tier and plan a migration if dedicated nodes fit the diagnosis.

  • Review MongoDB Search metrics for Search Process Memory, Search Index Size, Search Page Fault, and Search Process Throttling.

  • Identify whether page faults indicate an index-memory problem or whether latency follows database activity and indicates contention.

  • Check Search Max Replication Lag and replica set replication lag as separate metrics with separate investigations.

  • Review tips for sizing and scaling Search Nodes and MongoDB Vector Search production sizing.

  • Account for index build time and the temporary read load before evaluating post-migration performance.

event_model_payload.headline: What a repair layer can and cannot do on DSH's llm/stream seam
event_model_payload.summary:
A fused tool call once cost a whole turn: the provider streamed two JSON objects into one call index, the adapter threw MALFORMED_RESPONSE, and the turn ended.

dsh-remedy is a patch set I built for that and the neighbouring failures on DeepSeek Harness's seams. It runs as a resident plugin on llm/stream. It splits a fused call only when every fragment can be proven to parse on its own; otherwise it rethrows the provider's failure. A chunk the wrapper cannot read is passed through rather than turned into a new exception.

There is also an offline half. scan reads this host's session logs and reports fused calls, truncations and turns that ended without an answer. explain names which patch covers a failure class, without pretending an unread profile is "off".

Measured on this tree: 54 registered patches, 451 tests, six gates, and a cold install from the registry printing OK 8 fixture(s). npm latest is 0.4.20 on both packages. Those are build and host readings, not an audience estimate.

Three boundaries: it does not patch app.asar, it is not a plugin market, and macOS is only a CI job here. External bug reports stay leads until the shape is reproduced locally.

Repo: https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/dsh-remedy

What do you think about "rethrow rather than fake a fix" as the default for a repair layer?

event_model_payload.headline: WCAG 2.2 e nuova EN 301 549: cosa cambia per chi fa siti per la PA
event_model_payload.summary:
Lavoro su progetti per la pubblica amministrazione, dove l'accessibilità non è un'opzione: è un obbligo di legge. E da qualche settimana c'è una novità che chi fa siti per la PA, o per banche, e-commerce e trasporti, dovrebbe conoscere prima che diventi obbligatoria.

Il 2 settembre 2026 ETSI ha pubblicato la EN 301 549 v4.1.1, la norma europea sull'accessibilità a cui rimandano sia le regole per la PA sia l'European Accessibility Act. La novità principale è che passa dalle WCAG 2.1 alle WCAG 2.2. Ma non è l'unica, e secondo me nemmeno la più interessante.

A che punto siamo, oggi

Prima una cosa che ho dovuto chiarire anche a me stesso: una norma pubblicata non è ancora una norma in vigore. La v4.1.1 dà la presunzione di conformità solo quando la Commissione europea la cita nella Gazzetta ufficiale dell'UE. Al 19 novembre 2026 non è ancora successo, e le stime vanno da fine novembre a metà dicembre.

Quindi, se lavori su un sito oggi:

  • il riferimento obbligatorio in Italia resta WCAG 2.1 livello AA, tramite la EN 301 549 v3.2.1;
  • dopo la citazione, AgID dovrà aggiornare le sue Linee guida e le schede di controllo;
  • i criteri nuovi ti conviene sistemarli adesso, perché quasi tutti costano poco. Rifarli dopo, a norma cambiata, costa di più.

I sei criteri nuovi delle WCAG 2.2

Sono pochi e molto concreti. Te li elenco con il caso in cui li trovo più spesso nei siti pubblici:

  • 2.4.11 Focus non coperto. Premi Tab e il campo con il focus finisce sotto l'header sticky o il banner dei cookie. A me spesso è bastato scroll-padding-top sull'html.
  • 2.5.7 Trascinamento. Il caricamento dei documenti funziona solo con il drag and drop. Ti serve un visibile accanto.
  • 2.5.8 Dimensione dei bersagli. Icone di chiusura e numeri della paginazione sotto i 24 × 24 px. Di solito lo sistemi con un po' di padding.
  • 3.2.6 Aiuto coerente. "Contatta l'ufficio" sta in fondo in una pagina e in alto in un'altra, nello stesso percorso.
  • 3.3.7 Inserimento ridondante. L'indirizzo di residenza chiesto due volte nella stessa istanza. Ti basta precompilarlo, o mettere una casella "Uguale al richiedente".
  • 3.3.8 Autenticazione accessibile. Incolla bloccato nel campo password, autocomplete="off", codici OTP divisi in sei caselle che rifiutano l'incolla. Con SPID e CIE l'accesso avviene sul sistema del provider, ma il bottone e le credenziali alternative per gli operatori sono responsabilità del sito.

Il criterio 4.1.1 Parsing invece sparisce. Non festeggiare troppo, però: gli ID duplicati restano un problema, perché rompono etichette e descrizioni.

La parte di cui si parla poco: le preferenze dell'utente

La v4.1.1 riscrive il requisito sulle preferenze dell'utente e lo porta anche sul web, con la clausola 9.7. Il senso: la pagina non deve scavalcare le impostazioni che l'utente ha scelto nel sistema o nel browser. Dimensione del testo, zoom, contrasto elevato, tema scuro.

Questa parte non sta nelle WCAG, e axe non la controlla. Una pagina può passare tutte le WCAG e non rispettarla. E onestamente gli errori che vedo sono banali:

  • html { font-size: 16px }, che ignora la dimensione del testo scelta nel browser. Meglio font-size: 100% e misure in rem;
  • user-scalable=no o maximum-scale=1 nel meta viewport, che bloccano lo zoom su mobile;
  • icone fatte con background-image, che nel contrasto elevato di Windows spariscono. Le SVG con currentColor invece restano;
  • focus personalizzato che scompare in modalità colori forzati. Un outline: 2px solid transparent diventa visibile proprio lì.

La buona notizia è che la verifichi in cinque minuti, senza strumenti particolari:

  1. Chrome, Impostazioni, Aspetto, Dimensione carattere "Molto grande". Il testo deve crescere e la pagina non deve rompersi.
  2. Nei DevTools, pannello Rendering, emula forced-colors: active. Icone, bordi dei campi e focus devono restare visibili.
  3. Stesso pannello: prefers-color-scheme: dark e prefers-reduced-motion: reduce.
  4. Sul telefono, prova a ingrandire con due dita.

Se devi dichiarare la conformità, leggi il testo esatto della clausola nella norma ETSI. Io però con questi quattro controlli ho trovato quasi tutti gli errori che si vedono davvero.

Perché una scansione non basta

Ho provato tutto questo, per curiosità, sul sito del mio Comune, costruito bene con il tema AgID basato su Bootstrap Italia. La scansione automatica ha trovato un solo problema: il link del logo chiamato "Logo dell'ente".

Poi ho stretto la finestra a 320 px, che equivale allo zoom al 400%. La pagina scorreva in orizzontale per colpa di una griglia con colonne fisse da 350 px: chi ingrandisce il testo deve spostarsi di lato a ogni riga (criterio 1.4.10). La correzione è una riga di CSS:

grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(min(100%, 350px), 1fr));

Insomma, un report pulito non è un sito accessibile. E con la v4.1.1 la distanza fra le due cose aumenta, perché una parte dei requisiti nuovi uno scanner non la vede proprio.

Lo strumento che uso

Per tenere insieme tutto questo ho scritto a11y-agent-italia, sette skill open source per Claude, con licenza MIT. Fanno l'audit sui criteri WCAG con un report in italiano, propongono correzioni per React e HTML, guidano i test con tastiera e screen reader e preparano la dichiarazione di accessibilità per il form AgID. La skill /a11y-wcag22 fa la gap analysis verso la v4.1.1, compresa la clausola 9.7.

Lo installi in Claude Code con un comando:

npx a11y-agent-italia installa

E se ti serve solo la scansione, con axe-core e il controllo del reflow a 320 px:

npx a11y-scansiona https://tuosito.it --wcag22

Una regola l'ho tenuta ferma: nessuna skill dichiara conforme una pagina solo perché la scansione è pulita.

Se vuoi dare una mano

Io copro i casi che vedo nel mio lavoro, ma alla fine la PA italiana è fatta di migliaia di siti diversi. Ho aperto quattro issue per chi vuole iniziare a contribuire, e due non chiedono di scrivere codice: raccontare un caso reale trovato su un sito pubblico, e una checklist per i PDF dell'albo pretorio.

Il repo è qui: github.com/JacopoMarini/a11y-agent-italia

Fonti

  • ETSI, EN 301 549 V4.1.1 (2026-09)
  • AgID, Linee guida sull'accessibilità dei servizi, Determinazione n. 38/2026
  • Deque, EN 301 549 v4.1.1 is final
  • Hidde de Vries, New EN 301 549 adopted
  • W3C, What's New in WCAG 2.2

event_model_payload.headline: Railway app alternatives in 2026: 6 options and what they cost
event_model_payload.summary:
You want to know which Railway app alternatives are worth moving to, and what your bill will look like after the move. This guide prices the same small app on six platforms, shows where each one beats the others, and ends with a migration checklist you can follow tonight. It matters now for two reasons: Railway's railway.json and railway.toml files stop being read on 1 December 2026, and a usage-based bill is hard to predict until you price your own app.

Try it on Hubfly space: deploy the same app from Git or a Compose file and see the monthly estimate before you click Deploy.

Why people look for Railway alternatives

Railway is a good product, and its deploy flow is quick to learn. People still leave, usually for one of four reasons:

  • The bill is hard to forecast. Railway charges per second for CPU, RAM, volumes and egress. At its published rates, one vCPU running all month is about $20.29 and 1 GB of RAM about $10.14. A small app that keeps its full size busy all month can cost more than a fixed-price instance elsewhere.
  • Config as Code is going away. Railway has deprecated railway.json and railway.toml. Existing files are read until 1 December 2026, and new services can't opt in. That config has to move somewhere, for example to Railway's new TypeScript setup, so it's a natural moment to ask whether to move platforms instead.
  • Outages. On 19 May 2026 Google Cloud suspended Railway's production account, taking its API, control plane and databases offline for about 8 hours. Railway's own incident report says workloads in every region were unreachable at the peak.
  • Limits you hit later. Hobby volumes go up to 5 GB (plans docs), and HTTP requests through the public edge end after 15 minutes, or after 5 minutes with no data moving (specs and limits). WebSockets are exempt.

If none of these bother you, stay. Moving has a cost too.

The same app, priced on six platforms

Every row prices one always-on web service with about 0.5 vCPU and 512 MB RAM, plus the smallest paid Postgres each platform sells, for a 730-hour month. Prices are list prices as of 11 November 2026. Egress is left out because each platform counts it differently; see the table after this one.

Platform Web service Smallest paid Postgres Monthly total Catch
Fly.io shared-cpu-1x 256 MB $2.19 + 256 MB extra RAM at $6/GB = $3.69 Managed Postgres Basic $38 + 1 GB at $0.28 $41.97 HA, backups and pooling are included in that $38
Railway 0.5 vCPU + 0.5 GB at full use = $15.22 Postgres service, assumed at 0.25 vCPU / 512 MB + 1 GB volume = $10.30 up to $25.52 Full-use ceiling; Hobby's $5 counts toward usage
Render 512 MB, "less than 1 CPU" $7 256 MB Postgres $6, storage $0.30/GB $13.00 (+$0.30 if the 1 GB disk is billed separately) Free Postgres expires after 30 days
Heroku Basic dyno, 0.5 GB $7 Essential-0, 1 GB $5 $12.00 No rollback on Essential plans
DigitalOcean App Platform 1 vCPU / 512 MiB shared $5 Dev database, 512 MiB $7 $12.00 Dev database isn't backed up and is deleted with the app
Hubfly space Dedicated 0.5 vCPU / 512 MB / 4 GB, always on $2.23 Managed PostgreSQL Nano, 0.25 vCPU / 512 MiB / 10 GiB $2.02 $4.25 Managed Postgres has no automatic backups, point-in-time restore or replicas yet

How the two usage-priced rows add up:

  • Railway: 0.5 × $20.29 (vCPU) + 0.5 × $10.14 (GB RAM) = $15.22 for the web service. Postgres: 0.25 × $20.29 + 0.5 × $10.14 + 1 GB × $0.16 = $10.30.
  • Hubfly space: 0.5 vCPU × $0.004 × 730 h = $1.46, plus 0.5 GB × $0.002 × 730 h = $0.73, plus 4 GB storage × $0.00001536 × 730 h = $0.04, for $2.23. The managed Postgres Nano plan is a flat $2.02.

Egress per GB (the thing that surprises people later):

Platform Egress price
Railway $0.05/GB
Render 5 GB included on Hobby, then $0.15/GB
Fly.io $0.02/GB in North America and Europe
DigitalOcean App Platform 50 GiB included on the $5 plan, then $0.02/GiB
Northflank $0.06/GB

Check your own usage page for last month's egress before you compare.

The six Railway app alternatives, one by one

1. Render: the closest feel to Railway

Render gives you Git-push deploys and managed Postgres with fixed monthly prices per instance. That fixes the "what will I pay" problem. It also has a free web tier that spins down after 15 minutes without inbound traffic and takes about a minute to wake (free tier docs).

Pick it if you want Railway's workflow with a fixed bill. Watch out for bandwidth after the first 5 GB on Hobby and the 30-day expiry on free Postgres.

2. Fly.io: apps close to your users

Fly.io runs your Docker image as Machines in many regions. The compute is cheap; the managed database is not. Managed Postgres starts at $38 a month, but every plan includes high availability, automated backups and connection pooling.

Pick it if you need low latency in several regions. Watch out for the database price, and for the fact that most setup lives in a fly.toml file and the fly CLI.

3. Heroku: the old default, now in maintenance

Heroku has a long-standing add-on marketplace, and $7 + $5 is easy to budget. But Heroku moved to sustaining engineering in February 2026, which means fewer new features. Read what that means for you in Is Heroku shutting down?.

Pick it if you depend on a Heroku-only add-on. Watch out for Eco dynos sleeping after 30 minutes and no database rollback on Essential plans.

4. DigitalOcean App Platform: cheap and simple

$5 for 1 vCPU and 512 MiB is one of the lowest fixed prices here, and DigitalOcean has many regions. The cheap database is the catch: the $7 dev database is not backed up and is destroyed if you delete the app. For real data, add a Managed PostgreSQL cluster, which costs more.

Pick it if you already use DigitalOcean Droplets or Spaces. Watch out for the dev database.

5. Northflank: a free sandbox that doesn't sleep

Northflank's free Sandbox gives you 2 services, 2 jobs and 1 database, up to $20 of resources a month, always on with no sleeping (pricing). Paid compute starts at $12 a month for 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB. It can also run your apps in your own cloud account (BYOC).

Pick it if you want a free always-on test setup or need to run in your own cloud account. Watch out for the higher paid price for small apps. It's left out of the bill table because its Postgres add-on price isn't listed on the pricing page.

6. Hubfly space: the lowest bill for small always-on apps

Hubfly space runs your containers from Git, a Docker image or a Compose file, and prices CPU and RAM at $0.004 per vCPU-hour and $0.002 per GB-hour. That's why the same app lands at $4.25 a month. A few things that matter when you're coming from Railway:

  • Compose import. Paste your docker-compose.yml and Hubfly space creates the services, named volumes, healthchecks and depends_on order. Bind mounts are skipped, so move that data into a volume.
  • A hard budget cap. Set a cap per project. You get emails at 80% and 90%, and at 100% the workloads stop, so a runaway worker can't run up a surprise bill.
  • Auto Sleep when you want it. Turn it on for staging and pay compute only while the container is awake; volumes are still billed.
  • No seat, project or custom-domain fees. Custom domains get free TLS certificates.
  • A free allowance: 360 compute hours a month on the shared tier. Creating resources needs a one-time $5 deposit, which is prepaid credit you spend on usage, not a fee.

Where it falls short: managed Postgres has no replicas, high availability or point-in-time restore yet, and automatic backups are still coming. Railway, Render and Fly.io all do better there today. There are fewer regions too (a few in Europe and the US). If your app can't live without point-in-time restore, pick Render or Fly.io.

How to choose in one minute

If you care most about… Choose
A bill you can predict, same workflow as Railway Render
Users on several continents Fly.io
A Heroku add-on you can't replace Heroku
A $5 app next to your existing Droplets DigitalOcean App Platform
A free always-on sandbox, or your own cloud account Northflank
The lowest monthly bill for small always-on apps, with a hard budget cap Hubfly space
Railway's workflow and database point-in-time restore, and the bill is fine Stay on Railway

How to move off Railway: a checklist

These steps move a web service and its Postgres database. They use the Railway CLI (version 5.71.0 here) and the PostgreSQL 16+ client tools.

1. Export your variables. This prints raw values, so keep the file out of Git:

railway link
railway variable list --service shop-api --kv > shop-api.env
railway variable list --service Postgres --kv | grep DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL

Why: you need every secret on the new platform before the first deploy.

2. Write down what railway.json or railway.toml does. Build command, start command, pre-deploy command (often migrations), health check path and cron schedule. Each one becomes a setting on the new platform. If you stay on Railway, you have until 1 December to move these into its new setup.

3. Dump the database with the public URL from step 1:

pg_dump "postgresql://postgres:YOUR_PASSWORD@YOUR_PROXY_HOST:YOUR_PORT/railway" \
  --format=custom --file=shop.dump

Why: the custom format is compressed and lets pg_restore skip ownership. Use a pg_dump at least as new as the server version.

4. Create the new database, then restore into it:

pg_restore --no-owner --no-acl \
  --dbname="postgresql://shop_admin:NEW_PASSWORD@NEW_HOST:5432/shop" \
  shop.dump

Why: --no-owner and --no-acl make the new database user own every table, so you don't need a superuser on the new platform. Sequences keep their position, so new rows don't collide with old IDs.

5. Check the row counts on both sides for your biggest tables:

OLD_URL="postgresql://postgres:YOUR_PASSWORD@YOUR_PROXY_HOST:YOUR_PORT/railway"
NEW_URL="postgresql://shop_admin:NEW_PASSWORD@NEW_HOST:5432/shop"
psql "$OLD_URL" -tAc "select count(*) from orders"
psql "$NEW_URL" -tAc "select count(*) from orders"

6. Deploy the app from the same repo with the variables from step 1, and point DATABASE_URL at the new database. On Hubfly space, a root Dockerfile is used as-is; without one, the build detects the stack from your package files.

7. Cut over. Don't send real traffic to the new app before this step, and stop it while the restore runs, so it holds no locks and writes nothing that --clean would drop. Put the old app in read-only mode or stop it. Run step 3 again, then restore over the first copy with --clean --if-exists added, so old tables are dropped before the fresh ones load:

pg_restore --clean --if-exists --no-owner --no-acl \
  --dbname="$NEW_URL" shop.dump

Run step 5 again, then change your domain's DNS to the new platform. Keep the Railway project for a few days before deleting it.

For a click-by-click version, see How to move your app from Railway to Hubfly space, step by step.

What can go wrong

  • pg_dump: error: aborting because of server version mismatch. Your local pg_dump is older than Railway's Postgres. Install the matching client version, or run pg_dump from a container with the same major version.
  • ERROR: role "" does not exist during restore, on lines like ALTER TABLE public.orders OWNER TO …. You restored without --no-owner. Drop the new database, recreate it, and run step 4 again with both flags.
  • The new app can't reach the database. Railway's private hostnames (*.railway.internal) don't exist anywhere else. Replace every old host in your variables with the new database's connection string, and check that the database's network settings allow your app. If the database is open to all IPs, limit it to what your app needs.
  • Your Railway app never slept, so the bill was higher than expected. Railway's Serverless setting sleeps a service only after about 5–10 minutes with no outbound traffic, and an open database connection counts. Apps with a connection pool rarely sleep.
  • Long requests fail after the move. If you had requests near Railway's 15-minute limit, check the new platform's limit before cutting over, or move that work to a background job.

FAQ

What is the best alternative to Railway?

For most small apps, Render if you want the same workflow with fixed prices, and Hubfly space if you want the lowest bill for always-on apps. Pick Fly.io for multi-region apps.

Is Railway cheaper than Render?

Not for an always-on app at full size. A 0.5 vCPU / 512 MB service costs up to $15.22 a month on Railway and $7 on Render. Compare your real figure on Railway's usage page with Render's fixed price before deciding.

Does Railway have a free tier in 2026?

Railway has a 30-day trial with $5 of credit, then $1 a month of credit on the Free plan. Render, Northflank and Hubfly space each have a lasting free option.

Is Railway good for production?

Plenty of teams run production on Railway. Weigh the May 2026 outage, the 15-minute HTTP limit and the 5 GB Hobby volume cap against how much you value its workflow, and use the Pro plan for anything customer-facing.

What happens to railway.json after 1 December 2026?

Railway stops reading railway.json and railway.toml on that date. Move the settings into Railway's TypeScript configuration first, or into your new platform's settings if you're leaving.

Can I move a Railway app without downtime?

Close to it. Do a full copy first, then a short read-only window for the final pg_dump and a pg_restore --clean --if-exists, then switch DNS. The read-only window is usually the length of one dump and restore.

Do I need Docker to leave Railway?

No. Render, Heroku, DigitalOcean and Hubfly space build from source for common stacks. A Dockerfile makes the move easier, because every platform here can run one.

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Import a Compose file: bring a multi-service Railway project over in one paste.
  • Get a managed PostgreSQL database: create the Nano instance used in the price table.
  • Set a budget cap: stop a runaway bill before it happens.

Related reading: Heroku vs Render vs Railway vs Hubfly space pricing. Thinking of self-hosting instead? See Coolify vs Railway and Render.

Try it on Hubfly space: create a project, set a budget cap, and deploy your first service.

By Octave · drafted with AI, reviewed by Octave · Last updated 11 November 2026

event_model_payload.headline: Corners and Yellow Cards per Match by League: One Match Table, SQL and pandas, 2025/26 vs 2026/27
event_model_payload.summary:
Most football stat sites show you "corners per match" as a finished number. Computing it yourself takes about ten lines once all matches live in one table. Here is the exact approach we use for four leagues, with the real output for 2025/26 against 2026/27 so far. It is the same pipeline that produces our goal averages for every league, by TohaProBets, just pointed at corners and cards instead of goals.

The table

One row per match. Nothing is stored per team, because every team split can be derived later.

CREATE TABLE matches (
  league        TEXT,     -- 'APL', 'La Liga', 'Serie A', 'BR Serie A'
  season        TEXT,     -- '2526', '2627', or '2025', '2026' for Brazil
  date          TEXT,
  home, away    TEXT,
  hg, ag        INTEGER,  -- goals
  hc, ac        INTEGER,  -- corners won by each side
  hy, ay        INTEGER,  -- yellow cards
  referee       TEXT
);

A real row looks like this: ('2026-10-24', 'Arsenal', 'Everton', 2, 0, 12, 3, 1, 3, 'Tony Harrington'). Arsenal won 12 corners, Everton 3, and four yellows were shown.

Per-league averages in SQL 

SELECT league, season, COUNT(*) AS n,
       ROUND(AVG(hc + ac), 2) AS corners,
       ROUND(AVG(hy + ay), 2) AS yellows,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(hc + ac > 9.5), 1) AS corners_over_9_5,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(hy + ay > 4.5), 1) AS yellows_over_4_5
FROM matches
WHERE hc IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY league, season;

The WHERE hc IS NOT NULL line matters: friendlies and some cup games arrive without corner data, and averaging over NULLs silently shrinks the sample. In this dataset every league row has corners, so n equals the full match count.

The same in pandas 

df["corners"] = df.hc + df.ac
df["yellows"] = df.hy + df.ay
out = (df.dropna(subset=["hc"])
         .groupby(["league", "season"])
         .agg(n=("corners", "size"),
              corners=("corners", "mean"),
              yellows=("yellows", "mean"),
              c95=("corners", lambda s: (s > 9.5).mean() * 100),
              y45=("yellows", lambda s: (s > 4.5).mean() * 100))
         .round(2))

The output

European data runs to 8 November 2026, Brazil to 18 November.

League Season Matches Corners Over 9.5 Yellows Over 4.5
APL 2025/26 380 10.00 56.3% 3.75 33.9%
APL 2026/27 100 9.50 47.0% 4.01 39.0%
La Liga 2025/26 380 9.67 48.2% 4.41 44.2%
La Liga 2026/27 119 9.74 50.4% 4.44 48.7%
Serie A 2025/26 380 8.82 40.3% 3.70 30.8%
Serie A 2026/27 110 9.76 45.5% 3.22 26.4%
Brazil 2025 380 9.92 50.8% 4.93 56.3%
Brazil 2026 345 10.54 57.7% 4.58 49.0%

Three things jump out. England lost half a corner per match (10.00 to 9.50) but gained a quarter of a yellow (3.75 to 4.01). Serie A moved the other way on both: almost one extra corner (8.82 to 9.76) and half a card fewer (3.70 to 3.22). Brazil 2026 is the highest of all eight rows on both counts. The same aggregation for goals gives Serie A 3.11 per match against 2.43 last season.

Home and away splits

Split the sum back into its two columns and you get the home edge:

df.groupby(["league", "season"])[["hc", "ac", "hy", "ay"]].mean()

For 2026/27: APL home corners 5.00 against 4.50 away, La Liga 5.31 against 4.43, Serie A 5.03 against 4.74, Brazil 6.08 against 4.46. Away teams collect more yellows in England (2.23 against 1.78), while in Serie A the split is exactly level at 1.61 each.

Team level with one filter

The same table answers team questions. Newcastle's home corners this season:

SELECT AVG(hc), AVG(ac) FROM matches
WHERE league = 'APL' AND season = '2627' AND home = 'Newcastle';

Result: 3.6 won, 5.2 conceded over five games, down from 6.79 and 4.95 last season. A team-level number like this, set against the league baseline above, is the starting point for how Xpect turns match history into probabilities.

Pitfalls

  • Sample size. Ten rounds is 100 matches in England; a 0.5 shift is meaningful at league level but not for one team.
  • Season keys. Brazil runs on calendar years, Europe across two years. Keep the key as text and never sort it as an integer.
  • Corner direction. Store corners won by each side, not "for" and "against", and derive the latter per team. Otherwise the home and away views disagree.

event_model_payload.headline: Our log shipper reported nine pods out of nine on a cluster of twelve nodes
event_model_payload.summary:
Our route planning job runs every night and decides which van takes which parcels the next day. In August we gave it its own pool of three nodes, so its memory use could not crowd out anything else, and tainted them with workload=batch:NoSchedule. Only pods with a matching toleration can be scheduled there, which was the point. The job got the toleration. Nothing else did.

In October the job failed at three in the morning and the depots had no routes at six. The pods had already been cleaned up, so we went to our log store. There was nothing from the batch nodes, not that night and not any night since August. Our node dashboards had no data for them either.

Logs and node metrics both come from DaemonSets, one pod per node: Fluent Bit and node exporter. A DaemonSet's pods are scheduled like any others and respect taints. The DaemonSet controller adds tolerations of its own for the taints Kubernetes puts on nodes with problems, not ready, unreachable, disk or memory pressure, unschedulable, but not for taints we invent. Neither DaemonSet tolerated workload=batch, so neither had ever run on those three nodes.

What hid it for two months was the DaemonSet's own status. Desired, current and ready all said nine. The desired count is the number of nodes the DaemonSet is allowed to run on, not the number of nodes in the cluster, so a DaemonSet that excludes three nodes is perfectly healthy by its own measure. Our alert compared ready with desired, and they agreed.

We reran the job by hand and the vans left an hour late. The cause turned out to be a single depot with a malformed postcode, which took ten minutes to find once we had logs. Every agent DaemonSet now carries a toleration with operator Exists and no key, which tolerates every taint, because an agent belongs on every node. An alert compares count(kube_node_info) from kube-state-metrics with each agent's desired number scheduled, and any difference pages.

A DaemonSet's health is measured against the nodes it chose. Ours had quietly chosen to skip the three nodes we cared about that night.

– Sergey Shinder

event_model_payload.headline: `=?UTF-8?B?…?=` : lire et fabriquer des objets d'e-mail accentués sans casser les « é »
event_model_payload.summary:
Vous avez déjà ouvert la source d'un e-mail (« Afficher l'original » dans Gmail, « Code source du message » dans Thunderbird) et vu une ligne comme celle-ci ?

Subject: =?UTF-8?B?UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDog?=
 =?UTF-8?B?Y29tcHRlIHJlbmR1IGR1IDE4IG5vdmVtYnJl?=

Ce n'est ni du chiffrement ni un bug : c'est un encoded-word au sens de la RFC 2047. Les en-têtes d'un e-mail ont été pensés pour de l'ASCII ; dès qu'un objet contient « é », « ç » ou « œ », il faut un moyen de faire passer ces octets dans un canal 7 bits. Base64 en est un. Voici comment ça marche, les trois pièges qui finissent en « R�union » dans les boîtes de réception, et comment vérifier un en-tête à la main.

Anatomie d'un encoded-word

Le format est toujours le même : =?charset?encodage?texte?=

  • charset : le jeu de caractères des octets, aujourd'hui presque toujours UTF-8 (on croise encore ISO-8859-1 ou windows-1252 dans de vieux messages) ;
  • encodage : B pour Base64, Q pour une variante de quoted-printable ;
  • texte : les octets encodés.

Le client mail décode le Base64, puis interprète les octets avec le charset annoncé. Si ce charset est faux, le décodage Base64 réussit quand même… et le texte affiché est faux. Base64 ne connaît pas les caractères : il ne transporte que des octets.

Exemple pas à pas (objet illustratif)

Prenons un objet fictif : Réunion d'équipe : compte rendu du 18 novembre.

  1. En octets UTF-8 : 46 caractères, mais 48 octets, car chaque « é » occupe deux octets (C3 A9). « Réunion » donne 52 C3 A9 75 6E 69 6F 6E.
  2. En Base64 : 48 octets donnent 64 caractères (48 ÷ 3 × 4, sans = final puisque 48 est divisible par 3) : UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDogY29tcHRlIHJlbmR1IGR1IDE4IG5vdmVtYnJl
  3. En encoded-word : =?UTF-8?B? + 64 caractères + ?=, soit 76 caractères.

Problème : la RFC 2047 limite un encoded-word à 75 caractères. Notre objet dépasse d'un seul caractère. C'est exactement le genre de cas qui passe en test avec « Réunion » tout court et casse en production avec un vrai objet.

La solution : découper le texte (pas la chaîne Base64), encoder chaque morceau séparément, puis placer les morceaux sur des lignes de continuation qui commencent par un espace :

  • Réunion d'équipe : (21 octets) → UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDog, encoded-word de 40 caractères ;
  • compte rendu du 18 novembre (27 octets) → Y29tcHRlIHJlbmR1IGR1IDE4IG5vdmVtYnJl, encoded-word de 48 caractères.

Le blanc de pliage entre deux encoded-words adjacents est ignoré à l'affichage ; l'espace visible fait partie du premier morceau. Vérification avec le parseur de la bibliothèque standard Python :

import email, email.policy

raw = (b"Subject: =?UTF-8?B?UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDog?=\r\n"
       b" =?UTF-8?B?Y29tcHRlIHJlbmR1IGR1IDE4IG5vdmVtYnJl?=\r\n\r\n")
msg = email.message_from_bytes(raw, policy=email.policy.default)
print(msg["Subject"])
# Réunion d'équipe : compte rendu du 18 novembre

Et l'étape 2 en JavaScript (Node) :

const b64 = Buffer.from("Réunion d'équipe : ", "utf8").toString("base64");
console.log(`=?UTF-8?B?${b64}?=`);
// =?UTF-8?B?UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDog?=

Piège n° 1 : couper au milieu d'un caractère

La tentation, c'est de découper la suite d'octets tous les N octets. Si on coupe après 12 octets, le premier morceau se termine par C3, le premier octet de « é », et le second commence par A9 :

  • UsOpdW5pb24gZCfD, décodé seul : Réunion d'�
  • qXF1aXBlIDog, décodé seul : �quipe :

La RFC 2047 est explicite : chaque encoded-word doit représenter un nombre entier de caractères ; un caractère multi-octet ne doit pas être réparti sur deux encoded-words. Certains décodeurs recollent les octets (le module email.header de Python le fait), d'autres affichent deux �. Ne comptez pas sur leur indulgence : coupez sur des frontières de caractères (en JavaScript, itérez avec for…of ou Array.from(str) plutôt qu'avec des index d'octets), et pensez aux emojis, qui prennent quatre octets.

Piège n° 2 : coller tout l'encoded-word dans un décodeur

Pour vérifier un en-tête, collez seulement la partie entre ?B? et ?=. Si vous collez =?UTF-8?B?…?= en entier dans un décodeur Base64 qui se contente d'écarter les caractères hors alphabet, il garde le = initial ainsi que les lettres et chiffres de UTF-8 et B. La chaîne obtenue n'est plus du Base64 valide : vous récoltez une erreur au lieu du texte.

Piège n° 3 : choisir « B » quand « Q » serait plus lisible

Pour un objet surtout ASCII, beaucoup de bibliothèques préfèrent l'encodage Q. Python (EmailMessage avec policy.SMTP) produit par exemple, pour le même objet :

Subject: =?utf-8?q?R=C3=A9union_d=27=C3=A9quipe?= : compte rendu du 18
 novembre

Seuls les mots qui en ont besoin sont encodés, et le reste reste lisible dans les logs. B est plus compact quand presque tout le texte est non-ASCII (arabe, japonais…). Les deux sont valides ; l'essentiel est de laisser votre bibliothèque mail générer l'en-tête plutôt que de concaténer des chaînes à la main.

Et le corps du message ?

Dans le corps, Base64 apparaît avec Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64, typiquement pour les pièces jointes. Là, c'est la RFC 2045 qui s'applique : lignes de 76 caractères au maximum. Quant aux noms de fichiers accentués des pièces jointes, ils passent souvent par une autre syntaxe (RFC 2231, filename*=UTF-8''… en encodage pourcent), qui n'est pas du Base64 du tout.

Vérifier un en-tête en 3 étapes avec l'outil

  1. Ouvrez le décodeur Base64 en français et laissez Jeu de Caractères sur UTF-8.
  2. Collez uniquement la charge utile, par exemple SMOpbMOobmUgRHVwcsOp (nom fictif). Conversion en Direct étant activée par défaut, le résultat s'affiche aussitôt : Hélène Dupré.
  3. Si l'outil signale des caractères de remplacement, le morceau a sans doute été coupé au milieu d'un caractère, ou le charset annoncé n'est pas UTF-8. Choisissez Hexadecimal (libellé en anglais) pour voir les octets bruts : C3 A9 correspond à « é » en UTF-8, un E9 isolé à « é » en Latin-1.

Pour l'opération inverse, l'encodeur Base64 fonctionne de la même façon. Il produit le Base64 brut : il n'ajoute ni =?UTF-8?B? ni ?= et ne découpe pas un objet trop long, c'est à vous (ou mieux, à votre bibliothèque) de le faire. Notez aussi que l'option « Couper les Lignes (64 chars) » coupe en réalité à 76 caractères, soit la limite du corps MIME, pas celle d'un encoded-word. La conversion se fait dans le navigateur, mais l'historique de l'outil garde les entrées courtes en stockage local : utilisez des exemples fictifs plutôt que de vrais en-têtes contenant des données personnelles.

Transparence : cet outil est proposé par Mind vs Drive, l'équipe derrière ce blog.

À retenir

  • =?UTF-8?B?…?=, c'est un charset plus du Base64 ; ce n'est pas du chiffrement.
  • 75 caractères au maximum par encoded-word : découpez le texte, pas le Base64, et jamais au milieu d'un caractère multi-octet.
  • Pour déboguer, décodez seulement la charge utile et regardez les octets en hexadécimal.

Références : RFC 2047 (encoded-words, limite de 75 caractères, caractères non découpables), RFC 2045 (Content-Transfer-Encoding, lignes de 76 caractères), RFC 2231 (paramètres comme filename*). Exemples vérifiés le 19 novembre 2026.

event_model_payload.headline: How a boutique advisory maintains currency cross-rate tables for client hedging
event_model_payload.summary:
By Pradyumna Ghosh, Ghosh Para Capital Advisors, Siliguri

Data stamp. Every exchange rate in this article, and every figure calculated from one, comes from a single CurrencyScoop snapshot pulled on 19 November 2026. The provider timestamp is 07:52:19 UTC (13:22:19 IST). These are reference rates, not dealing quotes, and they will have moved since. The client examples are hypothetical.

When a client asks what a euro payment will cost in rupees, the answer should be a number with a date and a set of rules attached. Our home currency is the Indian rupee (INR). Our hedging watchlist has five currencies: the US dollar, euro, pound sterling, Japanese yen and Swiss franc. Six currencies make 30 directional pairs. If those pairs come from different sources, or from the same source at different moments, the table quietly contradicts itself.

This post sets out the method we use to keep the table consistent: one snapshot, one pivot currency, written assumptions, and checks that run on every refresh. The Python at the end is short enough to copy.

1. Pull one snapshot, not thirty quotes

One call goes to the CurrencyScoop latest-rates endpoint with USD as the base and the other five currencies as symbols. A second call, with INR as the base, is used only as a cross-check.

Table 1. Raw snapshot, as delivered

Currency Units per 1 USD (primary pull) Units per 1 INR (cross-check pull) Pulled
INR 93.3255633 (base) 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
USD 1 (base) 0.01071518 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
EUR 0.91113841 0.00976301 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
GBP 0.76024816 0.00814619 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
JPY 159.69790609 1.71119145 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
CHF 0.84330414 0.00903615 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC

Both responses carry the same provider timestamp. If they did not, we would pull again rather than compare numbers from two different moments.

2. The assumptions, stated before the numbers

  1. One source. All rates come from the CurrencyScoop (CurrencyBeacon) latest-rates API. Nothing is patched in from a bank screen or a website.
  2. One snapshot. Every figure comes from responses stamped 07:52:19 UTC on 19 November 2026. A table never mixes timestamps.
  3. USD is the pivot. USD is the provider's default base. Every cross is derived as (column currency per USD) ÷ (row currency per USD).
  4. One rate per currency, treated as a mid. The provider returns a single rate with no bid or offer. We treat it as a mid-market reference. It is not executable and includes no bank margin, forward points or value-date convention.
  5. Inverses are calculated, never sourced. GBP per EUR is exactly 1 ÷ (EUR per GBP), so the table cannot disagree with itself.
  6. Quotation. The home-currency view gives INR per unit of foreign currency. In the matrix, each row is a fixed amount of the row currency: 100 INR, 1 USD, 1 EUR, 1 GBP, 100 JPY, 1 CHF. Low-value currencies are quoted per 100 so that four decimals still carry enough precision.
  7. Precision. Provider values are read as exact decimals. Arithmetic uses Python's decimal module at 34 significant digits. Rounding happens only for display: four decimal places, round-half-even.
  8. Cross-check. The INR quotes are compared with reciprocals of the INR-base pull. Differences must fall inside that pull's precision floor (section 3).
  9. Freshness. A table is a valid reference for the Indian business day on which it was pulled. Its timestamp travels with every figure, including in client notes.
  10. Scope. No official fixings, pegs, forward points or forecasts are blended in.

3. The home-currency view: rupees per unit

Table 2. INR per unit of foreign currency

Currency Quote unit INR via USD pivot INR direct (cross-check) Difference Precision floor Pulled
US dollar 1 USD 93.3256 93.3255 +0.0021 bp ±0.0047 bp 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
Euro 1 EUR 102.4274 102.4274 < 0.0001 bp ±0.0051 bp 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
Pound sterling 1 GBP 122.7567 122.7568 −0.0051 bp ±0.0061 bp 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
Japanese yen 100 JPY 58.4388 58.4388 < 0.0001 bp < 0.0001 bp 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
Swiss franc 1 CHF 110.6666 110.6666 −0.0042 bp ±0.0055 bp 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC

The largest gap is 0.0051 bp, for sterling (pulled 19 Nov 2026). That is inside the precision floor of the cross-check data. The INR-base quotes arrive with eight decimal places. For a number as small as 0.00814619 pounds per rupee, that leaves six significant figures, so its reciprocal is only good to about ±0.006 bp. The gaps are rounding noise, not a disagreement. A gap outside the floor would stop the table until someone explained it.

Look at the USD row. The two values agree to within 0.0021 bp, yet they display as 93.3256 and 93.3255 (pulled 19 Nov 2026). A check that compared displayed numbers would raise a false alarm, so comparisons always use unrounded values.

4. The full cross-rate matrix

Read across. Each row is a fixed amount of the row currency. Each cell shows how many units of the column currency that amount buys at the snapshot.

Table 3. Cross-rate matrix (units of column currency per row amount)

Row amount INR USD EUR GBP JPY CHF Pulled
100 INR — 1.0715 0.9763 0.8146 171.1191 0.9036 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
1 USD 93.3256 — 0.9111 0.7602 159.6979 0.8433 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
1 EUR 102.4274 1.0975 — 0.8344 175.2729 0.9255 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
1 GBP 122.7567 1.3154 1.1985 — 210.0602 1.1092 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
100 JPY 58.4388 0.6262 0.5705 0.4761 — 0.5281 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC
1 CHF 110.6666 1.1858 1.0804 0.9015 189.3717 — 19 Nov 2026, 07:52:19 UTC

Each cell is: row amount × (column currency per USD) ÷ (row currency per USD), using the unrounded values in Table 1.

5. Checks that run on every refresh

  1. Same timestamp. Both pulls must carry the same provider timestamp. Passed: both read 07:52:19 UTC, 19 Nov 2026.
  2. Cross-check inside the precision floor. Passed: each gap sat inside its own floor; the largest, sterling's 0.0051 bp, against ±0.0061 bp (pulled 19 Nov 2026).
  3. Identities at full precision. A/B × B/A = 1 and A/B × B/C × C/A = 1 for every combination of the six currencies. The largest residuals on this snapshot were 4 × 10⁻³⁴ and 1 × 10⁻³³ (pulled 19 Nov 2026), which is zero at working precision. These identities hold by construction, so they test the process rather than the market. If anyone types a number into the table by hand, they fail.
  4. Move alert (illustrative setting). If any INR quote moves more than 1.5% from the previous business day's snapshot, check the data first. If the move is real, review the client hedges it affects.
  5. Stale label (illustrative setting). On weekends and Indian holidays the last snapshot stays in use, labelled "stale since …", until a new pull replaces it.

Why we never chain displayed numbers

Four-decimal figures are fine for reading and bad for calculating. Using the rounded values from Table 3:

  • EUR → GBP → EUR: 0.8344 × 1.1985 = 1.0000284, which is 0.28 bp too high (pulled 19 Nov 2026).
  • USD → GBP → CHF → USD: 0.7602 × 1.1092 × 1.1858 = 0.9998830, which is 1.17 bp too low (pulled 19 Nov 2026).
  • 1 INR at four decimals: 0.0107 USD, and 0.0107 × 93.3256 = 0.9985839, which is 14.16 bp too low. Quoting per 100 INR fixes this: 1.0715 × 93.3256 ÷ 100 = 0.9999838, only 0.16 bp low (pulled 19 Nov 2026).

A basis point looks trivial, but it scales with the notional, and it means two reports built from the same snapshot can disagree. Every published figure is recomputed from the raw snapshot, never from another rounded figure.

6. Using the table in a hedging conversation

Both examples are hypothetical. The arithmetic uses the unrounded rates pulled on 19 Nov 2026; displayed rates are rounded.

Example A: the rupee cost of a sterling payment. A family has a GBP 25,000 university instalment due in about 90 days.

  • At 122.7567 INR per GBP (pulled 19 Nov 2026), the payment costs INR 3,068,918 (about ₹30.69 lakh).
  • A 3% move in GBP/INR either way changes that by about INR 92,068, giving a range of INR 2,976,850 to INR 3,160,985 (at rates pulled 19 Nov 2026).
  • A forward contract would fix a rate that differs from this reference. The difference is the forward points, driven largely by the interest-rate gap between INR and GBP, plus the bank's margin. Neither is in the table. The table frames the size of the risk. The bank's quote at booking sets the price.

Example B: a cross exposure. A client earns US dollars and owes EUR 10,000.

  • At 1.0975 USD per EUR (pulled 19 Nov 2026), the payment needs USD 10,975.28.
  • The risk sits in EUR/USD, not in either currency against the rupee. Looking only at the INR column would make it look like two exposures when it is really one. That is why the table carries the crosses as well as the rupee column. Whether and how to hedge depends on the client's mandate and the instruments available to them. The table only makes the exposure visible.

7. What the table is not

  • Not a dealing rate. There is no bid or offer, bank margin or settlement convention.
  • Not a forward curve. There are no forward points or interest differentials.
  • Not an official fixing. Official reference rates and bank closing rates are taken at other times and can differ from this snapshot.
  • Not a forecast. It is a dated photograph.

8. The routine, end to end

  1. Pull both snapshots in the same minute: base USD with the five symbols, then base INR.
  2. Store the raw JSON with the request parameters, the provider timestamp and the retrieval time in an append-only log.
  3. Check that the timestamps match and that the INR cross-check sits inside the precision floor.
  4. Derive the INR view and the matrix from the raw USD-base values only. Never hand-edit a cell.
  5. Validate the identities, then apply the move alert and the stale label.
  6. Label every table and every quoted figure with the pull date and the provider timestamp.
  7. Use the table as a reference. Executable prices come from the bank at the time of booking.

The code 

# Rebuild the cross-rate matrix from one CurrencyScoop snapshot.
# Needs: pip install requests; set CURRENCY_API_KEY in your environment.
import os
from decimal import Decimal, getcontext, ROUND_HALF_EVEN

import requests

getcontext().prec = 34
URL = "https://api.currencybeacon.com/v1/latest"  # CurrencyScoop / CurrencyBeacon; confirm in your account docs
CCY = ["INR", "USD", "EUR", "GBP", "JPY", "CHF"]
SCALE = {"INR": Decimal(100), "JPY": Decimal(100)}  # rows quoted per 100 units

resp = requests.get(URL, params={
    "api_key": os.environ["CURRENCY_API_KEY"],
    "base": "USD",
    "symbols": "INR,EUR,GBP,JPY,CHF",
}, timeout=10)
resp.raise_for_status()
snap = resp.json(parse_float=Decimal)["response"]  # numbers parsed straight to Decimal
stamp = snap["date"]                                # provider timestamp: label every figure with it
per_usd = dict(snap["rates"], USD=Decimal(1))

def cross(row, col):
    """Units of col per SCALE[row] units of row, triangulated through USD."""
    return SCALE.get(row, Decimal(1)) * per_usd[col] / per_usd[row]

for row in CCY:
    cells = ["-" if row == col
             else str(cross(row, col).quantize(Decimal("0.0001"), ROUND_HALF_EVEN))
             for col in CCY]
    print(f"{SCALE.get(row, 1)} {row}", *cells, f"pulled {stamp}", sep=" | ")

Run against the 19 Nov 2026 snapshot (07:52:19 UTC), this prints the rows of Table 3.

Sources

  • Exchange rates: CurrencyScoop (CurrencyBeacon) latest-rates API (currencybeacon.com). Request 1: base USD, symbols INR,EUR,GBP,JPY,CHF. Request 2: base INR, symbols USD,EUR,GBP,JPY,CHF. Both pulled 19 Nov 2026; provider timestamp 2026-11-19T07:52:19Z. Usage subject to the provider's terms.

Further reading on Stack Exchange

Retrieved 19 Nov 2026. Community discussions, not house policy.

Cross rates and triangulation

  • How to determine the cross rate in a triangular arbitrage (Quantitative Finance SE)
  • Is this cross-rate bid/ask relationship formula correct for CAD/CHF derived from USD/CAD and USD/CHF? (Quantitative Finance SE; unanswered at retrieval)
  • Need to build a logic for a Forex Calculator with Cross rates (Stack Overflow)
  • Algorithm to determine exchange rate (Stack Overflow)

Precision and data handling

  • Why not use Double or Float to represent currency? (Stack Overflow)
  • In a currency exchange rate what is the maximum number of decimal places used? (Stack Overflow)
  • Do I understand currency exchange rates and bank buy/sell rates? (Personal Finance & Money SE)

Hedging practice

  • Why using 3 months forward to hedge fx risk on a fund of funds portfolio? (Quantitative Finance SE)
  • When to Choose FX Swap or Forward (Quantitative Finance SE)
  • Hedging a foreign currency purchase (INR/USD) for a real estate transaction? (Personal Finance & Money SE)
  • What does it mean to "hedge USD back to CHF"? (Personal Finance & Money SE)

General information only, not investment advice or a recommendation to deal. The examples are hypothetical. Rates are reference data pulled on 19 Nov 2026 and will have moved.

event_model_payload.headline: You Agreed to the Midnight Release at Ten in the Morning
event_model_payload.summary:
The planning meeting
was on a Tuesday morning.

Coffee.

Daylight.

A good night's sleep behind you.

Someone asked
who could run the release
at midnight on Thursday.

You said yes.

It sounded easy.

Two hours.

A checklist.

You had done it before.

On Thursday at eleven at night
you were a different person.

Tired.

Hungry.

Irritable.

Reading the checklist twice
and taking in half of it.

You would never
have agreed to this.

But you already had.

Here is the mechanism.

The psychologist
George Loewenstein
named it
the hot-cold empathy gap.

When you are calm,
rested and fed,
you badly underestimate
how much a different state
will change you.

Tiredness.

Hunger.

Stress.

Fear.

You can know
that you will be tired.

What you cannot do
from the cold side
is feel
how much
the tiredness will decide for you.

It works the other way too.

At midnight,
exhausted,
you swear never again.

By Tuesday's meeting
the feeling is gone
and the memory
is just a fact.

So you say yes again.

The gap
is not a lack of experience.

People who have done
a dozen night releases
still sign up for the next one
in daylight
with the same easy confidence.

Experience tells you the facts.

It does not
bring the feeling back.

What helps:

Do not trust
your morning self
to plan your night self.

Ask the person
who did the last late release
how it actually went.

Ask while they still remember.

Write the checklist
for the worst version of you.

Short steps.

No step that says
"check everything looks fine".

Put a rule in place
before you need it.

A second person
on every late change.

A stop time
that nobody argues with.

And when you notice yourself
saying "it will be fine"
about a version of you
that does not exist yet,
picture that version.

Eleven at night.

Cold coffee.

Ask that person
if they agree.

– Serguey Asael Shinder
