event_model_payload.headline: Deploying Industrial Edge Applications across Multiple Sites
event_model_payload.summary:
An industrial edge pilot can work perfectly while remaining difficult to reproduce.

The engineer knows which register requires scaling, which alarm is disabled and where the site-specific settings live. Deploying the same application elsewhere requires reconstructing those decisions.

A repeatable industrial edge deployment separates application logic from site configuration, node identity and runtime data. It also defines how each installation is validated, updated and recovered.

This guide explains the architecture and deployment practices behind that separation.

1. Define What Runs on the Node

An edge application may handle equipment acquisition, protocol conversion, local rules, operator screens, historical storage and upstream integration.

Document which functions belong locally and which depend on central services.

For each function, identify:

  • Required inputs.
  • External dependencies.
  • Expected behavior during disconnection.
  • Recovery behavior.
  • Resource requirements.

A local dashboard can still depend on remote authentication. A rule can still require a central API. Hosting software on site does not remove those dependencies automatically.

Keep safety functions and time-critical control within their engineered and validated implementations.

For background on acquisition, supervisory functions and deployment boundaries, see Iotellect’s SCADA architecture guide.

2. Separate the Deployment into Four Parts

Avoid copying an entire working installation to create another node.

Separate:

Application release: Reusable rules, screens, mappings and integration logic.

Site configuration: Equipment addresses, asset relationships and approved operating parameters.

Node identity and credentials: Unique identifiers and authorized connections.

Runtime data: History, events, operator actions and queued observations.

These categories need different handling.

An application update should not overwrite local history. A new installation should not inherit another node’s credentials. A rollback must account for persistent data and configuration compatibility.

3. Validate Site Configuration before Activation

Represent site differences as configuration rather than editing application logic at every location.

An illustrative configuration might look like this:

siteId: pumping-station-014
applicationVersion: 1.8.0
configurationVersion: 12

equipment:
  - assetId: pump-01
    deviceProfile: drive-profile-v3
    connection:
      protocol: modbus_tcp
      host: 192.0.2.10
      port: 502
      unitId: 1

telemetry:
  acquisitionIntervalMs: 2000
  staleAfterMs: 10000

storage:
  maximumQueueBytes: 4000000000

This is an application example, not an Iotellect configuration format.

Validation should check required fields, allowed values, supported device profiles and application compatibility.

A simplified validator could include:

def validate_config(config, release):
    require_nonempty(config.site_id)

    if config.application_version != release.version:
        raise ConfigurationError("Application version mismatch")

    if config.telemetry.stale_after_ms <= 0:
        raise ConfigurationError("Invalid freshness policy")

    for asset in config.equipment:
        if asset.device_profile not in release.supported_profiles:
            raise ConfigurationError("Unsupported device profile")

    return config

Production validation also needs schema checks, permitted operating ranges and appropriate error reporting.

Keep secrets out of ordinary exports. Use references to an appropriate credential-management mechanism.

4. Use Device Profiles to Normalize Equipment

Different equipment can expose the same operational concept through different representations.

One drive may report temperature as an integer requiring scaling. Another may expose a floating-point value.

A profile can map both into a shared measurement:

Source address
→ Data type
→ Scaling
→ Engineering unit
→ Application measurement

Document each profile’s:

  • Supported equipment and revisions.
  • Acquisition behavior.
  • Status mappings.
  • Timestamp origin.
  • Quality handling.
  • Available commands.
  • Confirmation method.

Test profiles against representative equipment. Protocol compatibility alone does not establish that the mapping is correct.

Preserve Observation Context

An application record might contain:

{
  "siteId": "pumping-station-014",
  "assetId": "pump-01",
  "measurement": "motor_temperature",
  "value": 61.7,
  "unit": "degC",
  "sourceTimestamp": "2026-11-18T08:30:00Z",
  "quality": "good",
  "profileVersion": "drive-profile-v3"
}

Preserve acquisition time separately from arrival time. An older observation may belong in history without replacing newer current state.

For platform-specific background, see the documentation on Data Table Timestamps and Quality.

5. Size Hardware against a Representative Workload

Tag count alone is insufficient for sizing an edge node.

Resource consumption also depends on acquisition frequency, protocol behavior, storage, calculations, operator sessions and recovery traffic.

Measure:

  • CPU and memory during normal operation.
  • Storage growth.
  • Dashboard response.
  • Queue growth during an outage.
  • Resource use during replay.
  • Application startup and recovery time.

Estimate raw storage using:

records per second
× average record size
× retention duration

For 50 records per second averaging 200 bytes:

50 × 200 × 86,400
= 864,000,000 bytes per day

That is approximately 864 MB per day, before indexes, logs and storage margin.

Measure the actual footprint and consider storage endurance for continuously writing workloads.

6. Specify Outage Behavior Explicitly

Define which functions must continue when the uplink becomes unavailable.

These may include acquisition, local visualization, approved rule evaluation and historical recording.

Notification delivery is a separate dependency. Local alarm detection can continue while an email or push channel is unavailable.

For buffering, specify:

  • When records become durable.
  • What acknowledgement permits deletion.
  • How repeated deliveries are recognized.
  • Maximum storage consumption.
  • Overflow behavior.
  • Replay rate limits.

Make data loss and queue health visible.

Also define how replay affects rules. Historical observations should not automatically create new live notifications without a documented policy.

7. Treat Updates as Versioned Changes

An application release can change interfaces, mappings, rules and persistent data.

Before deployment, establish:

  1. Supported starting versions.
  2. Configuration compatibility.
  3. Migration requirements.
  4. Backup procedure.
  5. Activation checks.
  6. Rollback conditions.

Start with a representative node or limited deployment group.

After activation, verify acquisition, local access, rules and upstream integration. A running process is only one health signal.

Check Rollback Compatibility

Restoring an older application package may not reverse a data migration.

Confirm whether the previous version can read the resulting configuration and storage format.

Test rollback using realistic runtime data rather than an empty installation.

8. Compare Desired and Reported State

A deployment request does not prove that a node activated the release.

Track intended and reported versions separately:

{
  "nodeId": "edge-014",
  "desiredApplicationVersion": "1.8.0",
  "reportedApplicationVersion": "1.7.3",
  "desiredConfigurationVersion": 12,
  "reportedConfigurationVersion": 11,
  "lastReportedAt": "2026-11-18T08:30:00Z",
  "deploymentStatus": "pending"
}

This is an illustrative record.

Keep report freshness visible. An offline node cannot confirm its current state.

Define how permitted local changes are recorded and reconciled. Otherwise, sites can gradually diverge from the approved deployment without a clear explanation.

9. Build on a Reusable Runtime

Teams can assemble edge applications from separate acquisition, storage, visualization and integration components.

A runtime that combines several responsibilities can reduce the number of independently maintained parts.

Iotellect Edge provides a low-code industrial application runtime for equipment connectivity, local logic, HMI, alarms, history and upstream integration.

The deployment team still needs validated profiles, appropriate hardware, site configuration and tested update procedures.

Document which capabilities are provided by the runtime and which depend on the deployment tooling or project-specific implementation.

Commissioning Checks for Every Installation

Use a repeatable acceptance process.

Verify that:

  • The node has a unique identity and appropriate credentials.
  • Equipment mappings match the installation.
  • Units, scaling and timestamps are correct.
  • Missing and stale data remain distinguishable.
  • Approved rules behave as expected.
  • Required local functions survive an uplink interruption.
  • Buffered data recovers according to policy.
  • Disk limits and queue health are visible.
  • Active application and configuration versions are recorded.
  • Backup and rollback procedures work.

Record exceptions before accepting the site.

A local adjustment that is necessary for operation should become an approved configuration difference or a tracked application change.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can one edge application serve different sites?

Yes, when site differences are represented through supported profiles and validated configuration. Hardware and operating requirements still need testing.

Should credentials be included in a reusable template?

Do not clone node credentials as part of a general application template. Provision identity and access for each installation.

Does local execution guarantee offline operation?

No. Required dependencies must also be available locally, and the node needs adequate resources and uptime.

What should a pilot prove before expansion?

It should demonstrate repeatable installation, configuration, normal operation, outage handling, updates and recovery.

event_model_payload.headline: idl-codegen: عميلان بأنواع محددة لـ TypeScript و Dart من Anchor IDL
event_model_payload.summary:
برنامج Anchor يصف نفسه في ملف IDL: تعليماته (instructions)، وحساباته، وأنواعه، وأحداثه، وأخطاؤه، وبذور (seeds) عناوين الـ PDA. جهة البرنامج تولّدها لك macros الخاصة بـ Anchor. أما جهة العميل (client) فمنها يبدأ العمل اليدوي. على أحدهم أن يكتب الدالة التي تحوّل الوسائط بترميز Borsh، وتضع أمامها الـ discriminator المكوّن من 8 بايتات، وترتّب الحسابات بالترتيب الصحيح مع أعلام signer وwritable الصحيحة، وتشتق عناوين الـ PDA من نفس البذور التي يستعملها البرنامج.

كتابة ذلك مرة واحدة أمر مقبول. لكن كتابته مرتين، بـ TypeScript لتطبيق الويب وبـ Dart لتطبيق Flutter، تعني نسختين يجب أن تبقيا متطابقتين مع البرنامج ومع بعضهما. وبايت واحد خاطئ في إحداهما يعطي معاملة تفشل على السلسلة برسالة خطأ لا تشرح الكثير.

idl-codegen يقرأ ملف Anchor IDL (مواصفة 0.30 وما بعدها) ويكتب العميلين معًا. والـ README يبدأ بتحذير يجب ذكره هنا أيضًا: المشروع لم يخضع لتدقيق أمني. العملاء المولَّدون يبنون التعليمات ويفكّون ترميز الحسابات، ولا يوقّعون ولا يرسلون شيئًا. راجع الكود المولَّد مقابل برنامجك قبل استعماله مع أموال حقيقية، وجرّب على devnet أولًا.

ماذا يقدّم

أمر واحد ينتج مجموعتين من الملفات:

  • TypeScript: الملفان .ts وborsh.ts، ويعتمدان على @solana/web3.js v1.
  • Dart: الملفان .dart وborsh.dart، ويعتمدان على package:crypto، وهما موجّهان لتطبيقات Flutter.

كل عميل يحتوي نفس المكوّنات.

معرّف البرنامج. الثابت PROGRAM_ID في TypeScript وProgramId في Dart.

الأنواع. في TypeScript تحصل على interfaces، وعلى الـ enums في شكل اتحادات { kind: ... }، وعلى دوال encodeX / decodeX. وفي Dart تحصل على أصناف (classes) فيها encode وstatic decode. الـ enums التي بلا بيانات تصبح enum عادية في Dart، والتي تحمل بيانات تصبح أصنافًا من نوع sealed.

بناء التعليمات. الدالة createXInstruction(accounts, args) تُرجع TransactionInstruction في TypeScript. ونسخة Dart تأخذ وسائط مسمّاة وتُرجع Instruction. الحسابات التي لها address ثابت في الـ IDL، مثل System Program، تأخذه كقيمة افتراضية. والحسابات الاختيارية تأخذ معرّف البرنامج كقيمة افتراضية، وهذا عُرف Anchor للتعبير عن "None".

فك ترميز الحسابات. الدالة decodeXAccount(data) تتحقق من الـ discriminator قبل الفك، وفي TypeScript توجد أيضًا isXAccount.

الأحداث (events). الدالة decodeXEvent(data) في اللغتين.

دوال PDA. الدالة findXPda(...seeds) تُولَّد من pda.seeds في الـ IDL: البذور الثابتة، وبذور الحسابات، وبذور الوسائط، وحالات seeds::program مثل حسابات التوكن المرتبطة (ATA). وعميل Dart يأتي بدالة findProgramAddress خاصة به.

الأخطاء والثوابت. في TypeScript: ERRORS وError.fromCode(). وفي Dart: Errors وException.fromCode(). ومعها قيم #[constant] المعرّفة في البرنامج.

تحويل الأنواع يتبع نفس الفكرة في الجهتين: u64 وi64 وu128 وi128 تصبح bigint / BigInt؛ والأعداد الصحيحة الأصغر تصبح number / int؛ وpubkey يصبح PublicKey / Pubkey؛ وbytes يصبح Uint8Array / Uint8List؛ وOption يصبح T | null / T?. أما tuple structs وtuple variants فتصبح values: [...] في TypeScript وfield0, field1 في Dart.

طريقة الاستعمال

تحتاج Node.js 20 أو أحدث. انسخ المستودع وشغّل المولّد من مجلد المشروع:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/idl-codegen
cd idl-codegen
pnpm install
pnpm gen target/idl/my_program.json --ts app/src/generated --dart mobile/lib/generated
# or after `pnpm build`:  node dist/cli.js  --ts  --dart

الوسيط الأول هو ملف الـ IDL الذي كتبه anchor build. والخياران --ts و--dart هما مجلدا الإخراج. كود TypeScript المولَّد يحتاج @solana/web3.js v1 في تطبيقك، وكود Dart المولَّد يحتاج package:crypto.

ثم في تطبيق الويب:

import { createIncrementInstruction, findCounterPda } from "./generated/counter_todo.js";
const [counter] = findCounterPda(wallet.publicKey);
const ix = createIncrementInstruction({ authority: wallet.publicKey, counter }, { by: 1n });

ونفس النداء في تطبيق Flutter:

import 'generated/counter_todo.dart';
final (counter, _) = findCounterPda(authority: me);
final ix = createIncrementInstruction(authority: me, counter: counter, by: BigInt.one);

المقطعان يشتقان نفس الـ PDA ويبنيان نفس بايتات التعليمة. التوقيع والإرسال يبقيان في كودك أنت، بالمحفظة وطبقة الـ RPC التي يستعملها تطبيقك أصلًا.

كيف اختُبر

الكود المولَّد لا ينفع إلا إذا وثقت في البايتات، ولهذا يدور أغلب قسم الاختبارات في الـ README حول هذه النقطة.

  • اختبارات golden. كل IDL في test/fixtures/ يُولَّد ثم يُقارن بايتًا ببايت مع test/golden/. الملفات هي counter_todo وescrow، وهما IDL حقيقيان من مشاريع Anchor مجاورة، وkitchen_sink المكتوب يدويًا ليغطي كل الأنواع: مجموعات حسابات متداخلة، وحسابات اختيارية، وenums تحمل بيانات، وtuple structs، وu128/i128، وf64، ومصفوفات ثابتة الطول، وseeds::program.
  • مترجمات صارمة. كود TypeScript المولَّد يمرّ من tsc --strict، وكود Dart المولَّد يمرّ من dart analyze --fatal-infos. ويُتجاوز فحص Dart إن لم يكن dart موجودًا في الـ PATH.
  • السلوك. دوال PDA تطابق PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync، بما فيها عناوين ATA. بيانات التعليمة هي الـ discriminator متبوعًا بوسائط Borsh. والحسابات تمرّ بدورة encode ثم decode وتعود كما كانت، مع التحقق من الـ discriminator.
  • بين اللغتين. برنامج Dart في test/golden/dart/bin/check.dart يبني نفس التعليمات وعناوين PDA وبايتات الحسابات، والاختبار يتحقق من أن ناتجه يطابق عميل TypeScript بايتًا ببايت.

هذا الفحص الأخير كشف خطأً حقيقيًا. على Dart 3.9 VM كانت الدالة BigInt.modPow تُرجع نتائج خاطئة لبعض المدخلات ذات 255 بت، فتعطّل فحص وقوع النقطة على منحنى ed25519 الذي تعتمد عليه findProgramAddress. لذلك يستعمل كود Dart المولَّد الآن خوارزمية square-and-multiply خاصة به.

ما يجب معرفته

  • غير مدقَّق. العملاء يبنون التعليمات ويفكّون البيانات فقط، لكن تعليمة خاطئة قد تحرّك أموالًا بعد أن توقّعها. قارن الناتج مع برنامجك وجرّبه على devnet أولًا.
  • الأنواع العامة (generics) مرفوضة. الـ IDL الذي يستعمل generics لا يُولَّد منه شيء.
  • بعض بذور PDA تصبح بايتات خام. البذور التي تقرأ بيانات حساب (path: "list.next_id") أو حقلًا من وسيط من نوع struct تتحول إلى وسيط bytes خام. وإن كانت تعليمة أخرى تشتق نفس الحساب من وسيط بسيط، يستعمل المولّد ذلك الشكل الأبسط.
  • coption لم يُختبر مع برنامج حقيقي. هو مدعوم في الترميز وفك الترميز، لا أكثر.
  • ملفات IDL القديمة تحتاج تحويلًا. ملفات IDL السابقة لـ Anchor 0.30 يجب تحويلها أولًا بالأمر anchor idl convert.
  • web3.js v1. ناتج TypeScript موجّه إلى @solana/web3.js v1.

لماذا بنيته

المشكلة هي التكرار. ملف الـ IDL يحتوي أصلًا كل ما يحتاجه العميل: أنواع الوسائط، وترتيب الحسابات، والـ discriminators، والبذور، ورموز الأخطاء. كتابة العميل يدويًا تعني نسخ هذه المعلومات إلى كود، ثم نسخها مرة ثانية عندما يوجد تطبيق موبايل بـ Dart بجانب تطبيق ويب بـ TypeScript. بعدها يجب تكرار كل تغيير في البرنامج في مكانين، ولا شيء ينبّهك عندما يتأخر أحدهما عن الآخر.

توليد العميلين من نفس الـ IDL يلغي خطوة النسخ، ويجعل اختبار أحد الناتجين مقابل الآخر ممكنًا. إذا أنتج عميل TypeScript وعميل Dart نفس البايتات لنفس المدخلات، ووافق عميل TypeScript مكتبة @solana/web3.js في عناوين PDA، يضيق المجال كثيرًا أمام اختلاف صامت. وخطأ BigInt.modPow مثال جيد على قيمة هذه المقارنة: لا شيء في كود Dart كان يبدو خاطئًا، ولم تكشفه إلا مقارنة البايتات.

الكود

المولّد، وملفات الاختبار، وملفات golden، والاختبارات موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/idl-codegen. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

event_model_payload.headline: tx-explainer: اقرأ معاملة Solana بلغة بسيطة
event_model_payload.summary:
العثور على معاملة (transaction) في Solana سهل، لكن قراءتها صعبة. المستكشف (explorer) يعطيك توقيعًا (signature)، وقائمة من مفاتيح الحسابات، وتعليمات (instructions) بياناتها سلسلة من البايتات. لتعرف ما الذي حدث فعلًا، عليك أن تتذكر أن أول بايت في تعليمة Token هو وسم (tag)، وأن المبالغ أعداد صحيحة بترتيب little-endian وبلا فاصلة عشرية، وأن برنامج Anchor يخفي اسم التعليمة خلف discriminator من 8 بايتات.

tx-explainer يقوم بهذه القراءة مكانك. تعطيه توقيعًا، أو بايتات المعاملة الخام، أو ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا في ملف، فيطبع ما فعلته كل تعليمة في جمل بسيطة، ثم الرسوم، ووحدات الحساب (compute units)، وتغيّرات الأرصدة.

هو أداة فك ترميز للقراءة فقط: لا يوقّع ولا يرسل أي شيء أبدًا. والـ README صريح في حدوده: المشروع لم يخضع لتدقيق أمني (not audited)، وهو موجّه أولًا إلى devnet وtestnet وlocalnet، والنص المبسّط اجتهاد قدر الإمكان ولا يغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج.

ماذا يقدّم

هذا ناتج الأداة على معاملة حقيقية من devnet موجودة ضمن ملفات الاختبار:

$ tx-explainer --file test/fixtures/devnet-memo.json
Transaction 5zhK…  [legacy]
Status: succeeded
Fee: 0.0000155 SOL (of which priority ≈ 0.0000105 SOL)
Compute units: 26,021 of 70,000 requested

What happened:
  1. [Compute Budget] Set compute unit limit to 70,000
  2. [Compute Budget] Set priority fee to 150,000 micro-lamports per compute unit
  3. [Associated Token Account] Create (if missing) the associated token account Expy…TCA6 for wallet 6a1w…BNqd and mint 4wMp…jY4y, paid by 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer)
  4. [SPL Token] Transfer 1,236.871165 tokens of mint 4wMp…jY4y from 55Xo…AmDQ to Expy…TCA6 (authority 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer))
  5. [Memo] Memo: "helm-payout-v1:…"

Token balance changes:
  55Xo…AmDQ (owner 2VyJ…TeEs): -1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y
  Expy…TCA6 (owner 6a1w…BNqd): +1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y

البرامج المدمجة. الأداة تعرف البرامج التي تظهر في أغلب المعاملات:

  • System: التعليمات CreateAccount وAssign وTransfer وCreateAccountWithSeed، وعمليات الـ nonce، وAllocate وTransferWithSeed.
  • SPL Token وToken-2022: تهيئة الـ mint والحسابات، وTransfer وTransferChecked، وApprove وRevoke وSetAuthority وMintTo وBurn وCloseAccount وFreeze وThaw وSyncNative وغيرها. أما تعليمات امتدادات Token-2022 فتُذكر برقمها فقط.
  • Associated Token Account: التعليمات Create وCreateIdempotent وRecoverNested.
  • Compute Budget: التعليمات SetComputeUnitLimit وSetComputeUnitPrice وRequestHeapFrame وSetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit.
  • Memo (الإصداران v1 وv2)، ويُعرض كنص UTF-8.

أي برنامج Anchor عبر الـ IDL. مرّر ملف IDL الخاص بالبرنامج بالخيار --idl (صيغة Anchor 0.30 وما بعدها)، فتعرض الأداة اسم التعليمة، والوسائط بعد فك ترميز Borsh (structs وenums وvec وoption والمصفوفات)، وأسماء الحسابات، وأسماء الأخطاء المخصّصة إن فشلت المعاملة.

بيانات الـ RPC الوصفية (metadata). عندما يأتي الإدخال من getTransaction، يضمّ الناتج أيضًا الحالة (مع أسماء أخطاء Anchor)، والرسوم، وتقديرًا لرسوم الأولوية (priority fee) يساوي حد وحدات الحساب × سعر الوحدة، ووحدات الحساب المستهلكة، والتعليمات الداخلية (CPIs)، وتغيّرات رصيد SOL، وتغيّرات أرصدة التوكنات بالخانات العشرية الصحيحة.

رسائل legacy وv0. الصيغتان مدعومتان. عناوين جداول البحث (address lookup tables) تُحلّ من meta.loadedAddresses. وفي الإدخال الخام، حيث لا توجد هذه البيانات، تُعرض بالشكل table[index].

ثلاث طرق للتشغيل. نفس منطق فك الترميز متاح كأداة سطر أوامر (CLI)، وكمكتبة TypeScript، وكواجهة ويب صغيرة تعمل كليًا داخل المتصفح وتتصل مباشرة بالـ RPC العام للشبكة المختارة. يضع الـ README رابطًا لنسخة تجريبية حية من هذه الواجهة: https://abdeldjalilchougui.github.io/tx-explainer/.

طريقة الاستعمال

تحتاج Node.js 20 أو أحدث. انسخ المستودع ثم ابنِه:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer
cd tx-explainer
pnpm install
pnpm build

ثم شغّل الـ CLI من مجلد المشروع:

node dist/cli.js <signature> --cluster devnet           # fetch via getTransaction
node dist/cli.js <signature> --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899
node dist/cli.js --raw <base64-or-base58 tx bytes>      # offline, no metadata
node dist/cli.js --file saved-getTransaction.json --idl target/idl/my_program.json
node dist/cli.js ... --json                             # machine-readable
node dist/cli.js serve --port 8787                      # web UI on 127.0.0.1

الشكلان الأولان يجلبان المعاملة من شبكة أو من الـ validator المحلي. الخيار --raw يعمل بلا اتصال على بايتات بصيغة base64 أو base58. والخيار --file يقرأ ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا، وهذا مفيد في تقارير الأخطاء والاختبارات. أما --json فيعطي نفس الشرح كبيانات منظّمة يستطيع سكربت أن يقرأها.

وكمكتبة، ثلاث دوال تغطي الحالة الشائعة:

import { explain, render, fetchTransaction } from "tx-explainer";
const e = explain({ rpc: await fetchTransaction(sig, "https://api.devnet.solana.com") }, { idls: [myIdl] });
console.log(render(e));

الدالة fetchTransaction تجلب المعاملة، وexplain تبني الشرح المنظّم، وrender تحوّله إلى النص الذي رأيته في الأعلى.

كيف يعمل من الداخل

يصف الـ README أربع وحدات صغيرة، ومعرفة هذا التقسيم تفيدك إن أردت إضافة decoder جديد:

  1. الملف message.ts يحلّل صيغة الإرسال (wire format) يدويًا: أطوال compact-u16، والتواقيع، وترويسة الرسالة، ومفاتيح الحسابات، والتعليمات المجمّعة، وجداول البحث في v0. ثم يستنتج من الترويسة إن كان كل مفتاح موقّعًا (signer) أو قابلًا للكتابة (writable).
  2. الملف programs.ts فيه decoder صغير لكل برنامج مدمج. كل واحد يقرأ وسم التعليمة (u32 في System وu8 في Token) وحقولها بواسطة Reader يعمل بترتيب little-endian.
  3. الملف anchor.ts يقارن أول 8 بايتات من بيانات التعليمة مع الـ discriminator لكل تعليمة في الـ IDL، ثم يفك ترميز الوسائط بـ Borsh انطلاقًا من شجرة الأنواع في الـ IDL.
  4. الملف explain.ts يجمع كل ذلك مع بيانات الـ RPC: أرصدة التوكنات تعطي الـ mint وعدد الخانات العشرية، والتعليمات الداخلية تعطي الـ CPIs، والأرصدة قبل وبعد تعطي الفروقات.

ما يجب معرفته

  • غير مدقَّق، والناتج اجتهاد. الجمل وسيلة مساعدة لقراءة المعاملة. لا تغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج، ولا ينبغي أن تبني عليها وحدها قرارًا يخص أموالًا حقيقية.
  • امتدادات Token-2022 تُعرض برقمها فقط. رسوم التحويل، والتحويلات السرّية، وباقي تعليمات الامتدادات لا تُحوَّل إلى جمل.
  • بعض البرامج يُذكر اسمها فقط. تعليمات Stake وVote وAddress Lookup Table والـ loader تُعرَّف بالاسم دون فك ترميزها.
  • رسوم الأولوية تقديرية. تُحسب بالصيغة ceil(limit × price / 1e6). وإن لم تحدّد المعاملة حدًّا، تفترض الأداة القيمة الافتراضية: 200 ألف وحدة حساب لكل تعليمة.
  • الإدخال الخام بلا بيانات وصفية. مع --raw لا توجد حالة ولا رسوم ولا تغيّرات أرصدة ولا تعليمات داخلية، لأن هذه المعلومات تأتي من الـ RPC وليس من بايتات المعاملة.
  • ما تم اختباره. الأمر pnpm test يستعمل فقط ملفات محفوظة في test/fixtures/. أربع منها معاملات اصطناعية يبنيها سكربت بمكتبة @solana/web3.js من مفاتيح عامة ثابتة. تُترك بلا توقيع، فلا يُنشأ أي keypair، وتحمل بيانات وصفية مكتوبة يدويًا: تحويل SOL مع memo وcompute budget، وإنشاء ATA مع TransferChecked وCPIs، وعملية mint بـ Token-2022 عبر lookup table في رسالة v0، ونداء Anchor فاشل. والخامسة معاملة حقيقية واحدة من devnet، التُقطت مرة واحدة عبر RPC للقراءة فقط.

لماذا بنيته

العرض الخام للمعاملة يجيب عن سؤال "ما البايتات التي أُرسلت"، بينما السؤال الذي يطرحه الناس هو "ما الذي حدث". الانتقال من الأول إلى الثاني يعني فك وسوم التعليمات، وقسمة مبالغ التوكنات على الخانات العشرية للـ mint، ومطابقة الـ discriminators في Anchor مع الـ IDL، وقراءة التعليمات الداخلية وفروقات الأرصدة من البيانات الوصفية. كل خطوة بسيطة، لكن تكرارها يدويًا مع كل معاملة بطيء، ومن السهل أن تخطئ في قراءة مبلغ.

أردت أداة واحدة تقوم بهذه الخطوات بنفس الطريقة في كل مرة، وتعمل على validator محلي كما تعمل على devnet، وتعمل بلا اتصال على البايتات الخام، ويمكن استعمالها من الطرفية (terminal) أو من الكود أو من تبويب في المتصفح. وتحليل صيغة الإرسال يدويًا، بدل إخفائها خلف مكتبة كبيرة، يُبقي الكود صغيرًا يمكن قراءته وتوسيعه.

الكود

الكود، وملفات الاختبار، والاختبارات، وواجهة الويب موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها، خصوصًا إضافة decoders للبرامج التي يُذكر اسمها فقط حاليًا.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

event_model_payload.headline: Top Automation Testing Courses for Senior Testers Moving Into Test Lead Roles: Projects, Frameworks and Class Format
event_model_payload.summary:
Senior testers preparing for test lead roles should choose automation testing courses that teach framework architecture, real-world project execution, CI/CD integration, and test strategy—not just scripting. Five options worth comparing are Simplilearn, StarAgile, Rahul Shetty Academy, KnowledgeHut, and Test Automation University. Simplilearn and StarAgile offer structured live training, Rahul Shetty Academy emphasizes technical depth, KnowledgeHut focuses on Agile automation strategy, and Test Automation University provides flexible self-paced learning.

The right course depends on your current automation experience, preferred class format, and readiness to manage quality across a team.

Why Senior Testers Need Advanced Automation Testing Skills

Moving from senior software tester to test lead involves more than learning Selenium or creating automated test scripts.

A senior tester typically executes test cases, identifies defects, maintains test scripts, and contributes to release quality. A test lead must also decide what to automate, establish framework standards, assign responsibilities, and communicate testing risks.

The most valuable automation testing courses for experienced professionals should develop five capabilities:

  • Framework architecture: Designing reusable, scalable, and maintainable automation solutions.
  • Automation strategy: Selecting appropriate tests based on business risk, execution frequency, and maintenance costs.
  • CI/CD integration: Connecting automated regression suites with development pipelines.
  • Project leadership: Reviewing automation code, mentoring junior testers, and coordinating testing activities.
  • Quality reporting: Measuring test reliability, coverage, execution performance, and defect trends.

A course that combines technical implementation with these responsibilities provides a stronger foundation for test leadership.

Top 5 Automation Testing Courses for Senior Testers

1. Simplilearn – Automation Testing Master's Program

Best for: Senior testers seeking comprehensive automation engineering training.

Simplilearn offers an automation testing program covering functional testing, API testing, performance testing, and AI-assisted testing. Its structured curriculum makes it suitable for experienced testers who want exposure to multiple automation technologies before assuming broader technical responsibilities.

Projects: The program includes practical assignments and capstone projects involving e-commerce, healthcare, and airline-booking applications. Learners work on functional automation and related testing workflows.

Frameworks: Topics include Selenium, Java, TestNG, Maven, REST Assured, Postman, JMeter, and Playwright-related learning modules.

Class format: Live online instructor-led sessions are combined with self-paced material, giving working professionals opportunities for structured learning and independent practice.

Test lead relevance: The broad curriculum helps learners understand how different testing approaches fit into an overall quality strategy.

Consideration: Senior testers should confirm how much training involves framework architecture, code reviews, and test leadership rather than introductory material.

2. StarAgile – Software and Automation Testing Certification Training

Best for: Senior testers seeking hands-on framework development with live instruction.

StarAgile offers software and automation testing training that combines programming, automation frameworks, practical assignments, and capstone projects. Its curriculum is relevant to experienced testers who want to strengthen their technical capabilities before taking responsibility for automation delivery.

Projects: Published examples include flight-booking automation, an e-commerce framework using Selenium and TestNG, and a telecom API automation framework.

Frameworks: The curriculum covers Selenium WebDriver, Java, Maven, TestNG, Page Object Model, Cucumber BDD, Selenium Grid, and REST Assured.

Class format: Live online instructor-led classes are supported by practical assignments, mentoring, and selected self-paced modules.

Test lead relevance: Framework implementation and multi-domain projects provide opportunities to practise automation design and understand testing workflows.

Consideration: Learners should verify whether their selected batch includes advanced architecture reviews, CI/CD implementation, and team-level automation planning.

3. Rahul Shetty Academy – Java SDET Automation Package

Best for: Experienced testers seeking deeper framework engineering skills.

Rahul Shetty Academy provides a Java-focused automation learning package covering web testing, API automation, mobile testing, and framework design. It is particularly relevant to testers who already understand testing fundamentals but need stronger programming and automation architecture knowledge.

Projects: Training includes practical web, API, and mobile automation exercises designed around real-world testing scenarios and reusable implementation patterns.

Frameworks: Key technologies include Selenium WebDriver, Java, TestNG, JUnit, Maven, Cucumber, REST Assured, and Appium.

Class format: The package is self-paced, allowing professionals to follow the learning sequence independently and revisit technical lessons when necessary.

Test lead relevance: Its design-pattern and framework-focused content can help testers establish coding standards and review automation solutions.

Consideration: Learners seeking structured mentoring, live feedback, or dedicated people-management training may require additional resources.

4. KnowledgeHut – Certified Professional Automation Agile Testing

Best for: Senior testers transitioning toward Agile test leadership responsibilities.

KnowledgeHut offers Certified Professional Automation Agile Testing (CP-AAT) training that emphasizes automation planning within Agile delivery. The course is relevant to experienced testers who already possess technical knowledge and want to make better decisions about automation strategy.

Projects: Practical activities include Agile testing case studies, acceptance-test design, BDD exercises, and collaborative problem-solving based on realistic testing situations.

Frameworks: Topics include TDD, ATDD, BDD, Cucumber, Gherkin, Selenium, JUnit, Maven, and Jenkins integration concepts.

Class format: The provider describes a two-day live instructor-led program featuring group activities, interactive discussions, and practical exercises.

Test lead relevance: The focus on testing strategy, risk assessment, and automation decisions closely matches responsibilities associated with test leadership.

Consideration: The short format is better suited to strategic development than building a comprehensive automation framework from scratch.

5. Test Automation University – Advanced Automation Learning Paths

Best for: Senior testers seeking flexible, specialized automation upskilling.

Test Automation University provides free online courses covering software test automation technologies and engineering practices. Its individual courses allow experienced professionals to strengthen specific skills without committing to a longer classroom-based certification program.

Projects: Practical exercises are available through selected courses, including Playwright-based test development, API interaction, test data management, and continuous integration activities.

Frameworks: Learning topics include Selenium, Playwright, API automation, Page Object patterns, CI/CD practices, and visual testing techniques.

Class format: Courses are self-paced, enabling learners to study independently and select modules according to existing knowledge and professional requirements.

Test lead relevance: Specialized courses can help senior testers evaluate modern frameworks and guide technical improvements within their teams.

Consideration: Learners must organize their own learning pathway and independently develop broader leadership and project-management capabilities.

Quick Comparison: Projects, Frameworks and Class Format

Course provider Primary focus Project approach Class format
Simplilearn End-to-end automation engineering Multi-domain capstone projects Live online + self-paced
StarAgile Applied framework development Web, API, and business application projects Live online + supplementary self-study
Rahul Shetty Academy Advanced Java automation Web, API, and mobile framework exercises Self-paced
KnowledgeHut Agile automation strategy Case studies and collaborative exercises Live instructor-led
Test Automation University Specialized technical upskilling Course-specific coding exercises Self-paced

These programs are not identical substitutes. They differ in technical depth, duration, instructor interaction, and leadership-oriented content.

Which Automation Frameworks Should Future Test Leads Master?

Senior testers do not need expertise in every automation tool. However, they should understand how to select and maintain frameworks that align with their organization's applications and development practices.

Selenium with TestNG or JUnit

Selenium remains relevant for automating web application testing. TestNG and JUnit support test organization, assertions, and execution management.

Test leads should understand how to build reusable test components, introduce parallel execution, and reduce maintenance overhead.

Playwright

Playwright supports modern browser automation and can be used with programming languages including JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, Python, and .NET.

It is useful for teams developing modern web applications that need reliable browser testing and integration with automated delivery pipelines.

Cucumber and BDD

Cucumber enables teams to describe expected application behavior using structured scenarios.

For test leads, the objective is not simply writing Gherkin files. It is improving communication between testers, developers, product owners, and business stakeholders.

REST Assured and API Automation

API testing helps identify defects before they appear in end-to-end user workflows.

Test leads should understand API validation, authentication, test data, negative scenarios, and the balance between API and UI coverage.

Jenkins and CI/CD Tools

Automation becomes more valuable when tests execute consistently within delivery pipelines.

A future test lead should be able to establish test execution policies, evaluate failures, and determine which tests belong in pull-request, nightly, and release-validation pipelines.

Three Practical Projects That Prepare Testers for Lead Roles

Course completion alone does not demonstrate readiness to lead testing activities. Senior professionals should develop portfolio projects that reflect architectural and management decisions.

Project 1: Enterprise E-Commerce Automation Framework

Build a reusable framework covering authentication, product search, checkout, and payment-related test scenarios.

Include Page Object components, test data management, parallel execution, reporting, and source control.

Leadership deliverable: Document framework standards, code review rules, and a regression maintenance plan.

Project 2: API Automation and CI/CD Pipeline

Create API tests for customer registration, account updates, authentication, and error handling.

Integrate the suite with Jenkins or another CI/CD platform and configure reports for failed executions.

Leadership deliverable: Define quality gates, execution schedules, and procedures for investigating failed builds.

Project 3: Automation Strategy for an Agile Team

Prepare an automation roadmap for a hypothetical application with limited testing resources.

Identify high-risk workflows, calculate automation priorities, and assign responsibilities across the testing team.

Leadership deliverable: Present an automation strategy containing milestones, estimated effort, maintenance ownership, and measurable outcomes.

These projects demonstrate the ability to plan, implement, and govern automation—not merely execute scripts.

How to Choose the Right Class Format

Live instructor-led courses are useful when learners want scheduled sessions, feedback, discussions, and support while developing automation skills.

Self-paced courses suit senior testers who already possess coding experience and need targeted learning around specific tools or frameworks.

Blended courses combine instructor interaction with independent learning and can work well for professionals balancing work and training.

Before enrolling, ask whether the program provides live code reviews, reusable project repositories, practical assessments, mentor access, and recordings. Confirm the current syllabus, schedule, fees, and exact certification awarded.

How to Measure Readiness for a Test Lead Role

After training, evaluate your progress against five practical outcomes:

  1. Framework ownership: Can you design a maintainable framework and explain its architectural choices?
  2. Test strategy: Can you prioritize automation based on risk, business value, and maintenance effort?
  3. Pipeline integration: Can you explain test failures, configure execution stages, and manage unreliable tests?
  4. Team guidance: Can you review scripts, establish standards, and mentor other testers?
  5. Reporting: Can you communicate release risks and test results clearly to engineering stakeholders?

Strong performance across these areas provides more meaningful evidence of leadership readiness than a certificate alone.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which automation testing course is best for senior testers becoming test leads?

The best choice depends on existing experience. Simplilearn and StarAgile are options for structured, project-based training. Rahul Shetty Academy supports deeper framework engineering, while KnowledgeHut emphasizes Agile automation planning. Test Automation University is useful for independent specialization.

Is Selenium enough to become a test lead?

No. Selenium is valuable for browser automation, but a test lead must also understand API testing, framework maintainability, CI/CD, test strategy, team coordination, and quality reporting.

Do senior testers need coding skills for test lead roles?

Coding proficiency is helpful, especially when reviewing automation frameworks, diagnosing failures, and mentoring automation engineers. The required depth varies by organization and whether the role is primarily technical or managerial.

Are live classes better than recorded automation testing courses?

Live classes can provide immediate feedback and structured accountability. Recorded courses offer flexibility and repeated access to technical material. Neither is automatically superior; project quality and practical application matter more.

Can automation testing certification guarantee a promotion?

No. Certification demonstrates learning but does not guarantee advancement. Employers also evaluate technical judgment, project ownership, communication skills, mentoring capability, and delivery experience.

Final Thoughts

The best automation testing courses for senior testers moving into test lead roles are those that develop both technical and decision-making skills.

Simplilearn, StarAgile, Rahul Shetty Academy, KnowledgeHut, and Test Automation University offer different learning approaches. Choose according to the gaps in your existing skills rather than provider popularity alone.

Ultimately, test leadership is about building reliable quality processes, guiding teams, and making informed automation decisions. A strong course provides the foundation, while practical project ownership turns those skills into leadership capability.

event_model_payload.headline: Our tests imported the repository and passed while the package we deployed was missing eleven templates
event_model_payload.summary:
Our label service is a Python package that turns a consignment into a carrier label. Every carrier zone has a JSON template, and the package ships them inside itself, under labels/templates. setup.py listed them with package_data and the pattern templates/*.json, which had been right since the first carrier.

In September we added the Highlands and Islands zones for a carrier that prices them separately, and the engineer put the eleven new templates in a subfolder, templates/zones. The tests for all eleven passed in CI. The pipeline built a wheel, the image installed it, and the first Highlands label in production failed with FileNotFoundError. Ninety two parcels for Inverness and Skye waited on the dock until the afternoon.

The pattern was easy to blame once we looked. templates/*.json matches files directly inside templates and nothing in a folder below it, so the wheel held every old template and none of the new ones. setup.py did exactly what it said.

The real question was why CI had been green. Our tests ran with python -m pytest from the root of the checkout, and that puts the current directory first on sys.path. import labels found the folder in the repository, holding every file anyone had committed, before it could find anything installed. For four years we had tested the source tree. The wheel that production ran had never been imported by a single test.

We moved the code under src/, so the package cannot be imported from the repository root at all and the tests have to use an installed copy. CI now builds the wheel once, installs it into a clean virtual environment, runs the suite against that, and puts the same file into the image. A short step lists every file under templates in the repository and fails the build if any of them is missing from the wheel. The package_data pattern now covers subfolders, but the check is what we trust.

A green run tells you about the code your tests imported. Ours imported the repository, and we shipped a package.

– Sergey Shinder

event_model_payload.headline: Network Security Basics Every Developer Should Know
event_model_payload.summary:
Most developers spend their time on code, but a weak network can undo all of that work. A leaked port, an unpatched router, or a shared Wi-Fi password can give someone a way in, no matter how clean your app is.

Here are the network security basics every developer should have covered. At ZIA Networks, these are the first things we look at when reviewing a setup.

1. Know what is exposed

You can't protect what you can't see. On a network or machine you own, check which ports are open:

nmap -sV your-server-ip

Only scan systems you own or have written permission to test. If you see a port open and you don't know why, that's your first thing to investigate.

2. Close everything you don't need

Default deny is a good rule. Allow only the traffic you actually use. On a Linux server with ufw:

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable

Check the result with:

sudo ufw status verbose

3. Lock down SSH

SSH is one of the most attacked services on the internet. A few small changes help a lot. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config:

PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no

Use key-based login instead of passwords, then restart the service:

sudo systemctl restart ssh

Make sure your key login works in a second terminal before you close your current session, so you don't lock yourself out.

4. Keep everything updated

Operating systems, routers, firewalls, and packages all need regular updates. Many real attacks use bugs that already have a fix.

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

5. Don't trust the network by default

Use HTTPS everywhere, even on internal tools. Keep dev, staging, and production separate, and don't reuse the same credentials across them.

6. Keep secrets out of your code

API keys and passwords don't belong in your repo. Use environment variables or a secrets manager, and rotate keys if one is ever exposed.

7. Log and monitor

If nobody is watching, an attack can run for days. Keep logs, set alerts for unusual logins, and review them regularly.

8. Test your backups

A backup you've never restored is only a hope. Do a test restore from time to time.

Quick checklist

  • [ ] Open ports reviewed
  • [ ] Firewall set to deny by default
  • [ ] SSH uses keys, root login off
  • [ ] Updates applied
  • [ ] Secrets out of the repo
  • [ ] Logs and alerts on
  • [ ] Backup restore tested

Wrapping up

None of this is complicated, but it does need to be done consistently. If you'd rather have an expert look over your setup, ZIA Networks helps businesses build and maintain secure, reliable networks with clear advice and dependable support.

What's one network security habit you wish you'd started sooner? Share it in the comments. 👇

event_model_payload.headline: AI companies pay billions for this data. I give it away for free.
event_model_payload.summary:
There is one thing AI companies want right now more than chips.

Data. Not any data. Recordings of coding that actually worked. Meta put 14 billion dollars into Scale AI. A company that sells training data. Not models. Data. And right now, Mercor pays engineers 80 to 200 dollars an hour to sit down and record real coding work for AI labs.

That is the food. It is real, it is rare, and it sits behind a paywall. I make that food. And I give it away. MIT license, Zero dollars, No signup.

Receipts: Meta's data deal and Mercor's own rates page.

What the food actually is

Not code. Not diffs. The whole work session.

A ticket. An agent reading a real repo. Tool calls. A test that fails. The fix. The retry. The pass. Every step in order. Every terminal output exactly as the tool said it. The AI world calls this a trajectory. I call it the struggle. A diff shows the answer. The struggle shows how someone got there. Models learn from the struggle.

Right now: 66 recordings. 2,541 real tool calls. Five real repos you already use: click, attrs, packaging, tenacity, cli.

"Free data is usually trash." Fair. Here is the difference.

  1. Everything ran for real, in a sandbox. No invented outputs. Ever.
  2. The answer was not in the room. I erase the git history, so the agent can not peek at the human fix.
  3. The tests are locked. The agent can not edit them to cheat.
  4. A recording ships only if the tests pass and the work stands next to the real human fix.
  5. The mistakes stay in. 60 failed runs, kept in order, with the fixes after them. Most sellers hide the mistakes. The mistakes are the lesson.
  6. You can check me. One command verifies all 66 files on your machine.

And this week I audited my own data. Found one bad episode. I did not delete it. I labeled it, locked it out of the training lists, and published the full report. Every flaw, in the open.

Show me a data seller who does that.

I said I would sell this. I changed my mind.

Some of you read my old post. I said this data was for sale. Here is why it is not.

The big labs trained on your code for free. Your repos, your posts, your answers. Then the cleaned up version got a price tag in the billions. I think the food should flow both ways. So the data is free. For the kid training a model on a free GPU. For the one person lab. For you.

And my selfish reason, straight up: a paywall with zero users is worth zero. I want people to train on it, break it, and tell me the numbers. That is worth more to me than money right now. The factory stays mine. The food is yours.

The numbers I promised, including the ugly ones

My last post promised real test numbers. Here they are. I trained a small Qwen model on this data. On my own test, correct tool calls went from 43% to 80%. Then the rest of my tests showed other scores got worse. But that was my engineering problem. Not a data issue.

I could have hidden that. Then I would be every other data seller. So it is in the README. I rebuilt the training pipeline and started retraining. No clean win yet.

And yes, 66 is small. One research team got a 47% jump on a tool use test from just 239 recordings. A little real data beats a mountain of fake data. And the factory does not sleep.

It is just there

I am not going to beg you to use it. It is just there. A door left open.

git clone https://github.com/Sumama-Jameel/megabit-trajectories.git
cd megabit-trajectories
python3 verify.py

That last line checks all 66 recordings. If it says 66/66, you have exactly what I published. Byte for byte. It ships in OpenAI chat format, with converters for other formats included.

Repo: https://github.com/Sumama-Jameel/megabit-trajectories

Train on it. Report the numbers. Even the bad ones. Especially the bad ones.

One last thing

Last time I opened a free door to 75 models. Models eat data. This is the free food. They trained on your code for free. Now training data sells for billions.

Should this food be free for everyone, or is selling it fair? Pick a side. I will be down there.

event_model_payload.headline: Fixing Silent Misconfigurations in GitLab Runner: Adding Concurrency Alias Support
event_model_payload.summary:
When operating self-hosted or cloud infrastructure for CI/CD pipelines, one subtle configuration mistake can cause unexpected resource exhaustion or build instability.

In my recent contribution to GitLab Runner (MR !7782), I solved a long-standing developer trap related to TOML configuration parsing that previously led to runners processing unlimited parallel jobs unintentionally.

Here is the story of how a small alias mapping prevents critical operational failures in production CI/CD environments.

The Problem: The "Concurrency" Trap

GitLab CI/CD documentation and community discussions frequently use the word "concurrency" to describe how many jobs a runner or worker pool can execute simultaneously. Furthermore, within a runner's specific configuration, settings like request_concurrency already use that exact terminology.

Consequently, DevOps engineers and system administrators frequently wrote:

concurrent = 1

[[runners]]
  name = "docker-runner"
  url = "https://gitlab.com"
  concurrency = 1  # ⚠️ Expected: Only run 1 job at a time
  executor = "docker"

Or at the global level:

concurrency = 4    # ⚠️ Expected: Maximum 4 global concurrent jobs

What actually happened?

Under the hood, GitLab Runner uses BurntSushi/toml to unmarshal config.toml into Go structs. Because Go struct tags strictly mapped:

  • concurrent to global Config.Concurrent
  • limit to runner-level RunnerConfig.Limit

Any key named concurrency was silently ignored without raising an error or warning!

Because limit defaulted to its zero value (0), and 0 in GitLab Runner represents unlimited, a runner meant to strictly execute one build at a time would suddenly pick up and run dozens of jobs in parallel. This often resulted in Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, CPU throttling, and failed deployments.

The Solution: Intelligent Alias Fallback

In Merge Request !7782, we implemented alias handling during configuration loading:

  1. Global Level: If concurrent is not set but concurrency is present in the configuration, concurrency is mapped directly to Config.Concurrent.
  2. Runner Level ([[runners]]): If limit is not explicitly set, concurrency is mapped directly to RunnerConfig.Limit.
  3. 100% Backward Compatibility: Canonical keys (concurrent and limit) take priority if both are specified, ensuring existing configurations remain unaffected. 
# Now fully supported and safe!
concurrency = 4

[[runners]]
  name = "production-runner"
  url = "https://gitlab.com"
  concurrency = 1   # Enforces single-job execution as expected
  executor = "docker"

Verifying with Table-Driven Tests in Go

To ensure this fallback works reliably across all combinations of configurations, we added comprehensive table-driven tests (TestLoadConfig_ConcurrencyAlias):

  • Scenario A: Only concurrency specified at root level → Maps to Concurrent.
  • Scenario B: Only concurrency specified in [[runners]] → Maps to Limit.
  • Scenario C: Both concurrent/limit and concurrency present → Canonical fields take precedence.
  • Scenario D: Unset values retain their standard defaults. 
go test -v ./common -run '^TestLoadConfig_ConcurrencyAlias$'

All test cases pass cleanly, safeguarding runner stability across minor and major upgrades.

Key Takeaways

  1. Developer UX matters in Infra Configs: If operators commonly guess a configuration key based on natural naming conventions or documentation phrasing, supporting it as an alias eliminates dangerous failure modes.
  2. Beware of Silent Unmarshaling: When unmarshaling TOML/YAML/JSON in Go, unused fields don't always produce syntax errors, which can leave critical limits at their uninitialized zero values.
  3. Open Source Contribution: Small, well-targeted improvements can resolve issues open for years (Issue #4793) and prevent real-world production outages.

Check out the merged implementation on GitLab:

👉 GitLab Runner MR !7782

Author: Manish Kumar

GitLab: @manishpatel00

event_model_payload.headline: 컨테이너처럼 쓰고, VM처럼 격리하기 4편 - IB 네트워크와 로컬 NVMe, vCPU 배치, 베어메탈 대비 성능
event_model_payload.summary:
3편에서는 Fabric Manager가 NVLink로 묶어 주는 GPU 조합인 fabric partition(이하 '파티션')을 DRA(동적 리소스 할당)로 할당하고 VM에 연결했습니다. 학습 작업을 실행하려면 GPU뿐 아니라 다른 서버와 IB(InfiniBand)로 통신할 NIC(network interface card), 모델과 데이터를 읽고 쓸 로컬 스토리지도 필요합니다.

이 연재는 다음과 같이 구성됩니다.

  • 1편: 컨테이너와 VM의 차이, Kata Containers의 Pod 실행 구조
  • 2편: GPU 패스스루 계층과 GPU 8장 VM의 부팅·메모리 구성
  • 3편: Fabric Manager 파티션과 DRA를 이용한 GPU 할당
  • 4편: IB 네트워크와 로컬 NVMe, vCPU 배치, 베어메탈 대비 성능

먼저 IB NIC와 로컬 NVMe를 VM에 연결하면서 겪은 문제를 살펴보고, 이어서 vCPU를 호스트 CPU에 잘못 배치해 생긴 문제와 해결 방법을 다룹니다. 끝으로 사용자가 작성하는 Pod YAML과 베어메탈 대비 성능을 정리합니다.

VM 안에서 IB 네트워크 쓰기

VM 안의 GPU가 다른 서버의 GPU와 데이터를 주고받으려면 무엇이 필요할까요? 분산 학습은 스텝마다 수 GB의 그레이디언트(gradient)를 서버 사이에서 주고받습니다. TCP 소켓으로 보내면 요청마다 시스템 콜과 커널 소켓 버퍼 복사를 거치므로 그 처리 시간이 학습 시간에 더해집니다.

서버 사이의 GPU 통신과 RDMA

RDMA(remote direct memory access)에서는 애플리케이션이 메모리 영역을 미리 등록하고 그 주소와 접근 키를 상대 서버와 교환해 둡니다. 그러면 NIC는 CPU와 커널 네트워크 스택을 거치지 않고, 등록된 메모리에서 데이터를 읽어 상대 서버의 등록된 메모리에 직접 씁니다. 저희 환경에서는 IB 네트워크로 RDMA를 사용합니다.

일반 RDMA가 다루는 대상은 호스트 메모리이므로 GPU의 데이터를 보내려면 먼저 호스트 메모리로 복사해야 합니다. GPUDirect RDMA(이하 'GDR')에서는 NIC가 GPU 메모리의 BAR(Base Address Register) 영역을 DMA(direct memory access)로 읽고 쓸 수 있어 이 복사가 필요 없습니다. NCCL(NVIDIA Collective Communications Library)은 GPU와 NIC가 가까이 연결되어 있으면 이 경로를 사용합니다.

IB NIC를 VM에 연결하기

호스트에서 RDMA를 사용할 때는 /dev/infiniband 아래의 장치 파일을 엽니다. 하지만 이 파일은 호스트 커널의 드라이버에 접근하는 인터페이스이므로 VM 안에서는 쓸 수 없습니다. 따라서 VM의 GPU로 RDMA 통신을 하려면 IB NIC 자체를 게스트에 연결해야 했습니다.

GPU와 같은 방식으로 NIC를 vfio-pci에 바인딩한 뒤 VFIO(Virtual Function I/O)로 게스트에 연결했습니다. 게스트에서도 NIC를 사용할 수 있도록 커널에 mlx5와 IB 드라이버를 넣어 빌드했습니다.

다만 NIC도 GPU처럼 한 번에 VM 하나에만 연결할 수 있습니다. B200 서버에는 GPU마다 짝지어진 컴퓨트 NIC 8개와 스토리지 네트워크용 NIC 2개가 있습니다. 컴퓨트 NIC는 GPU와 1:1로 짝지어 있어 그대로 연결하면 되지만, 스토리지 NIC는 2개뿐이라 VM 8개에 하나씩 연결할 수 없었습니다. 그래서 스토리지 NIC에는 SR-IOV를 적용했습니다.

NIC 하나를 여러 VM에서 쓰는 SR-IOV

SR-IOV(Single Root I/O Virtualization)를 켜면 물리 기능인 PF(Physical Function)가 가상 기능인 VF(Virtual Function)를 여러 개 만듭니다. VF마다 PCI 주소와 IOMMU(input-output memory management unit) 그룹이 따로 있으므로 각각 vfio-pci에 바인딩해 서로 다른 VM에 연결할 수 있습니다. 다만 같은 PF에서 만든 VF들은 대역폭을 나누어 쓰게 됩니다.

NIC 펌웨어에서 SR-IOV를 켠 뒤 sysfs에 필요한 개수를 쓰면 VF가 만들어집니다. 저희는 이 작업을 노드 설정 과정에 넣어 두었습니다. 아래 명령은 root로 실행합니다.

# 스토리지 NIC 하나에 VF 8개 생성
$ echo 8 > /sys/class/infiniband/mlx5_2/device/sriov_numvfs

$ cat /sys/class/infiniband/mlx5_2/device/sriov_numvfs
8

$ lspci -d 15b3: | grep -c 'Virtual Function'
8

생성한 VF는 lspci에서 장치 이름에 Virtual Function이 붙은 Mellanox NIC로 나타납니다. 정리하면, 저희 환경에서는 컴퓨트 NIC는 PF를 통째로, 스토리지 NIC는 VF로 나누어 연결합니다.

NIC 용도 연결 방식
컴퓨트 NIC(PF 8개) NCCL 통신 PF 전체를 VM에 연결
스토리지 NIC(PF 2개) 스토리지 네트워크 SR-IOV로 PF마다 VF 8개를 만들고 VM에 PF별 VF 1개씩 연결. VF의 포트 GUID(포트를 식별하는 64비트 ID)는 별도 커널 모듈로 설정

VM 크기별로 받는 NIC는 다음과 같습니다.

  • GPU 1장 VM: 컴퓨트 PF 1개, 스토리지 VF 2개
  • GPU 4장 VM: 컴퓨트 PF 4개, 스토리지 VF 2개

게스트에서는 PF와 VF 모두 mlx5_0 같은 일반 RDMA 장치로 보이기 때문에 PCIe 위치만으로 컴퓨트용인지 스토리지용인지 구분할 수 없습니다. 그래서 DRA 드라이버가 각 포트가 속한 IB 네트워크의 SM(subnet manager) GUID로 컴퓨트용과 스토리지용을 나누어 발행합니다.

GPU와 가까운 NIC 고르기

NIC를 VM에 연결하자 RDMA 통신은 가능해졌습니다. 하지만 B200 서버 2대의 GPU 16장으로 NCCL all_reduce를 실행했을 때 버스 대역폭(busbw)은 158GB/s에 그쳤습니다. 이 절에서 설명할 수정을 모두 적용한 뒤에는 약 700GB/s가 나왔습니다.

게스트에서 보이지 않는 PCIe 연결 구조

가장 큰 원인은 GPU와 NIC의 PCIe 연결 구조(topology)였습니다. 이 서버에서는 PCIe 스위치마다 GPU 하나와 컴퓨트 NIC 하나가 함께 연결되어 있습니다(2편의 서버 물리 구성 그림 참고). 같은 스위치의 NIC를 쓰면 경로가 짧지만 다른 스위치의 NIC를 쓰면 루트 컴플렉스까지 올라갔다 내려와야 하고, 경우에 따라 소켓 사이 연결도 지납니다. 그래서 NCCL은 실행되는 시스템의 sysfs에서 PCIe 트리를 읽고 GPU마다 같은 스위치에 연결된 NIC를 고릅니다.

문제는 Kata Containers(이하 'kata') 게스트의 PCIe 트리에 호스트의 스위치 구조가 나타나지 않는다는 점이었습니다. 2편에서 본 것처럼 콜드 플러그된 GPU와 NIC는 각각 독립된 가상 루트 포트 아래에 연결되기 때문입니다. 게스트에서 실행한 NCCL은 모든 GPU와 NIC가 같은 거리에 있다고 계산했고 그 결과 다른 스위치의 NIC를 선택하는 경우가 생겼습니다.

레일셋과 NCCL 토폴로지 파일

게스트의 NCCL이 GPU와 NIC의 거리를 모른다면 호스트가 알려 주면 됩니다. 그래서 DRA 드라이버가 호스트에서 GPU와 같은 스위치의 NIC를 골라 함께 할당하고, 그 짝을 게스트의 NCCL에 전달하도록 바꿨습니다.

드라이버는 노드의 PCIe sysfs에서 GPU마다 같은 스위치에 연결된 컴퓨트 NIC를 찾아 GPU와 NIC의 짝인 레일(rail)을 만듭니다. 그리고 파티션마다 그 GPU들의 레일 NIC를 레일셋(railset)으로 묶어 ib-railset 디바이스 하나로 발행합니다. NIC를 낱개로 요청하게 하면 할당된 GPU와 다른 스위치의 NIC를 스케줄러가 고를 수도 있기 때문에 묶음으로 만들었습니다.

레일셋 안의 NIC 순서는 파티션의 GPU 순서를 따르므로 게스트의 i번째 GPU와 i번째 NIC가 짝이 됩니다. NIC가 빠져 있거나 포트 링크가 끊겨 레일을 모두 갖추지 못한 파티션에는 레일셋을 발행하지 않으므로 레일셋을 함께 요청한 ResourceClaim(이하 '클레임')에는 그 파티션의 디바이스가 할당되지 않습니다.

레일 정보는 NCCL 토폴로지 파일로 넘겼습니다. NCCL은 NCCL_TOPO_FILE로 지정한 XML 파일이 있으면 sysfs 대신 그 파일을 읽습니다. 따라서 이 파일에 GPU와 같은 레일의 NIC가 같은 가상 PCIe 브리지 아래에 있다고 적어 주면 NCCL은 둘이 가까이 연결되어 있다고 판단합니다.

드라이버는 클레임을 준비할 때 이 파일을 호스트에 만들어 CDI(Container Device Interface)로 컨테이너에 마운트하고 NCCL_TOPO_FILE을 설정합니다. 파일은 virtio-fs로 게스트에 전달되고 클레임이 해제되면 함께 지워집니다. 파일을 만들지 못하면 클레임 준비를 실패시켜 잘못된 토폴로지로 학습이 시작되지 않게 했습니다.

다만 파일에는 게스트 안의 PCI 주소를 적어야 하는데, 파일을 만드는 시점에는 VM이 아직 부팅되지 않았습니다. 그래서 내부 수정본의 shim은 클레임에 할당된 GPU와 NIC 순서대로 루트 포트를 만들고, 버스 번호는 업스트림 kata가 NUMA(non-uniform memory access) 노드별로 정해 둔 값을 씁니다. 순서와 버스 번호가 정해져 있으니 VM을 부팅하기 전에도 게스트 주소를 계산할 수 있습니다.

토폴로지 파일을 적용하고 NCCL 알고리즘을 NVLSTree로 지정하자 all_reduce 버스 대역폭은 158GB/s에서 613GB/s로 올랐습니다. IB NIC는 HCA(host channel adapter)라고도 부르며, NCCL에서는 NCCL_IB_HCA로 사용할 NIC를 지정합니다. 이 설정으로 컴퓨트 NIC 8개를 지정하자 버스 대역폭은 620GB/s가 되었고, 이후 8GiB 메시지로 측정한 값은 697.6~712.4GB/s였습니다.

GPU와 같은 레일의 NIC를 함께 요청하기

GPU와 그 레일셋을 함께 할당하려면 둘이 같은 파티션에 속한다는 조건도 필요합니다. 3편의 DRA 드라이버는 파티션 하나를 DRA 디바이스 하나(이하 '파티션 디바이스')로 발행하고 레일셋에는 짝이 되는 파티션의 번호를 fmPartitionId 속성으로 붙입니다. 클러스터 관리자는 ResourceClaimTemplate에서 GPU와 레일셋을 함께 요청하면서 constraints의 matchAttribute에 이 속성을 지정합니다.

아래 템플릿은 GPU 8장짜리 파티션 디바이스와 같은 파티션의 레일셋을 한 클레임에서 요청합니다.

requests:
- name: gpu
  exactly:
    deviceClassName: kata-gpu.nks.ncloud.com
    count: 1
    selectors:
    - cel:
        expression: "device.attributes['kata-gpu.nks.ncloud.com'].size == 8"
- name: nic
  exactly:
    deviceClassName: kata-ib-vf.nks.ncloud.com
    count: 1
    selectors:
    - cel:
        expression: "device.attributes['kata-gpu.nks.ncloud.com'].deviceType == 'ib-railset'
                     && device.attributes['kata-gpu.nks.ncloud.com'].size == 8"
constraints:
- requests: ["gpu", "nic"]
  matchAttribute: "kata-gpu.nks.ncloud.com/fmPartitionId"

스토리지 VF는 같은 템플릿에 ibvf-storage 디바이스를 요청하는 항목을 NUMA 노드별로 하나씩 더 두어 2개를 받습니다. 관리자는 GPU 수별로 이런 템플릿을 미리 설치해 두고 사용자는 템플릿 이름만 적습니다.

각 NIC는 서로 다른 물리 포트에 연결되어 있어 GPU 수에 맞춰 NIC를 늘리면 사용할 수 있는 대역폭도 늘어납니다. 서버 2대 GPU 16장 DDP(distributed data parallel) 학습에서 이 차이를 확인했습니다. GPU 8장 VM 하나에 연결하는 컴퓨트 NIC를 2개에서 8개로 늘렸을 때 처리량은 424.6ktok/s(초당 천 토큰)에서 565.5ktok/s로 올랐습니다.

GDR 경로와 ACS DT 비트

NIC 배치를 바로잡은 뒤에도 GDR 경로에 문제가 남아 있었습니다. 2편에서 GPU를 VM마다 격리하려고 켠 ACS(Access Control Services)는 스위치 하위 포트 사이의 P2P(peer-to-peer) 요청을 루트 컴플렉스로 보냅니다. 그래서 같은 스위치의 GPU와 NIC 사이를 오가는 GDR 트래픽도 루트 컴플렉스를 거쳤습니다.

이 문제는 MLOps Platform 팀의 도움을 받아 함께 분석했고, ACS의 Direct Translated P2P(DT) 비트로 해결했습니다. PCIe 장치가 ATS(Address Translation Services)로 IOMMU에서 주소를 미리 변환해 '변환 완료'로 표시한 요청은, DT 비트를 켜면 IOMMU 검사를 다시 거치지 않고 스위치 안에서 바로 전달됩니다.

이 방식은 PCIe 장치가 이 표시를 올바르게 붙인다는 전제 위에서 동작합니다. 그래서 저희는 GPU와 같은 PCIe 스위치에 연결된 NIC에만 ATS를 켜고, DT 비트도 GPU와 NIC 바로 위의 스위치 포트에만 설정했습니다.

적용 후 B200에서 NIC가 GPU 메모리에 쓰는 링크당 대역폭은 32.0GB/s에서 43.9GB/s로 올랐습니다. 서버 2대 GPU 16장의 all_reduce(메시지 크기 8GiB)에서는 GDR을 켰을 때 버스 대역폭이 697.6712.4GB/s로, 껐을 때의 241266GB/s보다 크게 높았습니다.

로컬 NVMe를 여러 VM에 나누어 주기

다음은 스토리지입니다. 모델과 데이터를 빠르게 읽고 쓰기 위해 B200 서버에 NVMe 4장을 장착했고, 그중 2장은 호스트가 RAID(redundant array of independent disks)로 사용하고 나머지 2장을 VM용으로 남겼습니다.

기존 연결 방식의 공유·성능 한계

기존 연결 방식으로는 여러 VM이 디스크를 나누어 쓰면서 원하는 성능까지 내기는 어려웠습니다.

방식 게스트에서 NVMe까지의 I/O 경로 디스크 공유 순차 읽기
virtio-fs 게스트, virtio-fs, virtiofsd, 호스트 파일 시스템, NVMe 여러 VM에서 공유 가능 4.75GB/s
virtio-blk 게스트, virtio-blk, QEMU, 호스트 커널, NVMe 여러 VM에서 공유 가능 2.1GB/s
패스스루 VFIO로 게스트에 직접 연결 VM 하나가 NVMe 1장 독점 10.0GB/s

virtio 두 방식은 I/O마다 호스트의 여러 계층을 지납니다. virtio-blk에서는 게스트가 virtqueue에 요청을 넣고 호스트에 알릴 때 VM exit가 발생합니다. 요청을 꺼낸 QEMU는 요청마다 시스템 콜을 호출해 호스트 커널의 블록 계층을 거쳐 NVMe에 접근합니다.

패스스루를 쓰면 NVMe 1장의 성능이 그대로 나오지만 VM 하나가 디스크 하나를 독점하게 됩니다. GPU 8장 서버에서 GPU 1장 VM 8개가 VM용 NVMe 2장을 나누어 써야 하는 환경에는 맞지 않았습니다. NVMe를 여러 VM에 나누어 주면서 호스트 계층도 건너뛸 수 있는 경로가 필요했습니다.

SPDK와 vhost-user-blk

NVMe를 vfio-pci에 바인딩해 커널 드라이버에서 분리하면 SPDK(Storage Performance Development Kit)가 사용자 공간에서 NVMe를 직접 제어할 수 있습니다. SPDK는 전용 CPU 코어(리액터 코어)가 완료 큐를 계속 확인하는 폴링으로 I/O를 처리하므로 인터럽트 비용이 없는 대신 리액터 코어의 사용률은 항상 100%입니다.

여기에 vhost-user를 결합해 게스트의 virtio 요청도 QEMU 대신 SPDK가 처리하게 했습니다. 게스트가 virtqueue에 I/O 요청을 기록하면 SPDK의 리액터가 폴링으로 읽어 NVMe에 전달하고, 완료 결과를 같은 virtqueue에 씁니다.

virtio-blk와 달리 이 경로에서는 SPDK가 virtqueue를 계속 폴링하므로 게스트의 알림을 기다리지 않습니다. NVMe도 사용자 공간에서 직접 다루므로 요청마다 호스트 시스템 콜을 호출하지 않습니다.

SPDK가 virtqueue의 요청을 읽고 I/O 버퍼에 접근하려면 게스트 메모리도 직접 볼 수 있어야 합니다. vhost-user에서는 QEMU가 게스트 메모리를 담은 파일 디스크립터를 SPDK 프로세스에 넘겨 같은 메모리를 매핑하게 합니다. 이 때문에 게스트 메모리는 파일 기반 공유 메모리로 구성해야 했습니다. kata는 enable_hugepages = true로 게스트 메모리를 hugetlbfs 기반으로 구성하고, QEMU 메모리 백엔드의 share=on으로 공유 가능한 메모리로 엽니다.

SPDK 프로세스는 모든 게스트의 메모리를 매핑하는 만큼 호스트 커널과 같은 신뢰 수준의 구성 요소로 운영하고 있습니다.

SPDK 논리 볼륨(lvol)을 이용한 NVMe 분할

남은 문제는 NVMe를 여러 VM에 나누어 주는 방법이었습니다. kata의 CSI(Container Storage Interface) 드라이버(csi-kata-directvolume)에도 SPDK 기반 볼륨 경로가 있지만 백엔드로 호스트 파일 시스템 위의 파일을 사용합니다. 게스트 요청을 SPDK가 처리해도 저장 공간에 접근할 때는 호스트 커널의 파일 시스템 계층을 다시 거치는 구조입니다.

이 방식으로 NVMe 1장에서 100GiB 순차 쓰기(큐 깊이 32)를 3회 측정한 결과는 6.5~7.0GB/s였습니다. PVC(PersistentVolumeClaim)마다 파일을 만들고 용량을 관리해야 하는 방식도 운영에 맞지 않아 다른 백엔드가 필요했습니다.

SPDK는 블록 장치 위에 lvstore라는 풀을 만들고 그 안에서 논리 볼륨을 나누어 쓸 수 있습니다. lvstore는 SPDK 사용자 공간 안에 있으므로 논리 볼륨을 vhost-user-blk로 게스트에 연결하면 데이터 경로에 호스트 커널이 들어가지 않습니다.

kata의 CSI 드라이버에는 논리 볼륨을 직접 사용하는 볼륨 유형이 없어 그 경로를 추가했습니다. 볼륨이 게스트에 나타나기까지는 다음 순서를 거칩니다.

  1. 노드가 시작될 때 초기화 스크립트가 SPDK용으로 예약된 NVMe 2장을 RAID 0으로 묶어 lvstore를 만들거나 기존 lvstore를 재사용합니다.
  2. StorageClass에는 쓸 lvstore 이름만 지정하고 CSI 드라이버는 PVC 하나를 논리 볼륨 하나에 대응시킵니다.
  3. PVC가 만들어지면 CSI 드라이버가 논리 볼륨을 생성하고 vhost-user 소켓을 노출합니다.
  4. kata shim이 그 소켓을 QEMU의 vhost-user-blk 장치로 추가하면 게스트에서는 볼륨이 /dev/vdb 같은 블록 장치로 보입니다.

SPDK에 넘길 NVMe는 커널 장치명(nvme0n1) 대신 PCI 주소로 지정했습니다. 커널 장치명은 부팅 순서에 따라 달라질 수 있어서, 목록이 한 칸만 밀려도 호스트가 쓰는 RAID 멤버를 vfio-pci에 바인딩할 위험이 있었기 때문입니다.

사용자는 일반 Pod처럼 PVC를 만들고 volumeMounts에 적으면 됩니다.

네트워크·스토리지 적용 전후 비교

GPU와 NIC 배치, GDR 경로, NVMe의 SPDK 경로를 적용하기 전후를 다음 조건에서 비교했습니다.

  • 서버: B200, 컴퓨트 IB NIC 400Gb/s
  • 로컬 디스크: 같은 VM에서 virtio-fs와 SPDK 경로를 같은 fio 명령으로 측정. SPDK는 NVMe 2장 RAID 0
  • ib_write_bw: perftest의 RDMA 쓰기 대역폭 측정 도구. -q4는 QP(queue pair) 4개
  • 단위: ib_write_bw는 Gb/s, fio 랜덤 읽기는 IOPS(input/output operations per second), 나머지는 GB/s

결과는 다음과 같습니다.

구분 항목 적용 전 적용 후
네트워크 서버 2대 GPU 16장 all_reduce 버스 대역폭(GPU와 NIC 배치) 158GB/s(토폴로지 파일·NVLSTree·NIC 지정 없음) 셋 모두 적용 620GB/s
네트워크 서버 2대 GPU 16장 all_reduce 버스 대역폭(NCCL_IB_HCA로 컴퓨트 NIC 8개 지정, 메시지 크기 8GiB) GDR 끔 241~266GB/s GDR 켬 697.6~712.4GB/s
네트워크 ib_write_bw -q4 업스트림 kata에는 DRA로 할당한 NIC를 VM에 연결하는 경로 없음 게스트 VF 387.2Gb/s(같은 NIC의 호스트 PF 387.3Gb/s)
로컬 디스크 fio 순차 읽기 virtio-fs 4.75GB/s SPDK 19.8GB/s
