event_model_payload.headline: Biz AI Agent: stop drawing agent flows — build real AI agents with a skill and an AI coding tool (fully open source)
event_model_payload.summary:
AI coding changed in the last year. Describe a feature to Claude Code or Codex and it designs, implements, tests, checks its own work and reports back.

Yet when people build AI agents or workflows, the default is still a drag-and-drop flow builder such as Dify. That is great for a prototype. For an agent that runs a real business process, it starts to hurt:

  • permissions (who may read what), approvals (who decides) and exceptions are hard to express as boxes and arrows;
  • reviewing, testing and rolling back a flow change — routine in software — is awkward;
  • the most capable developer we now have, the AI coding tool, can barely touch a flow that lives in a canvas.

Biz AI Agent takes the opposite approach. It is an open-source AI agent framework (Apache-2.0):

An agent is first an ordinary IT system — so you build it with AI coding.

  • Repository: https://github.com/ITC-cloud-soft/biz-ai-agent
  • Website: https://biz-ai.myaiportal.net/en/biz-ai-agent.html

1. A skill plus an AI coding tool

The repository ships the agent-builder skill for AI coding tools. Clone it and open your tool at the root — the skill is picked up automatically.

git clone https://github.com/ITC-cloud-soft/biz-ai-agent.git
cd biz-ai-agent && npm install
claude        # Claude Code loads .claude/skills/agent-builder
# codex       # Codex discovers .agents/skills/agent-builder

Then ask in your own words:

Use the agent-builder skill to build a "travel expenses" AI agent:
- employees ask about the expense rules and check their own claims on Slack;
- managers approve their team's claims; above $1,000 finance approves too;
- finance gets a monthly count report;
- the rules are in docs/travel-rules.md.

Following the skill, the AI:

  1. asks people first — who uses the agent, what it may read, who approves, who may read which document, what a correct answer is — writes it into AGENT_PLAN.md and waits (no guessing);
  2. writes the business system and its manifest and passes the Bridge v1 conformance suite: 52 / 52;
  3. adds permission-aware knowledge, the "why did this reach me?" graph, evals written before any tuning, the settings screens, SNS approvals and the DeepSeek Harness (DSH) profile;
  4. verifies every step with commands and reports the results, what is not verified and what is still to confirm.

examples/equipment-loans in the repo was built from scratch by an AI that followed only this skill.

A no-code tool is for people drawing flows. This is AI writing code, with tests guarding it. Branches, permissions and exceptions are plain code and tests — there is no ceiling on what the agent can do.

2. Build, deploy and maintain it like a web app

What the AI produces is an ordinary Node.js project in examples//:

file what
bridge.manifest.yaml the system's self-description: roles, events, the AI's tools
src/app.mjs the business system: data, sign-in, business rules, API, settings screens, knowledge, graph
knowledge/*.md company documents, with their visibility written inside
evals/, test/ evals and tests for business rules, permissions and conformance
dsh-profile/ the AI plane's configuration

Deploying is the same as any website: NODE_ENV=production node src/server.mjs behind an HTTPS reverse proxy. The AI plane (DSH) is one more process on the same machine, reached only through a gateway inside the web app.

Maintenance is the same too: git, reviews, tests and CI just work. Want a change? Ask the AI coding tool again — the tests (52 conformance checks, business rules, permissions, eval floors) tell you nothing broke.

3. Talk to it on chat — and it talks to you

The AI employee works in the chat your staff already use: LINE, Slack, Teams, WeCom, DingTalk, Feishu and more (13 SNS).

Employee → agent

  • "What is the daily allowance for a business trip?" — it searches company documents with that employee's own rights and answers with sources (links to the business screens). What you cannot see, the AI cannot see.
  • "Why did this approval reach me?" — it explains, from the manifest.

Agent → employee

  • a claim comes in → an approval card goes to the approver only (never the requester); one tap to approve;
  • business changes are notified only to the people the business system names;
  • reports with counts only, on schedule.

It answers when asked and reaches out when needed — two-way, proactive agents. People still decide: the AI's only write is a proposal; confirming, approving and amounts stay with people, enforced by code and configuration, not by prompts.

4. Fully open source — let's build it together

Apache-2.0: source, manual, skill, examples and tests are all public.

npm test       # about 900 tests, 0 fail
npm run e2e    # a real DSH + mock model + mock LINE: 15 / 15 PASS

"I built an agent for this process", "I need it on that chat platform", "this part of the skill is unclear" — issues, PRs and stars are all welcome. People who know the business plus people who drive AI coding tools make smarter agents.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/ITC-cloud-soft/biz-ai-agent
  • Website (the most complete explanation): https://biz-ai.myaiportal.net/en/biz-ai-agent.html

event_model_payload.headline: What CISA’s new cyber strategy means for how you ship software
event_model_payload.summary:
On October 26, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency released CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, three pillars of a four-year strategy for securing the nation’s critical infrastructure. The focus is on operational technology, but the pillars apply to anyone building and shipping software for the government.

CISA has given itself 60 days to review its current services, 180 days to publish an implementation plan, and a year to report progress. That plan is what agencies, and the vendors who supply them, will be measured against. In this article, you'll learn what each pillar asks of your software factory, and where GitLab fits in to your strategy.

Why the timing matters

CISA's plan lands as AI accelerates both sides of security. The same models that let agents write and ship code at machine speed also make old weaknesses cheaper to find and exploit. The Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) mid-year forecast projects 2026 at roughly 66,000 CVEs, up from the 59,000 it projected in February. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report puts the median time to fully patch a known-exploited vulnerability at 43 days, up from 32, and finds only 26% of those vulnerabilities were fully remediated.

Attackers often have a working exploit within days of disclosure, and sometimes hours. Most teams still need weeks to fix a known vulnerability. Closing that gap is much of what CISA 2030 is about.

Defend: Lead national cyber defense

The Defend pillar sets four objectives: coordinated defense across federal, state, local, and industry partners; stronger protection for operational technology; published guidance that makes software security a strategic advantage; and secure adoption of emerging technologies like AI. The last two describe a software factory where security is built in and where people and AI agents operate under the same rules.

Consider a typical week. A critical CVE drops in a library your agency uses in a dozen services. The advisory tells you the flaw is exploitable. It does not tell you whether the vulnerable code path is reachable or who owns each affected service. By the time someone has manually investigated your exposure, the exploit is public.

That investigation is what GitLab Duo Agent Platform takes off your plate. Security Analyst Agent draws on GitLab Orbit’s live knowledge graph of your code, pipelines, and deployments to rank the new finding against your backlog by exploitability, reachability, and blast radius. Agentic vulnerability resolution then writes a root-cause fix, opens a merge request, and validates it in your real pipelines before a developer reviews it. Both agents run under a composite identity, so they can only do what the agent and the person who triggered the agent are both allowed to do, inside an isolated environment that is torn down when the task ends.

The same pipeline produces the evidence CISA is looking for. In March 2025, one compromised access token poisoned a widely used CI action and exposed secrets in more than 23,000 downstream repositories. Each affected team had to figure out on its own whether it was impacted. GitLab generates a software bill of materials (SBOM) for every build and signed provenance for every artifact, so the answer to ‘did this touch us?’ is a lookup, not a hunt.

Harden: Prioritize national infrastructure security

The Harden pillar is about focus: using threat intelligence and infrastructure data to decide what is most at risk, working with international partners, and concentrating effort on the systems that would do the most damage if they failed. For a software factory, that means fixing the vulnerabilities that are actually exploitable rather than addressing everything a scanner flags.

GitLab’s vulnerability management is where that gets enforced. GitLab brings every scanner finding into a single report that shows its severity, exploitability, and status. GitLab Orbit connects each finding to the line of code where the vulnerability lives, the pipeline that built that code, and the team responsible for the code. A security engineer, or an agent, can then sort the queue by what is actually reachable in production instead of by a raw CVSS score. False positive detection takes the noise off the top of the queue, so what remains is the work that matters.

Ranking the queue only helps if the fix follows. Agentic vulnerability resolution takes the top finding and writes the fix, and when the same flaw appears across many projects, it fixes all of them under one policy. The security engineer’s job shifts from chasing findings to approving fixes.

The controls that make this safe are set once and inherited everywhere. A policy defined at the group level injects required scans into every pipeline beneath it and blocks a merge on a critical or known-exploited finding until a designated reviewer approves. Neither a developer, nor an agent, can change the policies that review their own work.

Prevail: Mobilize national resilience

CISA makes clear that a strong defense won’t stop every intrusion. The Prevail pillar speaks specifically to what happens next. It involves detecting adversaries quickly, evicting them decisively, and keeping critical operations running. For a software factory, that means you can still build and ship a fix when shared infrastructure is disrupted, and you can see exactly what an attacker, or a compromised agent, touched.

The development environment is a prize for an adversary: compromise it and you have a path into everything built there, starting with the credentials. GitLab Secrets Manager takes that path away. Secrets stored as CI/CD variables are visible to every job in the pipeline by default. Secrets Manager scopes them instead because a job must request each secret by name and gets only the ones it has been granted. A compromised dependency can reach only the secrets its job was allowed to use, and every time a secret is retrieved, that access is logged.

Keeping operations running also means you can still ship when something upstream fails. If a dependency or a shared service goes down mid-incident, the agency that can still build, test, and deploy an emergency patch is the one that can recover. That takes a deployment inside a boundary you already control. GitLab runs on your own infrastructure, including air-gapped environments, or on GitLab Dedicated for Government, a fully managed, single-tenant SaaS with FedRAMP Moderate and GovRAMP authorizations. Both options support disaster recovery and run AI agents.

If a vulnerability does get through, you don't have to reconstruct events from memory. Every agent action lands in the same audit system as the human actions, tied to the agent and the person who sent it, so you can see what an agent did, in what order, and under whose authority. The response is fast and specific: stop the task, pull its access, and roll back what it changed, with a full record of events already in hand.

A standard for earning autonomy

Every pillar in CISA 2030 comes back to one question: How do you let AI do more of the work without losing control of the outcome? GitLab’s answer is the GitLab Security Standard, published in October 2026 and applied to our own software factory.

An agent earns autonomy the way a new engineer does, one level of trust at a time. The standard defines five stages (Authorize, Isolate, Verify, Release, and Respond), each mapped to the frameworks your compliance team already reports against, including NIST SP 800-53, NIST SSDF, and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. The stages are cumulative: An agent that has proven the early ones can recommend changes, and one that has proven all five can fix, test, and merge on its own, with humans reviewing by exception.

How to get started

You don’t need to wait for CISA’s implementation plan to request a free GitLab Security Standard assessment and find out which stage your agents have earned. You can also learn how GitLab helps you create guardrails for your software supply chain.

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing eve 1.0
event_model_payload.summary:
Today we're announcing eve 1.0, the open-source framework for building production-ready agents.

Since the public preview in June, we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available.

We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite.

With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead.

Build production agents on a harness you own

The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in.

For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation.

Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product.

Thousands of businesses already run eve in production for internal and customer-facing agents. Rillet built a software factory on eve that takes in customer requests, converts them into specs, tests the changes, and opens PRs for human review. Rillet tripled its shipping rate in three months. Clay built monty, a data agent that answers employees’ questions in Slack. Just over two months in, 30–40% of the company used it every week.

Lindy's agent framework roundup names eve “Best for durable backend agents”.

Collaborate in multiplayer agent sessions

Multiplayer lets several people work with an agent in one shared session. eve keeps track of who said what and directs approvals and sign-ins to the right person. You can set up memory for each user or the whole team.

In the native Slack channel, each thread is one shared session. Approvals appear as buttons that only the right person can answer, and a live task card shows progress and timing. You can follow up in the thread without mentioning the agent again, cancel the current turn, or reset the session from Slack.

Ambient mode lets an agent listen in channels you choose, even without being mentioned. Guided by goals you set per channel, it decides when to speak up, help, or take on a task, and when to stay quiet. To limit model costs, a small decision model screens every message first, and only the ones that might be for the agent start a turn.

Slack is one of several native channels, alongside Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, GitHub, Linear, Twilio, Web Chat, and iMessage. The Chat SDK channel adds support for any Chat SDK platform adapter, including WhatsApp, Messenger, Google Chat, and email. Each channel is one file, and the same agent can work across all of them. See the integrations directory for the full list.

Build agent UIs with Next.js and other frameworks

eve 1.0 expands our native integrations for Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, TanStack Start, and Vite. The framework integrations build your agent alongside your app and set up its routes. On Vercel, you can deploy the agent and your site as one project, or host them separately.

The client libraries let you work with tool calls, approval requests, and questions in a consistent way across frameworks. Use that session data to build custom UIs: stream replies into agent chats, embed an agent in a page, or show the agent's tool calls in your own components.

Use eve add channel/web to scaffold a chat app with AI Elements components, or add eve's React, Vue, or Svelte bindings to an existing UI.

Build multi-tenant agents

One support-agent deployment can connect to each customer's ticketing system with their own credentials and apply that customer's approval rules.

Your application authenticates the user and identifies which tenant they belong to. You can then set memory, connection credentials, and approval policy for that tenant and user.

Before each model call in the main agent loop, dynamic definitions load the agent's capabilities from the session and external data. In 1.0, they cover models, connections, and subagents as well as tools, skills, and instructions.

Give agents memory across sessions

We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself.

Built-in fileMemory keeps data in memory in eve dev and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel.

Other providers include claude-mem, Hindsight, Kybernesis Arcana, Memanto, memco, Supermemory, and Upstash AgentKit.

Trace agents with OpenTelemetry

We rebuilt eve’s tracing around OpenTelemetry, so you can follow an agent’s work in the tracing tools you already use. eve dev records traces locally by default. If you host eve yourself, you can export them to an OpenTelemetry backend, including one you run yourself.

Tracing integrations include Raindrop, with more options in the integrations directory. Add one with eve add instrumentation/, or use the instrumentation APIs to build your own integration.

Traces now show when an agent is waiting for a person, including tool approvals, questions, budget prompts, and sign-ins. They record model selections and approval decisions alongside model usage and cost, and follow calls into MCP servers and remote agents.

You choose what eve collects for tracing. Content you exclude from collection stays out of every destination. You can filter out spans or redact inputs and outputs per destination. Private conversations in production send only metadata by default, without prompts or tool results. The OpenTelemetry guide explains these controls.

On Vercel, Agent Runs uses the same traces to show sessions, model calls, tool execution, subagent activity, and approval decisions in the dashboard. When eve deploy creates a new Vercel project, it sets up trace sampling automatically. See the Agent Runs guide for setup and configuration.

Lower agent turn latency

At the start of September, our hosted stress test on Vercel Workflows took a median of 3.036s per turn. In 1.0, the same 100-turn workload took 414ms. The test sends messages one at a time, with one immediate mock-model response and no tool calls per turn. We measure from sending a message until the turn finishes, capturing eve and Workflow overhead without the time a model takes to generate a response.

We worked with the Workflow team on spec 9, which gives each run a single orchestrator so background steps no longer replay the workflow. The team also moved event and stream writes to WebSockets and cut redundant history reads. eve agents get these improvements through Workflow SDK.

eve also caches the information it needs to route messages to each session and can move idle sessions to a newer deployment between turns. Web UIs can prewarm a session before the first message arrives, so the first reply starts sooner.

Lower workflow costs for long agent sessions

For a 50-turn Evo Docs session, the estimated Vercel Workflows cost drops from 5.4¢ to 1.3¢, about 76% lower. That assumes roughly two model steps per turn and 30-day retention. eve now uses Workflow SDK 5.5 and saves only the conversation data that changed between turns. We've also cut repeated work in workflow steps, checkpoints, and sandbox setup:

  • Workflow steps save changes and refer back to data already stored, instead of repeatedly copying a growing conversation into each step. Steps that don't need history no longer receive it.

  • Checkpoints store references to image files returned by tools, so they don't have to copy the image bytes each time.

  • Sandboxes from prepared snapshots skip repeated setup. Stop a sandbox and keep its files for reuse. Cleanup starts when the session ends.

The storage changes are part of the open-source Workflow SDK, so agents you host yourself on other Workflow backends also store less duplicate session data. The cost estimate above uses Vercel Workflows pricing.

On Vercel, workflow steps run on Fluid compute. They need extra storage writes for inputs above the payload size limit, so sending less session data helps keep turn times consistent as sessions grow. Images and files can still require those writes.

For model calls, tool and skill listings can stay out of the initial prompt until they're needed. Connection tools run through eve__search and eve__tool, so each search no longer has to expand the model's tool list. We also changed how eve marks parts of a prompt for provider caching, so more content can be reused between calls.

During an earlier migration to eve, an engineer at Evisions reported:

Share agent capabilities with extensions

Since the preview, we've added extensions so teams can share tools, skills, instructions, connections, channels, schedules, hooks, and subagents without copying files between agents. You can use extensions from the extensions directory or create your own with npx eve@latest extension init .

For example, agent-browser adds browser automation, Mux Video adds tools for video assets and clips, and Link adds wallet and purchase tools.

eve builds workspace extensions from source and reloads changes during development. You can update shared capabilities in one package and try the changes in your agents as you work.

Build coding agents with eve’s shared tools

The 1.0 code extension builds on eve’s default file tools, adding coding instructions and skills that follow your repository’s AGENTS.md. It's included in the eve package, so there's nothing extra to install. Give it a repository in its sandbox and your agent can investigate code, edit files, and run the project's checks. It uses the same harness and extension system as your other agents, so you can replace or disable tools, override skills, and add your own instructions.

See the benchmark results for comparisons with other coding harnesses using the same tasks and model.

Add the coding extension to your agent:

The companion eve/extensions/git adds GitHub and pull request workflows, using credentials and authorization you configure. On Vercel, the optional remote self-modification extension lets your agent propose changes to its own source in a draft pull request. You review the changes, merge them, and deploy.

Build with the same public APIs eve uses

We built eve's subagents, sleep, and question tools on the same workflow system you can use through defineWorkflowTool. Your tools can return a result, start a background task, or keep accepting messages as a resumable task. They can wait for a person, webhook, or timer without keeping compute running, and their runs survive restarts. You don't need a separate background-job system to coordinate that work.

Once you've defined a reviewer subagent, this tool returns a receipt immediately. The task body waits for the reviewer's result, which is delivered to the model in a later message:

Upgrade to eve 1.0

If you already have an eve agent, the 1.0 upgrade guide walks through the changes to extension builds, agent APIs, session events, clients, and saved history. Follow it before deploying your upgrade.

eve follows semantic versioning, so breaking changes to stable APIs only happen in major releases. Experimental and internal APIs, including experimental fields, can change between major releases.

event_model_payload.headline: Ask HN: Who's really winning with AI-Coding?
event_model_payload.summary:
I've noticed the same pattern across three different Claude-coded projects now. Initial velocity is strong, but starts to fade until returns are negative.

It seems a combination of changes in model behavior and increasing code base size—emphasis on the latter. The larger the code base and documented history/progress (e.g. through updates to completed work and instructions, as in .md files), the more drift starts to set in.

At a certain point, you get collapse. This is where it can't maintain consistency within a single unit of work. It can manifest, for example, as adding a similar element to a view, but styling it in a completely different manner than existing elements. It literally feels random.

It can also manifest as incoherent or poorly implemented logic and behavior. I've followed different advice, restructured projects, entered plan mode, added deterministic checks, styles, rules, etc. But, it feels like whack-a-mole and it's unclear that it actually adheres to these rules in the first place.

Then, there's the question of it moving the problem. In response to my complaints of inconsistent UI generation, it recommended a style check to run after its UI changes. Of course, that begs the question of why it doesn't just apply those rules in the initial generation.

But, I am at a place now where it spins up AI agents to do a full UI/UX review—Playwright and all. Yet, it's still drifting and not catching it. This is consistent with its unit tests—on my latest project it has now generated a suite of hundreds of somewhat time consuming tests that it constantly runs pre-commit, and not a single test has ever failed. Meanwhile, there have been a number of bugs. When questioned, it said it had been testing the "wrong layer" and had essentially generated self-confirming tests.

My question is who is really winning here? When querying Google, it points to so many claims of success and approaches that supposedly contribute to that success. But, when you break down the underlying source for those claims, it appears to be largely Reddit.

Yet, pressing it further reveals that virtually every actual study shows either little to no productivity gains or actual regression—particularly where experienced engineers are concerned. And some of those studies debunk the self-reported claims of exactly the kind you see on Reddit, etc.

So, who here has developed a quality production application of any complexity using AI coding? If anyone, which harness/model, and what techniques did you use? Also, can you point us to your repo?

event_model_payload.headline: Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend
event_model_payload.summary:
The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a service proxy implementation with better performance than the iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API, and the ipvs backend was never able to implement all of the edge cases of Kubernetes Service functionality correctly.

In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33. Part of the plan behind adding the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace both the iptables and ipvs backends. Because the ipvs backend in particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it as of Kubernetes 1.35. Although it currently remains available in kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40. All ipvs users should therefore be planning to migrate to either the nftables or iptables backends.

Why was the ipvs backend written?

The ipvs backend was originally designed to fix two different kinds of performance problems in the iptables backend:

  • First, iptables had problems with data plane latency (the speed at which clients could establish new connections to services), because kube-proxy would write a separate iptables rule to match each service IP, so every new connection would need to be matched against a long series of rules that was O(n) in the number of services in the cluster.

  • Second, it had an even larger problem with control plane latency (the speed at which kube-proxy could process changes to services and endpoints and update the data plane rules), because kube-proxy would rewrite the entire iptables ruleset every time any service or endpoint changed. While the list of rules itself was only O(n) in the total number of endpoints, the amount of time, RAM, and CPU that it took to process the updated ruleset grew faster than that. In very large clusters, kube-proxy would use 100% of one CPU all the time just to process iptables updates. (In fact, the control plane scaling problem was bad enough that for most users it was not even possible to grow the cluster to the size where the data plane scaling problem became noticeable.)

The ipvs backend solved both of these scaling problems. The data plane problem was solved mostly automatically, because the kernel IPVS subsystem uses hash tables rather than linear lookup. The control-plane problem was solved by not rewriting the entire ruleset on every update. (The kernel IPVS API doesn’t have a way of doing batch updates anyway, so this was essentially forced.)

Why is the ipvs backend now being deprecated?

Almost from the start, the ipvs backend also had problems.

The first version didn’t have 100% compatibility with the iptables backend, but it was assumed that this would be fixed over time. Unfortunately, the original authors moved on to other things outside the Kubernetes ecosystem (as inevitably sometimes happens in open source), and it took a while to find new people interested in maintaining the code.

Meanwhile, as people began using the ipvs backend in larger and larger clusters, its own scaling problems started to emerge. In particular, the lack of batch update operations in the IPVS API meant that while the ipvs backend was faster than iptables when making a few small changes, it was potentially slower when making a large number of changes at once. And because the IPVS API is fairly limited in what it can do, kube-proxy's ipvs backend needed to fall back to using iptables to implement various features of Kubernetes Services beyond basic "load balancing", making it run into some of the same scaling problems the iptables backend has. While the ipvs backend tried to mitigate this by using ipset for some of its rules, this again ran into the problem of not having a batch update API. Additionally, the fact that the ipvs backend uses iptables means that it has the same long-term support problem as the iptables backend: Red Hat's plan to remove the iptables API entirely from Red Hat Enterprise Linux means the ipvs kube-proxy backend will also no longer be available to Kubernetes users on RHEL.

What about IPVS schedulers?

Beyond performance, the other reason some users were excited about the ipvs backend was the ability to pick from among various IPVS "schedulers" for distributing traffic to endpoints, rather than relying on the simple random selection used by iptables (and nftables).

Unfortunately, the way IPVS is used by kube-proxy prevents it from being able to use most of the IPVS schedulers in a useful way. The problem is that kube-proxy is a distributed service that runs on all nodes in the cluster, but the kube-proxy processes on different nodes do not share their IPVS scheduler state, so each node picks endpoints without knowing what is happening with clients on any other node. Even the schedulers that are designed to work in a distributed way generally don't work better than random selection in the context of kube-proxy. For example, the mh scheduler uses Maglev Hashing to select endpoints, which theoretically allows for extremely efficient distributed load balancing. But that efficiency is only in the context of a specific sort of two-layer load-balancer design, and kube-proxy does not have the right architecture to be able to act as either of the two layers in that design.

Switching away from ipvs

Switching to nftables

If you are running Kubernetes 1.36 or later, and your nodes are running a Linux distribution with kernel 5.13 or later, and you use the ipvs proxy mode, then Kubernetes recommends switching to the nftables mode of kube-proxy. (Although the nftables backend is GA —and fully usable—as of Kubernetes 1.33, there have been some performance- and scaling-related fixes since then that that weren't backported to releases earlier than 1.36.)

The nftables backend is fully supported, feature-complete, and even has very slightly better performance than ipvs:

(Taller bars represent longer latency. The "p50" group is the average connection establishment latency. Note that even the largest numbers in this graph are quite tiny; the point is not to claim that nftables is (noticeably) faster than ipvs, just to show that, unlike iptables, it's not slower.)

Switching is as easy as changing the kube-proxy configuration and restarting kube-proxy. For example, in clusters deployed via kubeadm, change mode: ipvs to mode: nftables in the kube-proxy ConfigMap and then restart the kube-proxy pods, as described in the documentation on reconfiguring a kubeadm cluster. (If you are overriding other ipvs-specific kube-proxy configuration, you will also need to change those options to the corresponding nftables ones.)

Switching to iptables: "It's Not As Slow As You Think!"

If you can't switch to nftables, either because you are on an older version of Kubernetes, or because your cluster runs on an older Linux distribution that isn't new enough to support the nftables backend, you may be able to just switch to the iptables backend, which has improved greatly since the original creation of the ipvs backend in 2017:

  • The generated ruleset has been optimized to remove redundant and irrelevant rules (#57461, #60306, #96959, #108251), reducing data plane latency.

  • The code that generates the ruleset has been optimized to do fewer allocations, and to avoid unnecessarily recomputing the same information multiple times (#65755, #65902, #67948, #85617, #90103, #97238), reducing CPU and memory usage when resyncing.

  • Rather than doing “check the current state of the rules, then update them to the new state”, iptables kube-proxy now does “assume the current state is correct, update to the new state based on that assumption, and only explicitly check the current state if that update fails”. This greatly improves the resyncing speed, because it turns out that even reading the iptables ruleset is extremely slow in large clusters (#81517, #110334, #114181).

  • To the extent possible within the constraints of the iptables APIs, kube-proxy’s iptables backend now only updates iptables rules for services/endpoints that have changed since the last sync, rather than rewriting the entire ruleset every time (#110268 / KEP-3453).

The net result of this is that the iptables backend of 2026, while still not as good as the ipvs backend, is at least much better than the iptables backend of 2017 was, and many people who found iptables unusable in the past would not have problems with it now.

As with switching to nftables, switching to iptables is mostly just a matter of updating your kube-proxy configuration, although for technical reasons, in this case we recommend that you reboot each node after changing the kube-proxy configuration, rather than merely restarting kube-proxy.

Learn more

  • KEP-5495 gives the full timeline and plan for kube-proxy IPVS deprecation.

  • The blog post "NFTables mode for kube-proxy" has more information about nftables mode and its performance relative to ipvs and iptables.

event_model_payload.headline: Declare that your app uses only expiring Admin API tokens
event_model_payload.summary:
Turn on the Admin API token expiry card from your app’s Settings page in the Dev Dashboard and any API requests made from your app to the GraphQL or REST Admin API must use expiring tokens. Requests made with non-expiring tokens will be rejected.

What changed

When you enable Admin API token expiry for an app, it applies across every store where that app is installed. GraphQL and REST Admin API requests then fail if they use either:

  • A non‑expiring offline access token
  • A delegate access token with more than 24 hours remaining before expiry

Enforcement can take up to 30 minutes to take effect. Enabling the setting doesn’t migrate or revoke existing tokens.

You can turn the setting off if you encounter issues. Turning it off doesn’t change the April 1, 2027 enforcement deadline for public apps or the December 1, 2026 requirement for custom apps.

Who’s affected

This setting is available for all app types in the Dev Dashboard. It affects an app only after you turn it on for that app.

Expiring tokens are required for all apps:

  • **December 1, 2026: ** Custom apps created on or after must use expiring tokens.
  • January 1, 2027: Public apps that still use non-expiring offline access tokens are delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working.
  • April 1, 2027: Shopify rejects a GraphQL Admin API or REST Admin API request that presents a non-expiring offline token, and merchants lose access to your app until they re-authenticate.

What to do

We recommend turning on Admin API token expiry to give you peace of mind that your migration is complete ahead of the deadlines.

  1. Complete your migration using the Admin API token expiry migration guide, then review your app’s GraphQL and REST logs for affected requests. The Dev Dashboard highlights potential token‑expiry issues detected in the last 14 days, though detection can lag by a day.
  2. Open your app in the Dev Dashboard, go to Settings, and select Turn on in the Admin API token expiry card. Confirm that you understand that requests that don’t meet token‑expiry requirements will fail.
  3. Allow up to 30 minutes for enforcement to take effect. Then check your app’s workflows and logs for rejected requests, including requests from background jobs, to confirm that your app handles expiring tokens correctly.

​

​

발표 내용

'자율 그래프 주도 개발(Autonomous Graph-Driven Development)'에서는 사람의 직접적인 지시 없이 그래프가 프로젝트 진행을 주도합니다. 스펙 문서와 코드는 AI Agent 루프가 작성하고, 결정론적 코드가 이를 기계적으로 검사하며, 결함은 피드백 루프를 통해 자동으로 바로잡습니다. 사람이 AI를 호출하던 주도권이 역전되어 이제는 AI가 필요할 때만 사람을 호출합니다.

​

​

발표 대상

​

목차

1. AI가 다 해 주는데, 뭐가 문제지? (배경 및 문제 정의)

  • 여전히 사람이 주도한다

  • 요구사항은 항상 변한다

  • AI 협업에 남은 빈자리, 자율 진행

​

2. 어떻게 스스로 굴러가게 할까? (접근 방법 및 실행 과정)

  • Autonomous Graph-Driven Development (용어 정의)

  • Don't call us, we'll call you

  • 그래프의 핵심 원칙

  • 그래프 구조

    • 노드 ① Upstream — 기획서 변경을 요구사항으로 옮긴다

    • 노드 ② Spec-drive — 스펙을 확정한다

    • 노드 ③ Dev — 확정된 스펙을 구현한다

    • 노드 ③ Dev 사례 — 복잡한 AI 대화 구현, 토큰 비용 $199.61

    • 노드 ④ Verify — 배포된 코드를 E2E 테스트로 검증한다

    • 노드 ⑤ Audit — 스펙의 논리적 결함을 찾는다

  • 진행 현황 대시보드 — 어디까지 왔고, 왜 멈춰 있는가?

​

3. 처음부터 잘 굴러갔을까? (어려움 및 극복 과정)

  • 그래프 자체가 또 하나의 제품이었다

  • 어려움 ① 루프 안정화 — 루프는 눈치채지 못했다

  • 어려움 ② AI와 협업 — 그래프는 쉬지 않는다

  • 어려움 ③ 기획과 협업 — 애매한 문장은 AI도, 사람도 오해한다

​

4. 그래서, 무엇이 달라졌나? (성과 및 임팩트)

  • 사람은 도구를 만들고, 루프는 제품을 만든다

  • 성과 ① 리드타임 — 사람의 결정만 남는다

  • 성과 ② 인력 — 백엔드 개발 공수 86% 절감

  • 성과 ③ 토큰 비용 — 루프는 프런티어 모델이 아니어도 충분하다

  • 성과 ④ 전체 비용 — 사람 + AI를 합쳐도 71% 절감

  • 임팩트 ① 일하는 방식의 변화 — Human-in-the-loop

  • 임팩트 ② 확장 가능성 — 그래프 운영 도구에는 서비스 지식이 없다

​

마무리

  • 결정만 하면, 그래프가 알아서 합니다

event_model_payload.headline: AI Gateway now supports Private Inference
event_model_payload.summary:
Private Inference connects your own model endpoints to AI Gateway.

Enterprises running fine-tuned, self-hosted, or prerelease models used to need separate keys, client code, and logs for them. Those models can now run through the same authentication, SDKs and APIs, and observability as catalog models, so every model your team uses is managed in one place.

Use Private Inference to:

  • Switch between private and catalog models: Call private models through Chat Completions, Responses, or Messages. AI Gateway translates each request to your endpoint's format, so switching only changes the model ID.

  • Keep models scoped to your team: Only your Vercel team can view or call private models, and they aren't listed in the public catalog. Credentials are stored encrypted, and you can enable Zero Data Retention per provider.

  • Connect coding agents: Use private models in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents connected to AI Gateway.

  • Monitor traffic together: View private model requests alongside catalog traffic in logs, trace drains, and custom reporting. Observability charts break down requests, tokens, and time to first token by private model.

  • Configure fallbacks: Optionally fall back to a catalog model if your private endpoint fails.

To get started, open the Private Inference page and add your endpoint as a private provider. Enter its base URL, select its API format, and add its credentials. Then add the models it serves.

You can also register the provider and model with the Vercel CLI, version 65.16.0 or later:

Private model requests appear in AI Gateway logs alongside requests to catalog models.

event_model_payload.headline: Auditable AI billing without a blockchain: signed batches and their limits
event_model_payload.summary:
The difficult part of AI API billing is often the request that almost finished. The router sent the prompt, the provider began responding, and the connection disappeared before final usage arrived. A database can store a precise number for that request without making the number well justified.

I am building TeeRouter, and this led to two separate design questions: what evidence supports a charge, and how can someone later detect changes to the published accounting records?

The implementation borrows a useful idea associated with blockchains: publish cryptographically verifiable records that readers can inspect independently. It does not run a blockchain or claim decentralized consensus. This article examines the public source at commit 5c89b551; it is an implementation case study, not an independent certification of the deployed service.

First define what a charge means

A receipt should preserve the pricing decision used for that request. Looking up today's price when displaying last week's usage makes historical charges difficult to reproduce.

TeeRouter freezes the pricing revision, applicable rules, and pool multiplier at admission. Provider-specific calculators interpret native usage fields. The basis is public API list pricing multiplied by the pool's multiplier, not a claim about the merchant's actual subscription expenditure or negotiated invoice.

The billing implementation uses integer arithmetic, retains pre-rounding amounts, and rounds upward once per request to micro-USD. This makes the chosen calculation reproducible without promising to match a provider's monthly invoice rounding, taxes, or discounts.

For a simple illustrative quote, 10,000 ordinary input tokens at $2 per million plus 1,000 output tokens at $8 per million produces a $0.028 base cost. A 1.2 multiplier gives $0.0336. These are made-up rates, not a current model quotation. Real records must also distinguish cached input, applicable pricing dimensions, and how each provider reports usage.

A timeout is an observation, not a usage counter

The interrupted-request policy separates several outcomes:

Observed outcome Accounting treatment
Router rejects the request before forwarding No charge
Upstream rejects it with HTTP 3xx/4xx No charge; any reported counters are retained as waived usage
Sending fails before the complete request is flushed, with no generation evidence No charge
Complete request is flushed, then the connection fails before a reply Estimate input at ordinary input pricing; no unseen output
Generation starts, then delivery fails Use official counters where available and estimates for supported missing portions
A successful response has missing or invalid usage Preserve an explicit pending reason

A generated refusal inside a successful model response is different from an HTTP rejection: generation may have consumed billable tokens.

The controversial row is the timeout after a full flush. A successful local flush does not prove that the remote application received or executed the request. The policy chooses a financial treatment for that ambiguity; it does not eliminate the ambiguity. Customers need to know that an estimated input charge can occur at this boundary.

Estimation is restricted to failed or interrupted model requests and is labelled estimated or mixed, with partial coverage. Unknown hidden output is not invented. A downstream cancellation cancels the upstream operation rather than draining it in the background, although closing a connection cannot guarantee the provider immediately stops computing.

Publishing these distinctions matters more than making every row appear confidently “settled.” A signed estimate remains an estimate.

Sign a batch, retain the exact bytes

The current public receipt format signs batches of records. A manifest includes the boot and key identity, batch number, previous hash, sequence range, record digest, count, and calculated total.

Conceptually, verification follows this chain:

original record bytes -> SHA-256 digest -> manifest
manifest + protocol label -> Ed25519 signature
manifest -> reference to preceding batch

There is one signature per batch. The current public format does not have per-record Merkle inclusion proofs. A reader needs the original complete records_json to verify the records; reserializing JSON may change the bytes being checked.

The verifier distinguishes a valid signature from an independently trusted TEE signing identity. The latter also requires hardware evidence and an approved reference policy. It is not established by a public key or a “verified” label included in the downloaded bundle.

Hash links let readers check continuity between supplied batches. They do not create consensus, prove that an operator has disclosed the latest batch, or prove that no other history exists. Independently retaining known batch heads could strengthen monitoring, but that is a separate system property, not something the signature supplies automatically.

Storage acknowledgment is not settlement

Consider a batch that reaches external storage, followed by a lost acknowledgment. Regenerating it with new metadata would complicate duplicate detection. TeeRouter freezes the signed bytes before upload and resends those same bytes on a later cycle.

A valid durable-storage acknowledgment permits releasing the uploaded raw details. It does not reset consumption or update user balances. Per-user, per-batch summaries remain until a separate settlement acknowledgment applies a balance update through an identified uploaded head.

That boundary is necessary because requests may finish while settlement is happening. Retiring consumption only through the acknowledged head preserves newer charges. Revisions and idempotent retries prevent repeating the same settlement from applying it twice.

The default upload cycle is five minutes. That is a delivery schedule, not a guarantee of completeness or immediate publication.

What survives a restart?

The optional accounting journal stores committed events and delivery state in SQLite WAL with authenticated encryption. Frozen batches keep their original signatures after restart; new batches use the new process identity.

It protects successfully committed records. It cannot reconstruct an in-flight request that never produced an event, recover usage that was never observed, or prevent deletion or rollback of an entire journal copy. On a journal write failure or capacity limit, the implementation closes new admission instead of silently discarding accepted events.

This makes durability a concrete, bounded claim rather than “nothing can ever be lost.”

Public accounting without publishing conversations

Public batches exclude prompts, answers, credentials, and refusal text. They contain accounting fields and refusal categories. User pseudonyms rotate using a fresh public batch nonce and a private random identity, rather than hashing a short username.

That reduces direct linkage across batches but does not guarantee anonymity. Timing, model choices, merchant identifiers, and distinctive traffic volumes can still correlate activity.

The resulting ledger is useful because readers can check the bytes they received, inspect charge evidence, and distinguish estimates from observed usage. Deposits, withdrawals, externally managed balances, missing history, and provider-side execution remain separate questions. Keeping those boundaries explicit is what makes the evidence meaningful.

event_model_payload.headline: What a TEE can actually prove about an AI API router
event_model_payload.summary:
An AI API router sits in an awkward place. It needs to read a request to select an upstream account, enforce permissions, and calculate usage. That also gives its operator opportunities to change parameters, misuse credentials, or report a different price from the one the client expected.

Publishing the router's source helps people inspect those decisions. It leaves another question unanswered: is that the program handling my request?

I am building TeeRouter, an open-source router that explores this question using trusted execution environments and independently verifiable receipts. This is a case study of its public implementation at commit 5c89b551, rather than an independent audit or verification of a live deployment. The interesting part is how narrow the useful guarantees need to be.

Start with the connection

Suppose a service presents a valid hardware attestation report. If the report is unrelated to the TLS connection carrying your prompts, it tells you very little about where those prompts go. An untrusted frontend could show evidence from a legitimate enclave while processing requests somewhere else.

TeeRouter binds its current TLS certificate and a client-generated challenge into the attestation report. The binding in the channel implementation is:

REPORT_DATA = SHA512(
    UTF8("teellm:attested-channel:v1\0")
    || nonce32
    || SHA256(certDER)
)

The nonce gives the verifier a freshness challenge. The certificate digest connects the evidence to the certificate used for TLS. The protocol label separates this purpose from other uses of attestation data.

This only works if the client actually checks that binding and uses the corresponding authenticated connection. Downloading a report, displaying a green badge, and then sending traffic to an unrelated endpoint would discard the useful property.

A hardware signature is only the beginning

An authentic report can still describe a program you should not trust. A verifier needs an independently chosen policy defining which measurements and security state it accepts.

For the TDX path, the project checks certificate chains, revocation and trusted computing base information, measurements, the relevant event sequence, and the report-data binding. The security document makes the independence requirement explicit: evidence supplied by the server cannot also be the sole authority deciding what counts as trustworthy.

There is an operational consequence here. Updating the router is also a trust-policy problem. A client must have a defensible reason to accept the new measured software. Automatically trusting every measurement announced by the service would weaken the point of checking measurements at all.

The application also matters. A correctly attested program with a credential-export endpoint would still export credentials. TEE isolation does not repair bad authorization logic, unsafe dependencies, or mistakes in the approved code. It reduces particular infrastructure trust assumptions under its hardware and software threat model; it does not remove the need for review.

Separate the administrator from the person making a request

A router administrator needs to change balances and permissions. That does not mean the administrator should be able to impersonate a user and spend their balance.

The current user authentication protocol requires a client-owned Ed25519 signature as well as a valid Bearer credential. A user ID is derived from the public key; the signing seed stays with the client.

The signature covers the exact body bytes, method, path and query, relevant headers, a timestamp, a random nonce, and the router's boot ID. Including authorization and routing headers prevents someone from preserving the body while silently changing the account-pool selection or other signed instructions. Including a boot ID makes proofs from an earlier process invalid after a restart.

This is a deliberately limited separation of powers. An administrator can still deny service, change permission settings, or alter externally managed balances. What administrator authority alone cannot do, under the verified implementation, is produce a valid signature for the existing user's key.

Preserve the request, including the expensive details

AI requests carry more financially significant settings than a model name. Cache controls, service tiers, reasoning options, and tool definitions can all affect behavior or cost.

TeeRouter's documented forwarding boundary preserves native generation parameters instead of silently adding its own cache or retention choices. Account egress is explicitly configured, official upstream HTTPS certificates remain checked, and a failed proxy is not supposed to fall back to a direct connection. These are application properties to inspect in the approved version, not properties hardware provides automatically.

There is also a boundary the router cannot cross: the upstream provider still receives the prompt. Attesting an intermediary does not attest the provider's internal inference service, prove which model weights it ran, or establish how it retains requests. A router can preserve a requested parameter; it cannot turn that parameter into independently observed behavior inside another company's infrastructure.

Evidence needs more than one status flag

The project also signs consumption batches. Its standalone verifier distinguishes signature verification, record verification, and TEE verification.

That distinction is useful beyond this project. A mathematically valid signature says that a key signed particular bytes. Hardware evidence and an approved reference policy can establish more about that key's origin. Neither result alone establishes that every request appears in the supplied history or that the latest batch has been disclosed.

For someone assessing a deployment, I would want separate answers to these questions:

  • Which software and reference policy did I approve?
  • Is this evidence fresh and bound to the connection I am using?
  • Which operations remain possible for the administrator?
  • Which data and decisions still depend on the upstream provider?
  • Which failures can interrupt availability or leave accounting incomplete?

Those answers are more useful than a single “TEE verified” label. The practical value is being able to inspect a specific program, verify a connection to an accepted instance, and understand exactly which remaining promises still require trust.

event_model_payload.headline: Puzzles to learn python loops
event_model_payload.summary:
Problem : 1
Divide the Tiles Equally
A school is preparing a large square floor for its annual function. The floor has N tiles arranged in a single row. The teacher wants to divide these tiles into equal-sized groups without leaving any tile unused. For example, if there are 12 tiles, the teacher can make:

1 group of 12 tiles
2 groups of 6 tiles
3 groups of 4 tiles
4 groups of 3 tiles
6 groups of 2 tiles
12 groups of 1 tile

no = 12
divisor = 1
while divisor <= 12:
    if no % divisor == 0:
        print(divisor)
    divisor = divisor + 1

Problem : 2
The Special Lock Number

A treasure box has a number lock with a number N. The lock designer follows a special rule: A number is considered a Special Number if it can be divided equally into groups in only two ways:
One group containing all the items.
Groups containing one item each.
For example, if the number is 7, the items can be arranged equally only as:
1 group of 7 or 7 groups of 1. But if the number is 8, it can also be arranged as 2 groups of 4, so it is not a Special Number.

Write a Python program that accepts a number N and determines whether it is a Special Number or not.

N = int(input("Enter a number: "))

divisor = 1
count = 0

while divisor <= N:
    if N % divisor == 0:
        count = count + 1
    divisor = divisor + 1

if count == 2:
    print("Special Number")
else:
    print("Not a Special Number")

Problem : 3
Secret VIP Numbers

A security system assigns special numbers to the first few VIP lockers. A number is considered a VIP number if it can be divided exactly by only 1 and itself. The security officer wants the numbers of the first 5 VIP lockers. Write a Python program to display those 5 numbers.

num = 2
count = 0

while count < 5:
    divisor = 1
    factors = 0

    while divisor <= num:
        if num % divisor == 0:
            factors = factors + 1
        divisor = divisor + 1

    if factors == 2:
        print(num)     // 2 3 5 7 11
        count = count + 1

    num = num + 1

Problem : 4
16.2) The Special Numbers
A teacher is preparing a Number Exhibition for students. She writes the numbers 1 to 20 on 20 cards. She wants to select only the special cards. A card is special if its number can be divided exactly by only two numbers: 1 and the number itself.

The teacher asks the students:
“Check all the cards from 1 to 20 and display the numbers that are special.”

num = 1

while num <= 20:
    divisor = 1
    count = 0

    while divisor <= num:
        if num % divisor == 0:
            count = count + 1
        divisor = divisor + 1

    if count == 2:
        print(num)  //2 3 5 7 11 13 17 19
    num = num + 1

event_model_payload.headline: Enterprise Multi-Agent Orchestration: Managing Distributed State & Consensus
event_model_payload.summary:
The evolution of generative AI has transitioned rapidly from single-turn chat interfaces to autonomous, multi-agent enterprise swarms. While proof-of-concept architectures can easily manage two or three cooperating models in a controlled sandbox, scaling these swarms to handle dozens of concurrent builder, reviewer, and validator agents introduces complex distributed systems challenges.

When autonomous agents operate across asynchronous nodes without strict state governance, systems fail in unpredictable ways: split-brain scenarios emerge where competing agents overwrite code modifications, context drift distorts task objectives, and cascading hallucinations poison downstream dependencies. This masterclass dives deep into the production architecture required to build resilient multi-agent swarms using distributed state machines, consensus protocols, and strict Byzantine fault tolerance mechanisms.

1. The Distributed State Problem in Agentic Swarms

In standard microservices architecture, state is typically persisted in relational databases or distributed key-value stores with ACID guarantees. In contrast, multi-agent systems rely on probabilistic reasoning engines (LLMs) interacting with mutable file systems, git worktrees, and ephemeral execution environments.

Without rigorous state synchronization, agents experience three critical failure modes:

  • State Divergence: Agent A assumes a database migration has been applied, while Agent B—operating on a slightly delayed event loop—refactors the schema based on legacy assumptions.
  • Race Conditions on Shared Artifacts: Concurrent builder agents attempting to modify the same core configuration file create merge conflicts that break automated compilation pipelines.
  • Implicit Context Drift: As execution runs span hours, historical chat turns accumulate noise, causing agents to deviate from the immutable project specification (CONTEXT.md).

To overcome these challenges, enterprise swarms must abandon naive chat-passing loops and adopt a Deterministic State Machine (DSM) pattern where every agent transition is gated by cryptographic or immutable log verification.

2. Architectural Blueprint: The Replicated State Machine Pattern

To ensure consistency across distributed agent nodes, we implement a replicated state machine model inspired by consensus algorithms like Raft. Every agent action—whether it is writing a test, executing a build, or proposing a refactor—is treated as a discrete state transition command.

Swarm Layer Primary Responsibility Fault Tolerance Mechanism
Leader Node (Orchestrator) Dispatches work items, sequences task logs, and maintains the global execution index. Heartbeat timeouts and automatic leader election upon worker unresponsiveness.
Worker Nodes (Builders) Execute isolated code generation tasks inside ephemeral git worktrees and containers. Sandboxed resource limits and automatic rollback on non-zero exit codes.
Validator Nodes (Reviewers) Perform independent static analysis, security auditing, and test suite execution. Deterministic test suites and multi-model consensus voting.

3. Implementing Consensus and Quorum Voting for Agent Decisions

When a builder agent completes a complex feature, allowing a single LLM to review and approve its own work introduces severe security and logic vulnerabilities. Enterprise-grade pipelines require Quorum-Based Validation.

Before any pull request can be merged into the main trunk, it must achieve a cryptographic or weighted consensus score from at least three independent validator agents utilizing different model backends (e.g., combining a reasoning model like DeepSeek-R1 with a deterministic code model).

Below is a simplified Python harness illustrating how an orchestrator enforces consensus verification before advancing the task state machine:


python
import hashlib
import json

class AgentConsensusOrchestrator:
    def __init__(self, quorum_threshold: int = 2):
        self.quorum_threshold = quorum_threshold

    def evaluate_task_output(self, task_id: str, validator_reports: list[dict]) -> bool:
        approvals = 0
        rejections = 0

        for report in validator_reports:
            # Verify cryptographic integrity of the report payload
            payload_hash = self._hash_payload(report['output'])
            if payload_hash != report['signature']:
                continue # Discard tampered or corrupted agent reports

            if report['verdict'] == 'APPROVE':
                approvals += 1
            elif report['verdict'] == 'REJECT':
                rejections += 1

        if approvals >= self.quorum_threshold and rejections == 0:
            print(f"Task {task_id} achieved consensus. State advancing.")
            return True
        else:
            print(f"Task {task_id} failed consensus quorum. Triggering remediation.")
            return False

    def _hash_payload(self, data: str) -> str:
        return hashlib.sha256(data.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()

# Example execution harness
orchestrator = AgentConsensusOrchestrator(quorum_threshold=2)
reports = [
    {"validator": "node-1", "verdict": "APPROVE", "output": "test_pass", "signature": hashlib.sha256(b"test_pass").hexdigest()},
    {"validator": "node-2", "verdict": "APPROVE", "output": "test_pass", "signature": hashlib.sha256(b"test_pass").hexdigest()}
]
orchestrator.evaluate_task_output("TASK-1049", reports)
4. Byzantine Fault Tolerance in Autonomous Swarms
In distributed systems, Byzantine faults occur when nodes fail arbitrarily, transmit false telemetry, or behave maliciously due to prompt injection or context poisoning. In multi-agent swarms, an adversarial prompt embedded in an external GitHub issue can trick a builder agent into introducing subtle supply-chain vulnerabilities or backdoor logic.

To defend against Byzantine failures, enterprise infrastructure must enforce:

Zero-Trust Inter-Agent Communication: Agents never accept raw text instructions from peer agents without cryptographic signature verification and schema validation via structured JSON outputs (e.g., using Instructor or Pydantic guardrails).

Immutable Audit Logging: Every prompt, intermediate reasoning step, tool call, and terminal output is streamed to an append-only log storage backend, ensuring full forensic traceability if an anomalous state transition occurs.

Sandboxed Execution Boundaries: Agents execute commands strictly inside ephemeral gVisor or Docker containers with strict network isolation, preventing lateral movement or unauthorized external API calls.

5. Managing Network Partitions and Split-Brain Recovery
Cloud-native agent infrastructure is susceptible to intermittent network partitions—whether due to API rate-limit throttling by LLM providers, container bridge dropouts, or node resource exhaustion. When a worker node loses connectivity with the orchestrator, it must fail safely.

Robust orchestrators implement strict leasing mechanisms. Workers hold lease tokens with short TTLs (Time-To-Live). If a worker fails to heartbeat within 30 seconds due to a network partition, the orchestrator revokes its lease, reallocates its assigned slice to a healthy worker node, and quarantines the isolated worktree until state reconciliation can be safely executed.

Conclusion
Scaling autonomous AI swarms from experimental prototypes to enterprise-grade production systems requires shifting our focus away from prompt engineering and toward classical distributed systems engineering. By implementing replicated state machines, quorum-based validation, Byzantine fault tolerance, and strict consensus loops, engineering teams can harness the immense speed of autonomous agents without sacrificing system reliability or security.

event_model_payload.headline: I Kept Generated Video Templates Editable Without Letting Them Drift
event_model_payload.summary:
I needed a generated video to remain editable after a customer changed a headline, swapped an image, or asked for a different CTA. The dependable approach is to preserve one validated VideoJSON document, expose only the fields people should touch, then render from that same document. That keeps a template flexible without letting timing, branding, or media assumptions silently drift.

The tempting shortcut is to render the first MP4, let someone request changes in a separate editor, and hope the next version resembles the first. That loses the source of truth immediately. Instead, I treat the template as a small contract: generated data is an input, VideoJSON is the saved working document, an editor is the controlled change surface, and a renderer is the final delivery step.

The boundary that stopped template drift

A video template should not make every property editable merely because the timeline can support it. In a product, I divide fields into three buckets before opening an editor:

Field type Example Who can change it? Why
Locked structure scene order, duration budget, required legal frame developer or template owner protects the promise the template was designed to make
Safe content product name, price, image URL, CTA, locale generator and approved user controls expected variation
Guarded creative control crop, music level, transition choice user with validation can improve a result but can also break readability

That table is deliberately boring. It is also the part that prevents an innocent copy edit from becoming a 19-second product video with a missing CTA. If a field has a visual or compliance consequence, name its owner and validation rule before it gets into the UI.

VideoFlow is useful here because its core compiles an authored flow into portable VideoJSON, and the same document can drive a live preview, browser export, or server render. That is the important architectural detail—not that JSON is fashionable, but that preview, edit, and output are no longer three loosely related representations.

Generate data, then validate a video document

I do not send an LLM or a catalog row straight to an MP4 renderer. It should first produce a narrow input object, then a template function maps that object into the known video shape. The template owner remains responsible for defaults and timing.

import VideoFlow from "@videoflow/core";

type ProductInput = {
  title: string;
  imageUrl: string;
  cta: string;
};

export async function makeDraft(input: ProductInput) {
  const $ = new VideoFlow({ name: input.title, width: 1080, height: 1080, fps: 30 });

  $.addImage({ fit: "cover" }, { source: input.imageUrl });
  $.addText({ text: input.title, fontSize: 7, fontWeight: 800 });
  $.wait("2.5s");
  $.addText({ text: input.cta, fontSize: 4, fontWeight: 700 });

  return $.compile(); // save this VideoJSON before any render
}

In production I would validate title, imageUrl, duration, allowed font sizes, and asset domains around that function. The point is that the generated values fill known slots; they do not invent scene order, arbitrary effects, or a renderer configuration. This is the same principle behind the review gate in my earlier VideoJSON pipeline guide: make a structured draft inspectable before an expensive or irreversible step.

Let customers edit the document, not the output

When a person needs more than a form can offer, give them a constrained editing surface on the saved document. VideoFlow’s React Video Editor takes VideoJSON, offers a multi-track timeline and live preview, and returns changes through callbacks. Persistence remains my job.

import { VideoEditor } from "@videoflow/react-video-editor";
import "@videoflow/react-video-editor/style.css";

export function CustomerVideo({ video, save }: { video: unknown; save: (next: unknown) => Promise<void> }) {
  return (
    <VideoEditor
      video={video}
      theme="night"
      onChange={(next) => save(next)}
      onSave={async (next) => save(next)}
      onUpload={async (file) => ({ url: await uploadAsset(file), type: file.type })}
    />
  );
}

The component is not a permission system. I still enforce the contract server-side when saving: reject a changed frame rate, missing required layer, disallowed media URL, or a timeline beyond the duration budget. A UI restriction is a usability aid; validation is the actual safety boundary.

My four checks before an export enters a queue

Here is the small receipt I would save beside every render request:

  1. Source identity: template version, input ID, and a hash or revision of the VideoJSON.
  2. Structural validity: required scenes and layers exist; duration, resolution, and FPS meet the template rule.
  3. Asset readiness: every media URL is reachable and allowed by policy.
  4. Delivery choice: browser export for a user-operated, privacy-sensitive small job; server rendering for queues, batches, and APIs.

VideoFlow’s browser renderer can create an MP4 Blob client-side and supports progress plus cancellation; its server renderer is intended for headless Node jobs and queue-style work. I would choose based on where the job belongs, not based on where the template was authored. The document can stay the same.

That separation also makes failures explainable. If preview looks right but server output is wrong, compare the saved VideoJSON revision and renderer configuration. If a customer change breaks a scene, inspect the rejected validation rule rather than trying to reverse-engineer an MP4.

A practical rollout sequence

Start with one template, one input schema, and one user role. Store the compiled VideoJSON after generation, render a DOM preview, and let a tester change only copy and media. Then add the guarded controls one at a time.

For an example of why I keep a clear source-to-output handoff, see the publishing contract I added to an automation pipeline. The domain is different, but the discipline is the same: a saved contract gives reviewers something concrete to approve and debuggers something concrete to compare.

TL;DR

Keep VideoJSON as the editable source of truth. Generate data into a controlled template, validate every saved revision, expose only intentional edit controls, and render the exact approved revision in the environment that fits the job.

That is enough to make generated video feel flexible to customers without turning every request into a fresh manual timeline. What fields would you lock first in a customer-editable video template?

event_model_payload.summary:
Every week CISA adds vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. The bar for getting on that list is not "severe on paper" but "attackers are using it now". For a small team with limited patching hours, that makes KEV the most useful priority list there is.

Below: every entry added between 9 November and 15 November 2026, copied from the catalogue and linked to its NVD record, plus what Romania's national cyber security directorate and Have I Been Pwned published in the same days. Nothing is estimated or rewritten.

The 12 actively exploited vulnerabilities added this week

10 Nov Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability CVE-2026-111793 not known
10 Nov Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-111560 not known
9 Nov IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability CVE-2026-123218 not known
9 Nov OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability CVE-2026-123158 not known
9 Nov SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-116779 not known

Breaches added to Have I Been Pwned

  • YouHack: 7,160,849 accounts, added 11 November. Check the breach page
  • СберСпасибо (SberSpasibo): 3,288,711 accounts, added 11 November. Check the breach page
  • CastleRAT: 179,745 accounts, added 13 November. Check the breach page

If your team's work addresses may be in one of these, check the breach page and the password reuse question, not only the address.

How to use a list like this in an hour

  1. Start with what faces the internet. VPN and access gateways, firewalls, routers, mail servers and public web platforms are how many ransomware incidents start.
  2. Search your inventory by product name, not by memory. "We don't run that" is a claim, and the asset list is the evidence.
  3. Patch or apply the vendor mitigation, then confirm the version. A patch that was downloaded but not applied reads as done in a ticket and is still exploitable.
  4. If you cannot patch today, reduce exposure: restrict the management interface to known addresses, disable the affected feature, or put the service behind an access gateway you trust.

Where this comes from

A small collector reads official sources every hour: DNSC, CERT-EU, CERT-FR (ANSSI), CERT-Bund (BSI), the UK NCSC, CISA KEV, Have I Been Pwned and three specialist newsrooms. It copies each item exactly, with its source link, and publishes the result on one page:

https://devaland.cloud/alerte-live.html (in Romanian, with every title kept in its original language).

Nothing on that page or in this post is written by a model. A security page that paraphrases an advisory wrongly does more harm than no page at all.
