event_model_payload.headline: Enabling the parallel frontend on nightly
event_model_payload.summary:
TL;DR: We are enabling the parallel frontend of the Rust compiler on nightly by default, to find remaining issues in preparation for its stabilization.

Context

The Rust compiler has been using multiple threads to compile code in its "backend" part (using LLVM) for a long time. However, its "frontend" part (which includes type checking and borrow checking) has been executing sequentially, on a single thread, which of course limits the performance of the compiler. If you are interested in a more in-depth explanation of parallelism in the Rust compiler, see this previous post.

The compiler frontend actually had support for running in parallel for a long time, but it was not enabled by default due to various issues. Three years ago, we made it possible to opt into the parallel frontend on the nightly channel, with the plan to stabilize it in 2024. Clearly, we did not achieve that goal, but work on the parallel frontend was still slowly progressing in the meantime.

Last year, Vadim Petrochenkov, together with several other contributors, started a coordinated effort to finally get the parallel frontend over the finish line. Since then, many long-standing issues were fixed, and its performance was improved. Now we are at a point where we would like to make it widely available. But before that, we want to find out if people encounter issues with it in the wild, which is why we are enabling it by default only on the nightly channel. Once we will be confident enough that it is working well, we want to stabilize it.

The parallel frontend has been enabled on the nightly channel by default since nightly-2026-11-14.

Benefits

The primary benefit of enabling the parallel frontend is, of course, faster compilation of Rust programs.

We benchmarked the parallel frontend in our benchmark suite, which measures the duration to compile the leaf crate in a crate graph. As usual, the results were varied. In some benchmarks, the parallel frontend barely helped. In others, for example when performing a cargo check of the nalgebra, cargo or diesel crates, the compilation was almost three times faster, using 8 threads.

In the table below, you can find the aggregated wall-time mean change for the real-world benchmarks in our suite, when building a single crate from scratch across several configurations, compared to the same build using a sequential frontend.

Frontend threads / Profilecheckclippydebugopt
2-21.95 %-20.74 %-14.2 %-12.51 %
4-37.99 %-36.01 %-29.14 %-23.67 %
8-44.23 %-41.76 %-36.1 %-27.88 %

It is clear that the parallelization is not perfect, and we definitely plan to invest more effort into improving its performance. Nevertheless, with 8 threads, it can make the end-to-end compilation time of cargo check ~2x faster for several crates that we tested, which is still quite an improvement.

The performance benefits for incremental rebuilds are much more modest, and also very hard to compare, because the performance of rebuilds depends on what was changed and how were the codegen units laid out. In our benchmark suite, we saw a mean improvement of 3-5% for incremental rebuilds. But we currently do not have great benchmarks for this use-case, so your results might vary.

We can also zoom in on an individual crate. Here is a chart of how the wall-time scales when compiling the nalgebra 0.33 crate, for a full non-incremental build (full), full incremental build (incr-full) and an incremental rebuild (incr-patched) across several build configurations:

What is interesting to note is that enabling the parallel frontend can actually also make the backend faster, for reasons explained here.

It is important to note that all benchmark results presented above measured only the compilation of a single crate. When compiling a whole crate graph, your CPU cores might already be saturated because of backend (LLVM) parallelism or by Cargo compiling multiple crates in parallel. So the final performance effect will vary heavily based on the workload that you are running, and on the number of cores that you have available.

We also benchmarked cargo check end-to-end (checking the whole crate graph) on the cargo crate itself on a machine with 8 CPU cores. With 8 threads, it resulted in a ~15% end-to-end improvement:

  • 36.7s with 1 frontend thread
  • 35.1s with 2 frontend threads
  • 31.9s with 4 frontend threads
  • 30.8s with 8 frontend threads

As can be seen from the results above, when the CPU cores are already saturated with parallel crate compilation and LLVM, the positive effect of the parallel frontend is reduced.

Tuning the thread count

At the start, the nightly toolchain will default to the parallel frontend using only 2 threads. This is a conservative choice that should still allow us to find potential issues while not increasing memory usage a lot at the same time.

If you want to test out the performance with different thread counts, you can override the number of threads used for the frontend using the --jobs-frontend compiler flag. It can be specified either in the RUSTFLAGS environment variable, or you can put it into a .cargo/config.toml file:

[build]
rustflags = ["-Zunstable-options", "--jobs-frontend=8"]

Currently, the performance of the parallel frontend will likely not scale very well above ~8 threads, but you can try it on your workload to test what happens. Note that using higher thread counts will likely lead to higher memory usage of the compiler, and in extreme cases it might cause you to run out of memory.

Limitations and known issues

Due to the used parallelism, the produced order of diagnostics might not be deterministic when using the parallel frontend.

In some situations, the generated binary might also not be reproducible, though we currently consider these cases bugs, and we would like to identify them and fix them.

There are currently some known issues related to the reproducibility of the Rust compiler when using the parallel frontend, which are being worked on.

How do I opt out?

To reiterate: this is only being enabled on nightly for now. If you are using the stable toolchain, you will still be using the sequential frontend by default.

If you want to disable the parallel frontend on the nightly channel, pass -Zunstable-options --jobs-frontend=1 to rustc, either via the RUSTFLAGS environment variable, or with the .cargo/config.toml configuration file:

[build]
rustflags = ["-Zunstable-options", "--jobs-frontend=1"]

If you have to do this for some reason, please do tell us why on GitHub or on Zulip. We would especially like to know about any compiler crashes that you encounter, or the produced binaries not being reproducible when the parallel frontend is enabled.

What's next?

Over the next few months, we will be monitoring GitHub and Zulip for any reported issues about the parallel frontend. Once we have enough confidence that it is working well, and there are no major issues, we would like to move forward and finally stabilize it.

We would also like to improve its performance, and make more things parallel. So far, a lot of the work on the parallel frontend has been focused on making it work correctly, rather than tuning its performance down to the last percent. We thus expect that we might still be able to make further performance improvements to it.

We would also like to make more parts of the frontend actually parallel, as some parts are currently still sequential even if parallelism is enabled. There is some ongoing work on this. Last year, we had a Google Summer of Code project focused on enabling parallel macro expansion and name resolution, and there is also an open pull request for parallelizing the lowering of the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to the High-Level Intermediate Representation (HIR). More work remains to be done on this front.

event_model_payload.headline: Latchkey vs GitHub hosted runners, and where each one wins
event_model_payload.summary:
Latchkey vs GitHub hosted runners comes down to a number you can compute from two published rate cards: $0.0025 a minute against $0.006 is 58% cheaper per 2 vCPU Linux minute, but Latchkey charges a monthly plan fee and GitHub gives you a monthly dollar allowance, so the break-even sits near 7,700 Linux minutes a month. Below that, staying put is cheaper, and on a public repository nothing paid can compete at all.


A GitHub Team plan with $18 of included usage (3,000 Linux minutes at $0.006) against the $19 Latchkey Launch plan with 4,000 included minutes, at published rates read 20 September 2026 and GitHub's allowance read 12 November 2026. The lines cross at 7,714 Linux minutes a month.

GitHub-hosted runners are the default and the safe answer: nothing to install, an included monthly allowance, every platform GitHub sells, and larger runners up to 96 vCPU. The standard Linux runner on a private repository is 2 vCPU with 8 GB of RAM and 14 GB of disk; on a public repository the same label gives 4 vCPU and 16 GB, free and unlimited.

Latchkey sells managed runners you adopt with a runs-on change, at $0.0025 a minute for 2 vCPU and 8 GB with 100 GB of disk, rising to $0.02 at 16 vCPU. Its argument is the rate plus what happens when a job fails for a mechanical reason: the runner diagnoses the failure and retries inside the run rather than handing it back to you. Its limits are equally plain, and they are listed below rather than buried.

Every cell below was read from the vendor's own public pricing or documentation page on 20 September 2026. Where a vendor does not publish a number, the cell says "not published" instead of carrying a guess.

Comparison

GitHub-hosted Latchkey
Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.006 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD on a private repo; free on public repos) $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.012 as a larger runner; the free public-repo standard runner is already 4 vCPU and 16 GB $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)
Free tier $12 of compute a month on Free, $18 on Pro and Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud (2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes), private repos only, deducted at each runner's own rate; larger runners can draw from it on Team and Enterprise Cloud and are billed on public repos 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale
Billing granularity Every job is rounded up to the nearest whole minute Per minute
Runner sizes and OS Linux x64 and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64, macOS on Apple silicon and Intel; larger runners to 96 vCPU x64 and 64 vCPU arm64 2, 4, 8 and 16 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 only. arm64, Windows and macOS are not offered
Cache: type, limit, persistence actions/cache, 10 GB per repository, entries removed after 7 days without access, restorable only from the same or the default branch Size not published. latchkey-dev/cache-action@v1 replaces actions/cache with a restore step and a save step, keeping path and key (no restore-keys); entries are isolated per organization, versioned by OS, kept 14 days; a failed restore warns rather than failing the job
Docker build acceleration None built in. cache-to: type=gha writes into the same 10 GB store latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, layers held in a Latchkey-managed private registry per organization
Concurrency limits 20 concurrent jobs on Free, 40 on Pro, 60 on Team, 500 on Enterprise Cloud. macOS is capped separately at 5, or 50 on Enterprise Developer 20, Launch 40, Scale 80 busy runners per workspace; idle warm runners do not count
Where jobs run GitHub's own hosted fleet Latchkey's own AWS estate on m6a-class hosts, one job per runner, no inbound access, destroyed after the job
Self-healing or retries None. A failed job waits for a person, or for retry logic you wrote yourself Built in: transient failures are diagnosed and retried inside the run
Setup change required None; this is the default A runs-on label change. GitHub organization accounts only

Where GitHub-hosted wins

This is the section that decides the page, so it goes first. Four of these are structural, not a matter of taste, and on any one of them the comparison is over before the rate card matters.

  • Public repositories. Standard GitHub-hosted runners are free and unlimited there, on a 4 vCPU and 16 GB machine, which is a better runner than the 2 vCPU tier anyone sells and costs nothing at all.
  • Anything that is not Linux x86_64. Latchkey has no arm64, no Windows and no macOS runner. If your matrix builds an iOS app or a Windows binary, those jobs stay on GitHub-hosted and your bill has two vendors on it.
  • Low volume. GitHub includes $12 of compute a month on Free, $18 on Team and $300 on Enterprise Cloud, which is 2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes at $0.006, and Latchkey charges $5 to $49 a month before the first minute. Under a few thousand Linux minutes, the plan fee is larger than the saving.
  • Personal accounts. Latchkey works with GitHub organization accounts only, so a repository under a personal account cannot use it whatever the price.
  • Sizes above 16 vCPU. GitHub sells larger runners to 96 vCPU x64 and 64 vCPU arm64; Latchkey publishes four sizes and stops at 16.
  • Published concurrency. GitHub states 20 to 500 concurrent jobs by plan and 5 concurrent macOS jobs, 50 on Enterprise. Latchkey documents 20 busy runners per workspace by default, raised on request, in its runner limits read 2026-09-20, so a wide matrix queues sooner than it would on a Team plan. The same page caps a job at four hours.

The break-even, in one line of arithmetic

Both sides have a fixed part and a variable part, so a per-minute comparison on its own is misleading. On a GitHub Team plan, GitHub prices every Linux minute at $0.006 and subtracts the $18 of included usage, so you pay nothing for the first 3,000 minutes and $0.006 a minute after that. On the Latchkey Launch plan you pay $19 a month, get 4,000 included minutes, then pay $0.0025. Set the two equal and the crossover is 7,714 Linux minutes a month.

That is the number to check your own usage against, and it moves with the plan you would actually buy: on the $49 Scale plan, with 6,000 included minutes, the crossover is 14,857 minutes a month. Everything below assumes 2 vCPU Linux jobs on a private repository, which is the comparison most teams are actually making.

Linux minutes a month, 2 vCPU GitHub-hosted on Team Latchkey on Launch ($19) Cheaper
2,000 $0, $12 inside the $18 included $19, inside the 4,000 included GitHub-hosted
5,000 $12: $30 less the $18 included $21.50 for 1,000 billed minutes GitHub-hosted
7,714 $28.28 $28.29 Level
10,000 $42: $60 less the $18 included $34 for 6,000 billed minutes Latchkey
20,000 $102 $59 Latchkey
50,000 $282 $134 Latchkey

Speed

Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. We have not run the same workload on these runners ourselves, and until we have, there is no number here worth quoting.

The cheap way to get a real answer is to point one slow job at each candidate for a week, because runner selection is per job and the Actions run log gives you the timings for free.

Cost: the same month, both ways

The table above nets each side's included allowance off, because that is how a Linux-only bill actually arrives. The one below does not: it is the workload every comparison here uses, stated gross on both sides so the pages are comparable, at 10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes a month on a private repository.

10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU 2,000 macOS minutes Monthly total
GitHub-hosted $60 at $0.006/min $124 at $0.062/min $184
Latchkey $25 at $0.0025/min Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted $149 plus $5 to $49 a month for the plan

Read that table with the macOS column in mind, because it is doing most of the work. Latchkey has no macOS runner, so those 2,000 minutes stay on GitHub-hosted at $0.062 a minute in both rows, and the entire difference between $184 and $149 comes from the Linux line. Latchkey's own plan is $5 to $49 a month on top of that compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off, so the figure is gross on both counts.

One more line that catches teams out, and it is GitHub's, not ours: the included allowance is a dollar amount, and each runner spends it at its own rate. A macOS minute is $0.062, so a Team plan's $18 is gone after about 290 macOS minutes, which is why so many Actions bills turn out to be mostly macOS. If that is your shape, macOS runner cost is a more useful page than this one, and no Linux rate will fix it.

Reliability

GitHub publishes a status history rather than an Actions SLA, and Latchkey publishes no uptime figure either, so treat both as unmeasured on that axis and do not let either of us claim otherwise. What is different is documented behavior on a bad job. On GitHub-hosted, a step that dies because a registry timed out, a browser binary did not install, or the kernel killed the process fails the job, bills the minutes it burned, and waits for a person; the re-run bills again.

Latchkey runners diagnose that class of failure and retry inside the run. It is worth being precise about what that does not cover: a compile error, a failing assertion or a genuine out-of-memory in your own code are not transient, and retrying them would be a bug rather than a feature. The way to size the difference is to count the runs in your own history that passed on the second attempt with no code change between them, which is the same measurement exit code 137 in GitHub Actions walks through for one specific failure.

Switching: the exact diff

One label per job, and nothing else in the workflow moves: steps, actions, secrets, matrix and artifacts are untouched, and reverting is the same edit backwards. Runner selection is per job, so the sensible trial is one job for a fortnight rather than a repository-wide decision, and a mixed file with macOS jobs still on GitHub-hosted is the normal end state rather than a compromise.

jobs:
   test:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: latchkey-small

   build:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: latchkey-medium

   ios:
     # stays on GitHub-hosted: Latchkey has no macOS runner
     runs-on: macos-latest

The verdict

If your CI is public, low volume, or built on anything other than Linux x86_64, GitHub-hosted is the right answer and this comparison is not close. The case for Latchkey starts at roughly 7,700 private-repo Linux minutes a month on a Team plan, where the 58% lower rate finally clears the plan fee, and it gets stronger from there: at 20,000 minutes it is $59 against $102, and at 50,000 it is $134 against $282. The second half of the case is the one the rate cards cannot show, which is what happens to the jobs that fail for reasons that have nothing to do with your code, and the honest way to price that is to count your own re-runs rather than to take our word for it. Whatever you decide, the decision is one line per job and reversible in a minute, which is the strongest argument for testing it on one job instead of arguing about it.

FAQ

Is Latchkey cheaper than GitHub-hosted runners?

Per minute, yes: $0.0025 against $0.006 at 2 vCPU is 58% lower, and $0.01 against $0.022 at 8 vCPU is 55% lower. Per month it depends on volume, because Latchkey charges $5 to $49 for a plan and GitHub includes $12 to $300 of compute a month (2,000 to 50,000 standard Linux minutes). Comparing a GitHub Team plan with the $19 Latchkey Launch plan, the two are level at about 7,714 Linux minutes a month and Latchkey is cheaper above that. On public repositories GitHub-hosted is free, so nothing paid wins there.

Do Latchkey minutes count against my GitHub included minutes?

No. A third-party managed runner registers with GitHub as a self-hosted runner, and GitHub's billing documentation states that Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners, so those jobs are not metered by GitHub at all. Your included allowance stays available for the jobs you leave on GitHub-hosted runners, which in practice is usually macOS and Windows.

Is there a limit on usage by public repos?

Standard GitHub-hosted runners are free and unlimited on public repositories, subject to GitHub's usage limits on job and workflow duration, and the free public-repo Linux runner is 4 vCPU with 16 GB rather than the 2 vCPU and 8 GB a private repository gets. Larger runners are billed even on public repositories. There is no cost case for a paid runner on a public repo, and we are not going to invent one.

What does Latchkey not offer?

No arm64, no Windows and no macOS runners: Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 only, in four sizes from 2 to 16 vCPU. No support for repositories under personal accounts, since it works with GitHub organizations only. A default ceiling of 20 busy runners per workspace, and no published uptime SLA. And a plan fee of $5 to $49 a month whose included minutes are separate from, not netted off, the per-minute compute.

References

  • GitHub Actions per-minute rates by runner
  • GitHub Actions billing: included compute by plan, in dollars
  • GitHub-hosted runner specifications
  • GitHub Actions usage limits and concurrency
  • GitHub larger runner sizes, to 96 cores on Linux x64 and 64 on arm64
  • Latchkey pricing: plans, included minutes and per-minute rates

event_model_payload.headline: Microsoft 365 was down for over twelve hours: what the outage says about our dependency
event_model_payload.summary:
It started unspectacularly: Outlook could not connect to the mailbox. Anyone who assumed their own network was at fault restarted Outlook, then the computer, then the router. Two hours later it was clear the router was not the problem: Microsoft had a global outage hitting Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot and a long tail of other services — and it was still not fully over on Friday morning.

What happened on 12 November 2026

Microsoft published two incidents in the admin center. EX1550543 covers Exchange Online, the mailbox behind Outlook, starting at 11:17 a.m. Eastern — 17:17 CET. MO1550821 followed at 1:26 p.m. Eastern and lists the services dragged in with it: Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Defender XDR, plus Planner, To Do, Intune, Purview, parts of Power BI, Universal Print and, in some setups, Windows 365 Cloud PCs.

Important for scale: what was affected were the parts that depend on Exchange Online. In Teams, chat and running meetings kept working, but calendars and scheduling did not. Files in SharePoint still opened. It was not a total product failure, it was a failure of the shared middle — and in Microsoft 365 that middle hangs off one identity, one tenant and one mail service.

The timeline, as far as Microsoft published it

Time (CET) What Microsoft reported
17:20 Investigating a possible problem with Exchange Online.
18:45 Connection errors in the part of Exchange Online that accepts logins and mailbox requests.
19:27 Infrastructure under heavy load in several regions; restarts and traffic shifting begin.
20:30 The load is not coming from more requests: a large number of servers dropped out of service unexpectedly. Microsoft pauses its own deployments.
20:58 The servers fail automatic health checks — the fault may sit in the part that answers those checks.
23:03 The actions so far "have not provided the anticipated relief".
01:12 The overwhelmed process is the one that sets up secure connections (TLS). Microsoft starts rolling back a recent network configuration change.
02:48 Restarts show "positive results", first regions recover.

As of Friday morning there was no confirmed root cause, only a preliminary technical explanation. Microsoft stated repeatedly that it saw no indication of malicious activity. More than 130,000 reports piled up on Downdetector alone.

What the outage teaches technically

Three things stand out, and none of them is a Microsoft problem in the narrow sense.

First: the trigger was not an attack and not data loss, but a health check that removes servers from service. That is exactly the intended behaviour — it just caught too many servers at once, at the wrong moment. Automation without a manual escape hatch scales mistakes.

Second: a single overwhelmed process for secure connections was enough to make mailboxes unreachable. If you think of mail as "just storage", you underestimate the chain: DNS, TLS, auth, mailbox, client. Any link can stop the whole thing.

Third: the 99.9 percent availability in the SLA sounds like "almost always". A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes, 0.1 percent of that is 43 minutes. An outage of this length blows the monthly target for many customers. The remedy is a credit on the monthly bill — not automatic, on request, and it does not replace a lost workday.

The real dependency is identity

What actually failed during those twelve hours was not Outlook. It was the anchor everything else hangs from: if you cannot sign in, you cannot open files, see appointments, schedule a meeting, approve something and — with Teams Phone — you cannot even make a call. A mailbox today is rarely just a mailbox. It is the login, the calendar, the chat, the archive and often the second factor for authentication.

This is not a criticism of cloud, it is a description of the architecture. Putting office communication into one tenant buys convenience, versioning and operations — and pays with a shared failure point. That is a deliberate trade-off, as long as it is made deliberately.

What Nextcloud replaces — and what it does not

After a day like this the question is inevitable: "why not self-host everything?" The honest answer is more nuanced than either camp likes.

Building block Nextcloud Note
Files & sync yes, with versions and trash The desktop client keeps selected folders available offline.
Calendar & contacts yes (CalDAV/CardDAV) Works in Thunderbird, Apple Calendar, Android and iOS without the web login.
Chat & video calls yes (Talk) A good base for internal calls; it does not replace Teams telephony.
Editing documents via Collabora/OnlyOffice Solid for most documents, not feature-parity with Word.
Mailbox no Nextcloud is not a mail server. A mailbox needs its own MX or another provider.
Phone system no Anyone using Teams Phone needs a separate solution.

So Nextcloud covers a large part of the office day — files, calendar, contacts, chat, documents — but it is not an Exchange replacement and not a phone system. Claiming otherwise builds the next disappointment. Separating it cleanly wins exactly what this is about: a piece of infrastructure you can see yourself.

"Everything under control" does not mean "it never breaks"

Self-hosting is not automatically more reliable. A single server is a single point of failure, a forgotten update is a security risk, and a backup with an untested restore is data loss on a delay. The difference is not the probability of failure, it is the ability to act:

  • Logs: you can see which process did what and when, instead of waiting for a status message.
  • Update timing: you decide when to update — and you can plan a rollback instead of suffering one.
  • Data: files and calendars live where you can back them up and restore them.
  • Communication: you can explain what is going on, because you can trace the cause yourself.

Control is not a guarantee, it is the ability to act when it matters. Which is exactly what most Microsoft customers could not do on Thursday: they could wait and refresh the status page.

What I would check in one hour

Whether you run Microsoft 365, Nextcloud or both, these seven points are cheap and pay off during the next outage:

  • A contact list outside the system: key customers, vendors, mobile numbers. Printed, or in a notes tool that does not hang off the same login.
  • A second communication path: a Signal group, a phone chain or a chat outside the tenant — decided in advance and circulated, not on the day of the outage.
  • Files available offline: keep the five documents a workday cannot run without on the device (Nextcloud client or "always keep on this device").
  • One person who says "it's Microsoft": check the status page instead of reinstalling Outlook. Publicly reachable: status.cloud.microsoft.
  • Check scheduled jobs: scan-to-mail, Universal Print, automatic invoices, forms, voicemail-to-mail. These fail quietly and surface only when a customer asks.
  • Test restores, don't just own backups: restore one file and one mailbox per quarter — with a stopwatch.
  • Check your own reachability: MX, SPF, DMARC and the externally visible endpoints. The mail DNS check and the Nextcloud check run without a login and show what the outside world sees.

And Thursday's mail?

Usually delayed, not lost. A sending mail server must retry for at least four to five days before giving up, per RFC 5321. If you are waiting for a signed contract or a bid, call instead of waiting. And if you wrote messages during the outage: check the outbox, do not blindly resend.

Then comes the unpleasant part that follows every large outage: phishing with the story "your mailbox has been restored, please sign in again". No provider asks for a fresh login via an email link during or after an outage. The scam radar collects exactly these patterns.

Bottom line

Thursday's outage was not proof that cloud does not work. It was proof of how much now hangs off a single identity — and how little any one company can do when that identity disappears. If you know the dependency, you can shape it: a clear view of what is truly critical, a second path for communication, and a remainder you control yourself.

For me that means: files, calendars and contacts in my own Nextcloud, with the versions and their end-of-support dates in sight — and something I can check from the outside. Everything under control is not a state, it is a practice.

The dates when the versions in use leave support are in the end-of-life calendar, including a subscribable calendar file. The next outage is coming; the only question is whether it catches you by surprise.

Originally published at daniele-michelin.com. More guides, free checks (SPF, TLS, headers) and an error-message lexicon: daniele-michelin.com/en/.

event_model_payload.headline: The error told you to delete one line. Deleting it changed every answer.
event_model_payload.summary:
A breaking change that fails loudly, and a fix that changes your product silently.

The error told you to delete one line. Deleting it changed every answer your product gives.

What changed

Anthropic's API version 2026-10-21 removed temperature, top_p and top_k from the Messages API. Not deprecated with a grace period. Removed.

The migration guide states it plainly:

In 2026-10-21, a request that sends temperature, top_p, or top_k returns a 400 error, even at the parameter's default value.

So this is a loud failure. Your request breaks, the error names the parameter, and you know exactly what to do.

That part is fine. Loud failures get fixed.

The part that is not loud

The fix is to delete the parameter. The guide then tells you what happens next:

Without these parameters, a request samples with their defaults, including a temperature of 1.0, the same as a 2023-06-01 request that leaves them out.

Your line said 0.0. You deleted it. You are now sampling at 1.0.

And for the models where that difference was real:

On models that accept other values, such as Claude Sonnet 4.6, a request that lowered temperature for more consistent output loses that effect. No other setting replaces it.

No other setting replaces it. That sentence is the whole article.

The sequence, as it actually plays out 

# Before: 2023-06-01, pinned low for a structured extraction task
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    temperature=0.0,          # <- deliberate. consistency matters here.
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
)

You bump the SDK. The call fails with a 400 — something to this effect (exact wording illustrative; the documented behaviour is a 400):

anthropic.BadRequestError: 400 - temperature is not supported
in API version 2026-10-21

You do the obvious thing:

# After: the 400 is gone
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
)

Green. Tests pass. Ship it.

What actually happened:

  1. You upgraded. A 400 appeared. The error named the parameter.
  2. You deleted the parameter. The 400 went away.
  3. Your tests passed — because your tests assert on shape, not on distribution.
  4. Your product's output variance is permanently higher, and nothing in your pipeline said so.

Step 2 is where it happens. The fix that silences an error is not the fix that preserves behaviour. And an error message is written to be silenced — that is its entire job.

Why your test suite will not catch this

Most LLM test suites look like this:

def test_extraction():
    out = extract(SAMPLE_INVOICE)
    assert out["invoice_no"] == "INV-2291"
    assert isinstance(out["line_items"], list)
    assert out["total"] == 118000

That is a shape and value assertion on one sample. At temperature=0.0 it was close to a deterministic check. At 1.0 it is a sample from a distribution that now happens to pass.

It will keep passing. Right up until the day it does not, on a customer's document, in production, with no code change to blame.

What catches it instead:

def test_extraction_is_stable():
    runs = [extract(SAMPLE_INVOICE) for _ in range(20)]
    distinct = {json.dumps(r, sort_keys=True) for r in runs}
    # not "did it work once" but "does it work the same way"
    assert len(distinct) == 1, f"{len(distinct)} distinct outputs in 20 runs"

Slower. More expensive. The only thing that would have told you.

To be fair to the guide

The escape hatch is documented:

If a request relies on a non-default value, either stop sending the parameter, or keep that request on 2023-06-01.

It is right there. It sits in the paragraph most people stop reading after sentence one, immediately below the instruction that fixes their build.

That is not a documentation failure. It is a reading failure, and it is extremely common: when an error message and a fix appear in the same paragraph, the rest of the paragraph does not get read.

The discipline

When a breaking change hands you a fix, ask what the fix changes. "Remove it" is a behaviour change wearing an error message.

Treat sampling settings as product config, not tuning knobs. Write down which of your outputs depend on low variance — structured extraction, classification, anything feeding a downstream parser — and which genuinely do not.

Test distribution, not shape. Run one prompt 20 times and diff them. A schema check will never catch this.

Record the API version your behaviour was measured against, beside the measurement. An eval result without its API version is an incomplete artefact.

Two hard rules

An error you silenced is not a bug you fixed.

If removing a setting is the official fix, that setting was doing something.

While you are in there

From the same source, one dated item worth putting in a calendar:

Deprecated model Retires Recommended replacement
claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 30 November 2026 claude-sonnet-5-5

And the lifecycle definition, verbatim: "Retired: The model is no longer available for use. Requests to retired models fail."

That one, at least, is not silent.

Anthropic also states it provides "at least 60 days' notice before model retirement for publicly released models" — and the console has a usage export that breaks your traffic down by API key and model, which is the fastest way to find out whether a deprecated model is still in your path.

Honest limitation

I am reading Anthropic's own migration guide and model-deprecation page, and every quote above comes from them.

I have not measured the variance change on a production workload. How large it is depends entirely on your prompts: a tightly constrained extraction prompt with a rigid schema may move barely at all, while an open-ended generation task may move a lot. The point is not the size of the effect. The point is that the change happened and nothing told you.

Checkable references

  • "Migrating to API version 2026-10-21" — Claude platform docs
  • "Model deprecations" — Claude platform docs

One open question

When you removed temperature to clear that 400 — did anyone measure the output before and after?

event_model_payload.headline: Price comparison: Amazon, AliExpress, eBay, Walmart, Etsy with Python
event_model_payload.summary:
What does a ceramic mug cost online? It depends where you look: Amazon, AliExpress, eBay, Walmart and Etsy each show different products, different sellers, different shipping terms and very different prices for the same words. Sellers who source or price a product, and anyone building a price comparison page, need those five answers side by side, in the same columns. This tutorial does a price comparison across Amazon, AliExpress, eBay, Walmart and Etsy with Python: one keyword, one run, one table, then the cheapest product on each marketplace and a price summary per marketplace with pandas. The data comes from the Marketplace Price Comparison Actor on Apify, called through the official Python client.

What you need

  • An Apify account (the free plan is enough to try this) and its API token, from Apify Console → Settings → API & Integrations, exported as an environment variable: export APIFY_TOKEN=...
  • Python 3 and two packages: 
pip install "apify-client>=3,<4" pandas

The common table

The Actor searches every marketplace for the same keywords in one run and returns one flat row per product, with the same columns whatever the marketplace:

  • marketplace (amazon, aliexpress, ebay, walmart or etsy), searchQuery and rankInMarketplace, the product's position in that marketplace's best-match order;
  • title, url, imageUrl, platformProductId (the marketplace's own id) and, when shown, brand and category;
  • price and currency, originalPrice and discountPercent for a deal, inStock;
  • shippingFree, shippingCost, deliveryEstimate, shipsFrom;
  • rating on 5, reviewCount, soldCount (units sold, where the marketplace publishes it), storeType (platform, business, individual or unknown) and isSponsored.

A value a marketplace does not show is null, so a CSV export keeps the same columns from run to run. Private sellers are never named; review texts and their authors are never collected.

Step 1: the input 

run_input = {
    "searchQueries": ["ceramic mug"],
    "marketplaces": ["amazon", "aliexpress", "ebay", "walmart", "etsy"],
    "maxResultsPerMarketplace": 20,
    "country": "US",
}

This is the public task "Compare ceramic mug prices on Etsy, eBay and AliExpress", with Amazon and Walmart added. country picks each marketplace's site (amazon.com, ebay.com, walmart.com, etsy.com, AliExpress shipping to the US) and the currency, USD here. maxResultsPerMarketplace caps the products per keyword and marketplace, so this run returns at most 100 rows.

Choose the keyword with Etsy in mind: Etsy only has results for common product words such as "ceramic mug" or "phone case". For "wireless earbuds" or "air fryer", keep the default marketplaces (Amazon, AliExpress, eBay and Walmart). Other useful fields: condition (new or used), and priceMin / priceMax for a price range, applied by each marketplace's filter and checked again on every product.

Step 2: run it and save the table

Save this as compare_prices.py:

import os

import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

run_input = {
    "searchQueries": ["ceramic mug"],
    "marketplaces": ["amazon", "aliexpress", "ebay", "walmart", "etsy"],
    "maxResultsPerMarketplace": 20,
    "country": "US",
}

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("myth84/marketplace-price-compare-scraper").call(run_input=run_input)
rows = list(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())

for item in rows[:8]:
    print(item["marketplace"], item["rankInMarketplace"], item["price"], item["currency"], item["title"][:60])

df = pd.json_normalize(rows)
columns = [
    "marketplace", "rankInMarketplace", "title", "price", "currency", "shippingFree", "shippingCost",
    "deliveryEstimate", "rating", "reviewCount", "soldCount", "storeType", "isSponsored", "url",
]
df[columns].to_csv("ceramic-mug-5-marketplaces.csv", index=False)
print(df["marketplace"].value_counts())

pd.json_normalize turns each row into one line and flattens attributes, the small object of facts that only some marketplaces show, into columns such as attributes.condition (eBay and Walmart) or attributes.boughtPastMonth (Amazon's "bought in past month", a monthly lower bound). The CSV is the common table: one line per product, whatever the marketplace.

Step 3: the cheapest on each marketplace

Three things to know before calling a product "the cheapest":

  • Welcome deals. AliExpress shows part of its products at a price for first-time buyers only, flagged by attributes.newShopperDeal. That price is not one anybody can pay, so leave those rows out.
  • No featured offer. Amazon shows some products without a price, when no seller has the featured offer: price is empty, and the filter below leaves those rows out.
  • Shipping. price is the displayed price, shipping not included. shippingCost gives the shipping price when the marketplace shows it; shippingFree is true when shipping is free and empty when the marketplace says nothing.

Add this to the script:

welcome = df.get("attributes.newShopperDeal", pd.Series("false", index=df.index)).eq("true")
anyone = df[~welcome & df["price"].notna() & (df["currency"] == "USD")].copy()
anyone["withShipping"] = anyone["price"] + anyone["shippingCost"].fillna(0)

cheapest = anyone.sort_values("withShipping").groupby("marketplace").head(1)
print(cheapest[["marketplace", "title", "price", "shippingCost", "withShipping", "url"]].to_string(index=False))

summary = anyone.groupby("marketplace").agg(
    products=("title", "count"),
    lowest=("price", "min"),
    median=("price", "median"),
    highest=("price", "max"),
    medianRating=("rating", "median"),
    medianSold=("soldCount", "median"),
)
print(summary.sort_values("median"))

cheapest holds one line per marketplace: the lowest price shipping included, as far as each marketplace shows it, with the link. summary gives, per marketplace, the number of products compared, the lowest, median and highest price, the median rating and the median units sold (empty where the marketplace publishes no sales figure, such as Amazon and Walmart). The median is the number to look at: one very cheap accessory or one premium set can make the lowest and highest misleading, and the median says what the typical product of the first results costs.

The comparison stays within one currency: no exchange rate is applied, which is why the filter keeps the US dollar rows. For the full rows of a marketplace, filter the DataFrame on marketplace and sort it by soldCount or rating.

Several keywords, every day

searchQueries takes several lines; each keyword is compared separately, and searchQuery tells the rows apart. Group by ["searchQuery", "marketplace"] instead of "marketplace" and the summary covers your whole catalogue in one run.

To follow a market over time, run the script every morning with cron and append the summary to a CSV with today's date: the median price of each marketplace, day after day, shows who moves first. Without code, open the public task in Apify Console, change the keyword, save it as your own task and add a daily schedule; the Output tab has a Comparison view of the products and a summary record per keyword and marketplace with the lowest, median and highest price.

Good to know

  • Each marketplace's own best-match order, sponsored products included and flagged in isSponsored; rankInMarketplace is the position among the rows of the run.
  • One marketplace failing does not stop the others: its status and the reason are in the run log and the summary record. The run fails only when no marketplace returned anything.
  • Amazon is searched on amazon.com, .co.uk, .ca, .de, .fr, .it and .es, Walmart in the US and Canada only; for another country, the marketplace is skipped and the log says so.
  • eBay is searched for fixed-price ("Buy It Now") listings: an auction's current bid is not a price to compare.
  • A product found by two of your keywords on the same marketplace appears once, under the first keyword.
  • No personal data: products, prices, average ratings and review counts; sellers are named only when they are the platform itself or a registered business.

Pricing is pay-per-event: a fixed price per product row, $2.00 per 1,000 on Apify's Free plan, down to $1.29 on the higher plans, whatever the marketplace (this run of up to 100 rows costs at most $0.20). A marketplace that returns nothing costs nothing. Use the data for analysis, respect each marketplace's terms and local law, and do not republish listings.

Disclosure: I build these Actors and may earn a commission if you sign up to Apify through these links.

event_model_payload.headline: pnpm/action-setup: the step order setup-node needs, and one store cache
event_model_payload.summary:
pnpm/action-setup installs pnpm and puts it on PATH; it does not install Node.js, and since v4.3.0 it can cache the pnpm store itself. The order that works is checkout, then pnpm/action-setup, then actions/setup-node with cache: pnpm, because setup-node asks pnpm for its store path and fails if pnpm is not installed yet.


Each step reads something the previous one produced. Read from pnpm/action-setup v6.1.1 and actions/setup-node v7.1.0 source on 2026-11-12.

Most pnpm workflows have three setup steps and one install, and most of the failures come from the order of the first three or from two of them disagreeing about a version. The action reads package.json before it installs anything, setup-node runs pnpm store path before it restores anything, and both can cache the same store with different keys.

The version comes from one of two places, the version input or packageManager in package.json, and setting both to strings that differ fails the step even when they agree on semver. Set neither and you get no pnpm version is specified, which has its own page.

Seven inputs, and an undeclared cache-hit

Seven inputs and two declared outputs. The restore step also sets a third output, cache-hit, which action.yml does not declare; it is true only when the exact key matched.

Input Default What it does
version empty Exact version, a range such as 10 or ^10.9.8, or latest. Required unless package.json names pnpm
dest ~/setup-pnpm Where the bootstrap pnpm is installed
run_install off Run pnpm install inside this step: true, an object or a list
cache false Cache the pnpm store with this action
cache_dependency_path pnpm-lock.yaml File or newline-separated files hashed into the cache key
package_json_file package.json Manifest to read, relative to the repository root; package.yaml also works
standalone false Install @pnpm/exe for pnpm 11 and earlier; no effect on pnpm 12

From action.yml, src/inputs and src/cache-restore/run.ts at v6.1.1 (commit 73e4699), read 2026-11-12. Outputs: dest and bin_dest.

Which pnpm version gets installed

With version empty, the action reads devEngines.packageManager first and packageManager second, stripping any +sha512 suffix. With version set and packageManager also present, it compares the two as plain strings and throws Multiple versions of pnpm specified: when they differ. That comparison is not semver: version: 12 against "packageManager": "pnpm@12.18.0" throws, even though 12.18.0 satisfies 12. Pick one source.

The install itself is a bootstrap pnpm from a lockfile committed in the action, followed by pnpm self-update to your version. For pnpm 11 and earlier, the action also checks the node on PATH and installs the standalone @pnpm/exe when that Node is older than 22.13, whatever standalone says. pnpm 12 ships a native executable and needs no Node at all.

# package.json carries "packageManager": "pnpm@12.18.0"
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@73e46992e05b19abd31f2f3c20e0e7370d762115 # v6.1.1
        # no version input: the manifest decides

The step order, and why it is fixed

Checkout comes first whenever the version lives in package.json, because the action reads the file from the workspace and a missing file is silently treated as no version at all. pnpm/action-setup comes before setup-node whenever setup-node has cache: pnpm: setup-node finds the store with pnpm store path --silent, and without pnpm on PATH it stops with Unable to locate executable file: pnpm. A setup-node maintainer closed the report of that error as expected behavior, since pnpm must be installed before the setup-node step.

Keep the install as its own step after setup-node rather than using run_install. run_install runs inside the pnpm/action-setup step, so it runs before any later setup-node and uses whichever Node happened to be on PATH at that moment.

steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
  - uses: pnpm/action-setup@73e46992e05b19abd31f2f3c20e0e7370d762115 # v6.1.1
  - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
    with:
      node-version: 24
      cache: pnpm
  - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
  - run: pnpm test

Two caches for one store: keep one

Both actions cache the directory pnpm store path prints, and both hash pnpm-lock.yaml by default. They differ in the fallback and in the cleanup. setup-node passes no restore keys, so a lockfile change restores nothing. pnpm/action-setup passes a prefix restore key, so a lockfile change restores the previous store and pnpm downloads only the difference.

The README says the post step prunes the store for you. In the source it runs pnpm store prune only when run_install was set; with a separate install step it logs Pruning is unnecessary. and saves the store unpruned. Turning both caches on uploads the same directory twice under two keys.

One more reason the version matters for caching: the store path contains the store layout version, and an earlier bootstrap pnpm reported a different path from the one your pnpm wrote to, which broke both caches on a cold run. The action now self-updates to your version before asking for the path, and its source names issue #233 as the reason.

pnpm/action-setup cache: true setup-node cache: pnpm
Key pnpm-cache--- node-cache---pnpm-
Restore fallback Prefix pnpm-cache--- None
Store prune before save Only with run_install No
Step order constraint None beyond checkout pnpm must already be installed

Keys from src/cache-restore/run.ts in pnpm/action-setup v6.1.1 and src/cache-restore.ts in actions/setup-node v7.1.0, read 2026-11-12.

run_install, when you do want it

It accepts true (a recursive install), one object, or a list of objects, each with recursive, cwd and args. It is a convenience: a separate step after setup-node does the same work with the Node you chose, and the action exports PNPM_HOME either way, so global installs work in both places.

- uses: pnpm/action-setup@73e46992e05b19abd31f2f3c20e0e7370d762115 # v6.1.1
    with:
      run_install: |
        - recursive: true
          args: [--frozen-lockfile]
        - args: [--global, prettier]

From v2 to pnpm 12 support

v2 stopped working with newer Node.js versions, and the README tells anyone on it to upgrade. For pnpm 11 and later, the same maintainers also publish pnpm/setup, which installs pnpm and a JavaScript runtime in one step; pnpm/action-setup still supports pnpm 12 alongside setup-node.

Release Change
v3.0.0 Runs on Node.js 20
v4.0.0 Throws when version and packageManager disagree
v4.2.0 Fetches pnpm from the registry in a root .npmrc
v4.3.0 cache input added
v5.0.0 Runs on Node.js 24
v6.0.0 pnpm 11 support
v6.1.0 pnpm 12 support

From the GitHub release notes for each tag, read 2026-11-12.

FAQ

Why does setup-node fail with Unable to locate executable file: pnpm?

Because cache: pnpm makes setup-node run pnpm store path --silent during its own step, and pnpm is not installed yet. Move pnpm/action-setup above setup-node, or drop cache: pnpm and use the action's own cache: true, which has no ordering constraint beyond checkout.

How does pnpm/action-setup compare to run: corepack enable?

Both get a pinned pnpm onto the runner. A pnpm maintainer answered in the action's issue tracker that there is nothing wrong with corepack, and that pnpm's docs at the time recommended it for every CI except GitHub Actions. The action adds the store cache, the version input and the standalone executable on old Node.

Is the action's cache setup equivalent to actions/setup-node's pnpm cache?

They cache the same directory with different keys and different fallbacks. The action restores the previous store on a lockfile change through a prefix restore key; setup-node passes no restore key and starts cold. Use one of them, not both.

Why does pnpm/action-setup throw Multiple versions of pnpm specified?

Because version and packageManager are both set and are not the same string. A major-only version: 12 against pnpm@12.18.0 counts as a mismatch. Remove version to let the manifest decide, which is also what your local tooling reads.

References

  • pnpm/action-setup README and action.yml at v6.1.1 (read 2026-11-12)
  • pnpm/action-setup src/install-pnpm/run.ts: version resolution
  • actions/setup-node advanced usage: caching pnpm
  • actions/setup-node#530: Unable to locate executable file: pnpm
  • pnpm/action-setup#105: comparison with corepack

event_model_payload.headline: I built EmojiBridge to connect collecting memes, editing GIFs, and dragging out the result
event_model_payload.summary:
I am Neo, the maker of EmojiBridge, a free Windows x64 desktop tool. This is a look at its workflow and the choices behind it, rather than a benchmark or a claim that it replaces every image editor.

Disclosure: I use AI tools in development. This article was drafted with AI assistance from the project's features and release information.

The small gap I wanted to close

A funny image can pass through several places before it becomes useful: a browser, a downloads folder, an editor, another export folder, and finally a chat window. The individual operations are simple, but finding the right file again interrupts the flow.

EmojiBridge groups three steps: collect a source, make a variation, and use the finished file.

1. Keep the source within reach

The floating media library keeps images and GIFs above other windows. An image can also be pinned on screen, moved, and resized. This is a separate desktop window; it does not modify the webpage beneath it.

That distinction matters when describing the feature: the goal is to keep a reference handy while browsing, not to inject an editor into every website.

2. Make a variation without leaving the workspace

For video, select a time range and crop the picture before exporting a GIF. For image-based memes, combine captions, shapes, still images, and GIFs. Manga captions, collages, templates, and effects such as bouncing or rotation provide different starting points.

A practical example is taking a short video moment, cropping out the surrounding frame, and exporting only the reaction you want to reuse. Another is combining several panels with a caption rather than searching for an existing meme with exactly the right text.

3. Treat the finished file as the handoff

The finished-image area supports dragging the result into a folder or an application that accepts file drops. This removes the intermediate step of opening an export directory and locating the file again.

File-drop support belongs to both sides of that interaction. EmojiBridge can provide a file, but a destination application still has to accept it. It would be misleading to describe this as sending into every application automatically.

The desktop trade-offs

Bundling local processing components makes the full package larger, but reduces setup for the default workflow. The full download includes three cutout models and default local components. Larger speech models remain optional downloads, and a system without WebView2 may need that runtime installed.

There are also QQ and WeChat collection/transfer workflows. These depend on the installed desktop clients, and compatibility is still being improved. During automated QQ reading or transfers, leave the mouse and windows alone until the task finishes. WeChat transfers use your own File Transfer Assistant and create chat messages. I am focusing this introduction on the editing and file workflow because those are useful even without chat-client automation.

Try it and tell me where it breaks your flow

The current interface and demo screenshots are in Chinese. It runs on Windows x64. Download the full archive, extract everything, then run EB/EmojiBridge.exe; building the source is not required. The demo meme pack is a separate optional download.

  • Feature walkthroughs
  • Source code
  • Latest release

The project's own code is GPL-3.0-only; third-party components and media keep their respective licenses.

Which transition is most awkward in your own workflow: collecting a source, editing it, finding an old result, or moving it into another app? Specific examples and reproducible issues would help shape the next iteration. If the project is useful to you, a GitHub star is also appreciated.

event_model_payload.headline: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash spent 84% of my tokens thinking: real latency, real cost, and the settings that fix it
event_model_payload.summary:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash started streaming in 1.2 seconds on every run I made. It took 20 seconds to produce the first line of the code I asked for. In between, it wrote about 3,300 tokens of reasoning that I never saw, and paid for at the output rate.

That gap matters more than any per-token price, so this post measures it, shows which settings change it, and works out what one answer actually costs at the official price and at ours.

Disclosure: I work on growth at OceanToken, an OpenAI-compatible API that resells DeepSeek, and I ran the tests there. The official prices come from DeepSeek's Models & Pricing page, with the date I read them.

TL;DR

  • Reasoning is on by default and billed as output. On a small coding prompt, 84% of V4.1 Flash's output tokens were reasoning.
  • With max_tokens: 800, Flash used the whole budget thinking and returned no code, and the call was still billed.
  • reasoning_effort: "low" cut cost by 37% and time-to-answer by ~45%. thinking: {type: "disabled"} did nothing in my runs.
  • With a reasoning model, output price is what you pay for: input was under 1% of the bill.

What I tested

Prompt (68 input tokens) Write a Python function that parses an ISO-8601 duration string such as 'PT1H30M' into total seconds. Include 3 unit tests. Answer with code only.
Models deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash, -v4.1-flash-1017, deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
Calls Streaming chat completions, OpenAI-compatible endpoint
When / where Nov 14, 2026, 03:57–04:07 UTC, from New York
Metrics time to first token (any kind), time to first line of code, output tok/s, tokens, cost

Results

Round 1: V4.1 Flash, max_tokens: 800, 5 runs per model

Model First token Output speed Total Output tokens Code returned? Cost / run
V4.1 Flash 1.16 s 171 tok/s 5.8 s 800, all reasoning No $0.0007
V4.1 Flash (1017) 1.05 s 171 tok/s 5.8 s 800, all reasoning No $0.0007

Medians of 5 runs. Cost = tokens × list price (OceanToken tier 1).

Round 2: V4.1 Flash with room to finish

Setting First token First line of code Total Output tokens Reasoning share Cost / answer
Default, max_tokens: 8000 (3 runs) 1.19 s 20.4 s 22.7 s 3,858 84% $0.0033
thinking: {type: "disabled"} (3 runs) 0.99 s 19.1 s 21.5 s 4,092 82% $0.0034
reasoning_effort: "low" (2 runs) 1.03 s 11.1 s 13.2 s 2,452 75% $0.0021

Output speed held at 180–205 tok/s across every Flash run.

What surprised me

  1. "Fast first token" means almost nothing for a reasoning model. Every Flash run started streaming in about a second, but that first token was reasoning, not answer. For an interactive feature, measure time to the first content token.
  2. Too small a max_tokens wastes money. At 800 tokens, Flash never left the thinking phase. You pay for 800 output tokens and get an empty content.
  3. reasoning_effort: "low" is the setting that saves money. It returned code in every run at 63% of the cost. I didn't grade answer quality, so check it on your own tasks before switching.

Did the bill match the price list?

Yes, to the cent. OceanToken returns the charge in an x-oceantoken-cost response header:

Call Tokens (in / out) Header tokens × list price
V4.1 Flash 68 / 300 $0.0002663 68 × $0.21/M + 300 × $0.84/M = $0.0002663
V4 Pro 121 / 2,967 $0.009527 121 × $1.056/M + 2,967 × $3.168/M = $0.009527

Reasoning tokens are billed exactly like visible output tokens.

Price list: official vs OceanToken

Per 1M tokens. Official prices from DeepSeek's Models & Pricing page (read Nov 13, 2026); OceanToken prices read Nov 14, 2026.

Model Official OceanToken tier 1 OceanToken tier 3
V4.1 Flash Input $0.30 $0.21 $0.18
Output $1.20 $0.84 $0.72
V4 Pro Input $1.32 $1.056 $0.792
Output $3.96 $3.168 $2.376

Tier 1 applies from your first top-up; tier 3 is the top-up tier with the lowest price. Same price at any hour of the day.

The legacy names deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp still work on DeepSeek's API; they route to V4.1 Flash 1017 at the same price.

The same answer at each price

The median Round 2 answer (68 in / 3,858 out):

Price Cost per answer Per 1,000 answers
Official $0.0047 $4.65
OceanToken tier 1 $0.0033 $3.26
OceanToken tier 3 $0.0028 $2.79
OceanToken tier 1, reasoning_effort: "low" (2,452 out) $0.0021 $2.07

The last row is the point of this post: the setting saves more than any price difference.

The code I used 

import time, json, requests

BASE = "https://api.oceantoken.ai/v1"   # or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, e.g. https://api.deepseek.com
H = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"}

def run(model, **extra):
    body = {"model": model, "stream": True, "max_tokens": 8000,
            "stream_options": {"include_usage": True},
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}], **extra}
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); first = first_code = usage = None
    with requests.post(f"{BASE}/chat/completions", headers=H, json=body, stream=True) as r:
        for line in r.iter_lines():
            if not line.startswith(b"data:") or line.endswith(b"[DONE]"):
                continue
            ev = json.loads(line[5:])
            usage = ev.get("usage") or usage
            for c in ev.get("choices", []):
                d = c.get("delta", {})
                if (d.get("reasoning_content") or d.get("content")) and first is None:
                    first = time.perf_counter() - t0
                if d.get("content") and first_code is None:
                    first_code = time.perf_counter() - t0
    return first, first_code, time.perf_counter() - t0, usage

print(run("deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash", reasoning_effort="low"))

Point BASE at two endpoints in the same hour and you have your own comparison.

What I could not determine

  • Other endpoints' latency on my prompt. I only measured one.
  • Time of day. All runs were in one 10-minute window.
  • More than one prompt. One small coding task; longer prompts shift the input/output split.
  • Answer quality. I measured speed and cost, not whether each answer's code was correct.

FAQ

How much does DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cost?
The official price is $0.30 input / $1.20 output per 1M tokens. On OceanToken it is $0.21 / $0.84 from the first top-up, down to $0.18 / $0.72 at the top tier.

Why is my DeepSeek bill higher than the token count I expected?
Reasoning tokens. They're billed as output, and in my test they were 75–84% of output.

How do I make DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cheaper and faster?
Set reasoning_effort: "low" for simple tasks, give max_tokens enough room to finish, and pin the model version.

Is V4.1 Flash 1017 different from V4.1 Flash?
1017 is the October 17 update; DeepSeek's deepseek-flash alias now points to it. In my test the two had the same speed and token use.

Bottom line

  1. Set reasoning_effort. On simple tasks, "low" saved 37% and answered ~45% sooner.
  2. Leave headroom in max_tokens. Too little, and you pay for reasoning with no answer.
  3. Measure time to the first content token, not the first token, for anything interactive.
  4. Pin the model version so a silent alias update doesn't change your costs.

If you run the script against another endpoint, post your numbers and the hour in the comments. I'll add them to the table.

Official prices read Nov 13, 2026; OceanToken prices read Nov 14, 2026. Tests run Nov 14, 2026, 03:57–04:07 UTC, from New York; about $0.20 spent in total.

event_model_payload.headline: What Happens Second by Second in the Bama Bound Reference Clip? A Python Timeline of Banner, Motion and Sound (Tested)
event_model_payload.summary:
Checked November 14, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. The clip measured here is the "Imported field preview" shown on the site. The site labels it "an external reference of the sign clip. Not a result generated by this studio." I only measured it. It isn't re-published here, and there are no frames of it in this post.

People ask AI assistants things like "what does the Bama Bound video actually do?" or "why does my Bama Bound clip get louder halfway through?" The Bama Bound meme page says there's one preset, and that it keeps the red banner and the reference timing. The FAQ says the clip is about eight seconds, vertical 9:16, and "the original soundtrack stays".

That's the product description. I wanted the same thing as numbers: where the banner is in each second, how much the picture moves, whether there's a cut, and what the sound does. A reference-video generator follows the reference's timing, so these numbers are also a checklist for your own result. If your clip's loud moment comes half a second early, the timeline shows it.

This post builds that timeline with one Python file (NumPy + ffmpeg, about 100 lines), runs it on the reference, and then tests it on two altered copies so you can see it notice the changes.

What ffprobe says first

Before any pixels:

video  h264 High, level 3.1, 720x1280, 24 fps, 193 frames, yuv420p, about 5.9 Mbit/s
audio  aac LC, 32000 Hz, stereo, about 130 kbit/s
format duration 8.096 s
frame types: 1 I, 49 P, 143 B
container tag: AIGC = "This content is generated by AI"

Two details stood out:

  • One keyframe in 193 frames. The only I-frame is frame 0. Players and editors seek by jumping to a keyframe and decoding forward, so scrubbing near the end of this file means decoding most of it. Re-encode with -g 24 (one keyframe per second) if you want snappy scrubbing.
  • The AIGC tag. The reference file carries a format-level metadata tag saying it was generated by AI. I expected a plain stream copy to keep it. It doesn't. ffmpeg's MP4 muxer only writes standard keys unless you ask for custom ones: 
$ ffprobe -v error -show_entries format_tags=AIGC -of default=nw=1 
source:            TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}
-c copy -> (no tag)
-c copy -map_metadata -1 -> (no tag)
re-encode (libx264) -> (no tag)
-c copy -movflags +use_metadata_tags -> TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}
re-encode -movflags +use_metadata_tags -> TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}

So every ordinary edit, even a lossless trim with -c copy, silently drops the AI label. Add -movflags +use_metadata_tags if you want it kept (and label the post on the platform too; I haven't checked which apps read this tag).

The script

timeline.py decodes the clip at 180x320 (small enough that grain averages out, big enough to find the banner), and computes three things per frame:

  • banner area: the share of pixels that look like the banner's crimson (r > 1.6·g, r > 1.2·b, r − g > 25). On the reference, the banner cloth measures around RGB (77, 34, 52), dark crimson rather than bright red, which is why the thresholds are ratios and not "r > 200".
  • banner top: the first row (as a fraction of frame height) where at least 25% of the row is banner-coloured. That row-coverage rule stops a few reddish skin pixels from counting as the banner.
  • motion: the mean absolute grey-level change against the previous frame, 0-255.

For sound it mixes to mono at the file's own sample rate and takes RMS in dBFS per half-second. It also looks for the biggest "step up" in loudness: 0.1 s RMS blocks, the median of the next 0.5 s minus the median of the previous 0.5 s. A frame counts as a cut when its motion is over 6x the clip's median and over 12.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Per-second timeline of a short vertical clip: banner position, motion, cuts, sound.

usage: python3 timeline.py clip.mp4 [--csv frames.csv]
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and NumPy. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Per frame (decoded at 180x320):
  banner_area  share of pixels that look like the crimson banner (r > 1.6*g, r > 1.2*b, r-g > 25)
  banner_top   first row (0..1 of frame height) where >= 25% of a row is banner-coloured
  motion       mean absolute grey-level change vs the previous frame (0..255)
Per 0.5 s of audio (mono mix at the file's own sample rate): RMS in dBFS,
plus the biggest 'step up' in loudness (0.1 s RMS, median 0.5 s after minus before).
A "cut" is a frame whose motion is > 6x the median motion and > 12.
"""
import json, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

W, H = 180, 320

def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-show_entries",
        "stream=codec_type,width,height,r_frame_rate,sample_rate,channels:format=duration",
        "-of", "json", path], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    return json.loads(out)

def frames(path):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-vf", f"scale={W}:{H}",
        "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8).reshape(-1, H, W, 3)

def audio(path, rate):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-vn", "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(rate),
        "-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32)

def main():
    path = sys.argv[1]
    csv = sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--csv") + 1] if "--csv" in sys.argv else None
    info = probe(path)
    v = next(s for s in info["streams"] if s["codec_type"] == "video")
    a = next((s for s in info["streams"] if s["codec_type"] == "audio"), None)
    num, den = map(int, v["r_frame_rate"].split("/")); fps = num / den
    f = frames(path).astype(np.int16)
    r, g, b = f[..., 0], f[..., 1], f[..., 2]
    mask = (r * 10 > g * 16) & (r * 10 > b * 12) & (r - g > 25)
    area = mask.mean(axis=(1, 2))
    rows = mask.mean(axis=2) >= 0.25
    top = np.array([np.argmax(x) / H if x.any() else np.nan for x in rows])
    grey = f.mean(axis=3)
    motion = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.abs(np.diff(grey, axis=0)).mean(axis=(1, 2))])
    med = float(np.median(motion[1:]))
    cuts = [i for i in range(1, len(motion)) if motion[i] > 6 * med and motion[i] > 12]
    print(f"file      {path}")
    print(f"video     {v['width']}x{v['height']} @ {fps:g} fps, {len(f)} frames, "
          f"container duration {float(info['format']['duration']):.3f} s")
    if a:
        print(f"audio     {a['sample_rate']} Hz, {a['channels']} ch")
    print(f"motion    median {med:.2f}, max {motion.max():.2f} at frame {int(motion.argmax())} "
          f"({motion.argmax() / fps:.2f} s)")
    print(f"cuts      {len(cuts)}" + (": " + ", ".join(f'{c / fps:.2f}s' for c in cuts) if cuts else ""))
    print(f"banner    visible (area >= 3%) in {int((area >= 0.03).sum())}/{len(f)} frames; "
          f"area {area.min():.3f}-{area.max():.3f}; top edge {np.nanmin(top):.3f}-{np.nanmax(top):.3f} of height")
    snd = None
    if a:
        rate = int(a['sample_rate']); x = audio(path, rate); hop = rate // 2
        snd = [20 * np.log10(np.sqrt(np.mean(x[i:i + hop] ** 2)) + 1e-9) for i in range(0, len(x) - hop + 1, hop)]
        h10 = rate // 10
        fine = np.array([20 * np.log10(np.sqrt(np.mean(x[i:i + h10] ** 2)) + 1e-9)
                         for i in range(0, len(x) - h10 + 1, h10)])
        rise = [(np.median(fine[k:k + 5]) - np.median(fine[k - 5:k]), k / 10) for k in range(5, len(fine) - 4)]
        db, t = max(rise)
        print(f"sound     biggest step up: {db:+.1f} dB at {t:.1f} s (median of 0.5 s after vs before)")
    print("\n  second | banner area | banner top | motion | sound dBFS (two halves)")
    for s in range(int(np.ceil(len(f) / fps))):
        sl = slice(int(round(s * fps)), int(round((s + 1) * fps)))
        if sl.start >= len(f):
            break
        snd_txt = ""
        if snd:
            pair = snd[2 * s:2 * s + 2]
            snd_txt = " / ".join(f"{d:6.1f}" for d in pair)
        print(f"  {s:>2}-{s + 1:<3} |    {area[sl].mean():.3f}    |   {np.nanmean(top[sl]):.3f}    | {motion[sl].mean():6.2f} | {snd_txt}")
    if csv:
        with open(csv, "w") as fh:
            fh.write("frame,t,banner_area,banner_top,motion\n")
            for i in range(len(f)):
                fh.write(f"{i},{i / fps:.4f},{area[i]:.4f},{top[i]:.4f},{motion[i]:.3f}\n")
        print(f"\nwrote {csv}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The reference, second by second 

$ python3 timeline.py ref.mp4 --csv frames.csv
file      ref.mp4
video     720x1280 @ 24 fps, 193 frames, container duration 8.096 s
audio     32000 Hz, 2 ch
motion    median 7.86, max 19.08 at frame 124 (5.17 s)
cuts      0
banner    visible (area >= 3%) in 193/193 frames; area 0.091-0.177; top edge 0.103-0.191 of height
sound     biggest step up: +8.9 dB at 3.5 s (median of 0.5 s after vs before)

  second | banner area | banner top | motion | sound dBFS (two halves)
   0-1   |    0.167    |   0.110    |   5.49 |  -21.8 /  -19.2
   1-2   |    0.148    |   0.118    |   7.23 |  -20.2 /  -19.9
   2-3   |    0.142    |   0.128    |   9.49 |  -22.2 /  -22.7
   3-4   |    0.145    |   0.143    |   9.15 |  -22.1 /  -13.1
   4-5   |    0.129    |   0.154    |  10.82 |  -13.5 /  -14.7
   5-6   |    0.107    |   0.159    |   8.71 |  -14.6 /  -13.4
   6-7   |    0.113    |   0.155    |   7.03 |  -13.5 /  -14.1
   7-8   |    0.124    |   0.139    |   7.64 |  -16.6 /  -14.3
   8-9   |    0.112    |   0.147    |  11.29 | 

wrote frames.csv

What that says, in plain words:

  • No cuts. It's one continuous shot. The biggest frame-to-frame change is 19.08 at 5.17 s, about 2.4x the median of 7.86. That's movement, not a cut (the cut test below gives a sense of scale).
  • The banner is always on screen, in all 193 frames, and it's high. Its top edge starts at 10.3% of the frame height and drifts down to 19.1% at about 4.8 s, then comes back up a little. Its area shrinks from 17.7% of the frame to about 9-12% in the second half, so it gets smaller or turns away from the camera. Caption stickers in the top fifth of the frame will sit on the banner. Put text lower down.
  • The motion is constant. It's 5.5 at the start and 7-11 for the rest. The median of 7.86 is high for a 180x320 decode, so expect handheld-style movement throughout, not a locked-off camera.
  • The sound steps up about 9 dB at 3.5 s. The first 3.5 seconds sit around −19 to −23 dBFS, and from 3.5 s on it's about −12 to −15 dBFS. That step explains the "why does it get louder halfway" question. It's in the reference soundtrack, which the clip keeps.

Does it notice when something is off?

A timeline is only useful if it moves when the clip changes, so I made two altered copies.

Copy 1: half a second trimmed off the start, scaled to 480x854, re-encoded. This is what a careless trim in an editor does.

ffmpeg -ss 0.5 -i ref.mp4 -vf scale=480:854 -c:v libx264 -crf 26 -preset veryfast -c:a aac -b:a 96k shifted_480.mp4

file      shifted_480.mp4
video     480x854 @ 24 fps, 181 frames, container duration 7.596 s
audio     32000 Hz, 2 ch
motion    median 7.79, max 19.03 at frame 112 (4.67 s)
cuts      0
banner    visible (area >= 3%) in 181/181 frames; area 0.089-0.160; top edge 0.109-0.191 of height
sound     biggest step up: +9.0 dB at 3.0 s (median of 0.5 s after vs before)

  second | banner area | banner top | motion | sound dBFS (two halves)
   0-1   |    0.151    |   0.118    |   6.67 |  -19.3 /  -20.4
   1-2   |    0.137    |   0.124    |   7.59 |  -20.0 /  -22.4
   2-3   |    0.135    |   0.136    |   9.18 |  -22.9 /  -22.3
   3-4   |    0.134    |   0.150    |   8.85 |  -13.1 /  -13.5
   4-5   |    0.103    |   0.160    |  11.58 |  -14.8 /  -14.6
   5-6   |    0.111    |   0.161    |   6.32 |  -13.5 /  -13.5
   6-7   |    0.110    |   0.143    |   7.41 |  -14.2 /  -16.7
   7-8   |    0.119    |   0.145    |   7.41 |  -14.4

The loud step moved from 3.5 s to 3.0 s (+9.0 dB, the same size), and the frame count dropped from 193 to 181. The banner numbers barely changed with the resolution, because the script always decodes at 180x320. So a resolution change won't move the timeline, but a timing change will.

Copy 2: a hard cut. The first 2 s of the reference followed by 2 s of a synthetic test scene (a red "TEST BANNER" box over a green field from make_field_test_clip.sh, no people), no audio.

./make_field_test_clip.sh field.mp4 720x1280 24 3
ffmpeg -i ref.mp4 -i field.mp4 -filter_complex \
  "[0:v]trim=0:2,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,fps=24[a];[1:v]trim=0:2,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,fps=24,setsar=1[b];[a][b]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0[v]" \
  -map "[v]" -c:v libx264 -crf 20 -preset veryfast cut_test.mp4

file      cut_test.mp4
video     720x1280 @ 24 fps, 96 frames, container duration 4.000 s
motion    median 3.09, max 68.66 at frame 48 (2.00 s)
cuts      1: 2.00s
banner    visible (area >= 3%) in 96/96 frames; area 0.117-0.176; top edge 0.103-0.400 of height

  second | banner area | banner top | motion | sound dBFS (two halves)
   0-1   |    0.167    |   0.111    |   5.46 | 
   1-2   |    0.148    |   0.118    |   7.17 | 
   2-3   |    0.119    |   0.400    |   4.98 | 
   3-4   |    0.119    |   0.400    |   2.09 |

The cut shows up as motion 68.66 at exactly 2.00 s, about 22x that clip's median, and it's the only frame flagged. The banner top jumping from about 0.11 to 0.400 is the test banner, which sits lower in its frame.

Using it on your own result

  1. Run timeline.py on your clip and on a reference you have the right to download (or just keep this post's numbers).
  2. Compare the sound step time first. In the reference it's 3.5 s. If yours is earlier, something trimmed the start. If yours is later, something added frames (a title card, a frozen first frame).
  3. Compare cuts: the reference has none. A flagged cut in your clip is an edit, not the preset.
  4. Compare banner top: if the banner's top edge is far lower than 0.10-0.19, the framing changed (for example a crop to 4:5).

The numbers are about the reference. A generated clip puts your photo's person in the banner holder's place, so expect the banner area and motion values to differ a bit. The structure (one shot, banner high, a loudness step around 3.5 s) is what the preset is meant to keep.
