event_model_payload.headline: Customer data erasure requests updated from 10 days to 5
event_model_payload.summary:
As of November 10, 2026, customer data erasure requests will no longer be held in a pending state for 10 days.

Erasure requests will now be processed 5 days after the request was submitted, regardless of when the customer's most recent order was placed. For recipients of gift cards that have been scheduled to send, the erasure request will remain in a pending state until the gift card has been delivered.

This update simplifies the overall experience for managing customer data requests.

event_model_payload.headline: Storefront MCP policies and FAQs tool is being deprecated in favor of UCP MCP Ask tool
event_model_payload.summary:
Storefront MCP search_shop_policies_and_faqs is deprecated. Migrate to UCP MCP's ask_business tool by January 15, 2027.

What's changing

The search_shop_policies_and_faqs tool on the Storefront MCP server (https://{shop}.myshopify.com/api/mcp) is deprecated in favor of the UCP Ask MCP tool.

UCP MCP implements the UCP ask capability (dev.ucp.common.ask) and exposes the following tool at the https://{shop-domain}/api/ucp/mcp endpoint:

  • ask_business: Answer a buyer's question about the store's policies and services, using the store's knowledge base and policies.

The deprecated tool will be maintained until January 15, 2027, but all documentation will refer to Ask MCP.

What you should do

If you're building with search_shop_policies_and_faqs:

  • Migrate calls to ask_business, and update endpoints to use https://{shop-domain}/api/ucp/mcp.
  • Include a meta object carrying ucp-agent.profile in every request. Your agent profile must declare dev.ucp.common.ask.
  • Send the question in ask.query, and optional buyer context (such as country or preferred language) in ask.context.
  • Note that ask_business returns a written answer in result.structuredContent.answer.plain, not raw knowledge base facts or full policy text. Update any code that parses the old response.
  • Use tools/list to check whether a store offers ask_business for your agent profile.

See the documentation for Ask MCP (https://shopify.dev/docs/agents/ask) for more details.

event_model_payload.headline: Shopify App Store submission requirements: build, grow, then expand
event_model_payload.summary:
We’re updating the Shopify App Store submission requirements so that the apps you list are apps merchants use. These changes apply to new app submissions, resubmissions of rejected apps, additional app listings, and listed apps with zero. They introduce new thresholds you must meet to submit and keep apps listed.

These policies apply to new submissions, resubmissions, and listed apps starting today.

What changed

We’ve updated the Shopify App Store submission and listing policies in four ways:

  • Minimum adoption before listing additional apps: Each of your existing apps must have at least 10 installs on full-priced Shopify stores before you can list an additional app. For details, see the submission limits in the App submission review guide.
  • Escalating cooldowns for rejected app submissions: Rejected submissions are subject to escalating cooldown periods before resubmitting. Cooldowns get longer with each repeated rejection, so resubmitting without meaningful changes leads to a longer wait. If a submission was rejected, make sure to address the review feedback before you resubmit so you don’t extend the cooldown period. For details, see the App submission paused section in App submission review and suspensions.
  • Identity verification for new apps: Identity verification is now a required step for developers who submit new apps so merchants know who’s behind the apps they install. You can complete identity verification from your partner account before you submit a new app.
  • Removal of apps with zero installs after six months: Apps with zero installs after six months are automatically removed from the Shopify App Store. For details, see the App usefulness check.

What you should do

Before submitting or resubmitting an app, confirm that you meet the applicable adoption and identity verification requirements and that any submission cooldown has ended.

For listed apps, review install counts to identify apps subject to automatic removal.

Who’s affected

These changes apply to you if any of the following are true:

  • You want to list an additional app in the Shopify App Store.
  • You’re resubmitting an app that was rejected in the Shopify App Store review.
  • You’re submitting a new app to the Shopify App Store.
  • You have an app listed in the Shopify App Store with no installs.

These changes don’t affect apps that already meet the install thresholds and remain installed on at least one full-priced Shopify store.

event_model_payload.headline: Remove your app from the Shopify App Store yourself
event_model_payload.summary:
You can now start sunsetting your app and remove it from the Shopify App Store yourself, from the Partner Dashboard. You no longer need to contact Shopify Support.

What's new

  • In the Partner Dashboard, go to Apps > your app > Distribution, and click Remove from App Store.
  • Choose a sunset date at least 30 days from now. This gives your merchants time to prepare and find an alternative.
  • Shopify removes your app from the Shopify App Store right away. Merchants can no longer find or install it there.

Removing your app from the Shopify App Store can't be undone. To list the app again, you need to submit it for review as a new app.

What happens to existing merchants

Removing your app from the Shopify App Store doesn't immediately affect merchants who already have it installed. They can keep using your app until your scheduled sunset date, when your app is sunset and removed from their stores.

Shopify doesn't email your merchants, cancel their charges, or uninstall your app for you. Before your sunset date, you're responsible for:

  • Telling your merchants about the sunset and reminding them before the sunset date
  • Cancelling app subscriptions with appSubscriptionCancel
  • Uninstalling your app from any remaining stores with appUninstall

Related docs

  • Sunsetting your app

event_model_payload.headline: Market.metafields matches keys in any case as of Storefront API version 2027-01
event_model_payload.summary:
As of Storefront API version 2027-01, the metafields field on the Market object matches each requested key in any case, as Market.metafield already does. This is a breaking change for apps and custom storefronts that request a market metafield key in a different case from the stored key, or that read a key that the buyer's markets store that differ by letter case. If your app does either, review its Market.metafields queries before you move it to 2027-01.

What changed

In version 2027-01, Market.metafields returns a metafield when the requested key matches the stored key in any case. In earlier versions, Market.metafields returns a metafield only when the requested key and the stored key have the same case.

For example, a market stores a metafield with the namespace custom and the key colour:

  • In version 2026-10 and earlier, the entry for { namespace: "custom", key: "Colour" } is null.
  • In version 2027-01, the entry returns the stored metafield.

Who's affected

The change applies to apps and custom storefronts that query metafields on a Market object, from Localization.market or Country.market, with Storefront API version 2027-01 or later. Your app is affected only if one of these conditions is true:

  • It requests a key in a different case from the key that the market stores.
  • The buyer's markets store the same key in different cases.

Your app isn't affected if it requests each key in the case that the markets store it, or if it uses only Market.metafield, which already matches keys in any case. Versions 2026-10 and earlier don't change.

Why this matters

In earlier versions, Market.metafield and Market.metafields can return different results for the same key: Market.metafield finds the metafield, and Market.metafields returns null. In 2027-01, both fields return the same metafield, so your storefront shows the same value whichever field it queries.

What to do

Market.metafield already matches keys case-insensitively, and it returns the metafield from the buyer's most specific market. So on the version that you use today, Market.metafield returns the result that Market.metafields returns in 2027-01. You can compare the two fields to find out whether the change affects your app.

  1. For each market metafield that your app reads, query Market.metafield and Market.metafields with the same namespace and key, and compare the results.
  2. If the results are the same for every key, then you don't need to make changes.
  3. If a result is different, then check whether the difference has a material impact on your app or your storefront.
  4. If it does, then update your app and your metafields so that they don't depend on the case of keys. For example, request each key in the case that your markets store it, and use one case for each key on every market.
query CompareMarketMetafields @inContext(country: CA) {
  localization {
    market {
      metafield(namespace: "custom", key: "Colour") {
        key
        value
      }
      metafields(identifiers: [{ namespace: "custom", key: "Colour" }]) {
        key
        value
      }
    }
  }
}

Related docs

  • Market object in the Storefront API
  • Storefront API 2027-01 reference
  • Retrieve metafields with the Storefront API
  • About Shopify API versioning

event_model_payload.headline: Market metafields break ties between equally specific markets by market handle
event_model_payload.summary: When a buyer matches two or more equally specific markets that set the same metafield, Market.metafield and Market.metafields now return the value from the market with the lowest handle, instead of the value that was updated most recently. This behavior change applies to the Storefront API, Liquid, and Function APIs on every API version. If your app or theme reads market metafields on stores with overlapping markets, check which value buyers get in a tie.

event_model_payload.headline: IP allowlists are now required for custom apps installed outside your organization
event_model_payload.summary:
We're enhancing protection of merchants by requiring IP allowlists for custom apps, if those apps are installed on stores outside of the organization that owns them.

  • Starting November 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET: Apps must have an IP allowlist for new installs.
  • Starting January 1, 2027 at 11:59 PM ET: Allowlists are required for existing installs.

What apps are affected

  • Custom apps installed on stores outside the organization that owns the app.
  • Partners who own multiple apps. From January 1, 2027, one app without an allowlist affects your ability to install any app on stores outside your organization.

What apps are unaffected

  • Apps installed only on stores within your own organization
  • Apps created by merchants either in the Dev Dashboard or in the admin
  • Public apps, which are covered by a separate requirement

Why we're making this change

Leaked tokens can be used from any network location. IP allowlists reduce the impact of a credential leak by limiting the networks from which your app can invoke the Admin API.

What to do

Configure your app's allowed IPs in the Dev Dashboard:

  • If your app calls Shopify from static IP addresses, configure your IP allowlist based on static IPs or CIDR range.
  • If your app's egress IP addresses are dynamic, allow your hosting provider's ASNs and list the countries your app runs in.

Audit every app you've installed on stores outside your organization, and configure an allowlist on each one before January 1, 2027.

For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

event_model_payload.headline: App security updates: Thank you, plus what's required next
event_model_payload.summary:
Thanks to you, we've already seen the vast majority of apps that run bulk operations adopt an IP allowlist. That's a big step toward keeping merchants protected heading into the busiest weeks of the year.

Here's what's required, what's new, and what's coming next.

Action required

  • All public apps that call the Admin API: Turn on an IP allowlist by November 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET. Apps without one will be delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working. For apps that are delisted, we'll relist apps automatically once they add an IP allowlist. Set up your IP allowlist
  • Bulk operations: We're beginning enforcement on bulk queries and mutations from public apps without an IP allowlist. Turn on your allowlist to restore them.
  • Enable bulk operations for partner-created apps: Before your app can run bulk queries or bulk mutations, enable them from API access requests in the Partner Dashboard. If your app doesn't start a bulk query or mutation for 31 days, you'll need to enable it again. Read the changelog
  • Custom apps installed outside your organization also need an IP allowlist: These apps need an IP allowlist for new installs from November 20, 2026, and for existing installs from January 1, 2027. From January 1, one app without an allowlist blocks you from installing any of your apps on stores outside your organization. Apps installed only within your organization, and apps created by merchants, aren't affected. Read the changelog

New this week

  • You can now use IP addresses and ASNs together. Your allowlist can include IP addresses, CIDR ranges and your hosting provider's ASNs at the same time, with up to 250 IP addresses or ranges. A request is allowed if it matches any entry. Country restrictions apply only to ASNs. For the strongest protection, use specific IP addresses wherever you can. Read the changelog

Coming soon

  • MFA on every partner account. Starting next week, multi-factor authentication will be required on all partner accounts. We recommend passkeys. Turn on MFA now so it doesn't interrupt your work later. Protect the accounts that control your app

Get help

If you see something suspicious, tell us right away at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You're responsible for fixing it and notifying affected merchants, and we'll support you through it.

For general security questions, contact Shopify Support.

Everything lives in the App Security Hub, and we answer questions on the App Security board in the developer community.

event_model_payload.headline: App IP allowlists now support IP addresses and ASNs together, and up to 250 IPs
event_model_payload.summary:
Your app's IP allowlist in the Dev Dashboard can now include IP addresses and autonomous system numbers (ASNs) in the same allowlist. This helps apps whose requests come from a mix of static and dynamic IP addresses. You can also now configure up to 250 IP addresses or ranges, up from 100.

What changed

The IP allowlist section of your app's Settings page no longer makes you choose between IP addresses and networks. You can enter up to 250 addresses or ranges in IP addresses or CIDR ranges, up to 10 ASNs in Networks (ASN), or both. Under Limit ASNs to countries, you can choose up to 10 countries. Countries limit only your ASNs, not your IP addresses.

Requests are allowed if they match one of your configured IPs or ASNs. Requests from outside your allowlist fail with a 403 status code.

What to do

IP allowlists will soon be required for all public and custom apps. Shopify strongly recommends all apps use an IP allowlist.

Allow specific IP addresses wherever you can. This is the most secure option, because only your own servers can use your app's access tokens. An ASN allows every address on your hosting provider's network, including addresses used by the provider's other customers. Add ASNs only for requests that come from dynamic addresses, such as serverless functions, and limit them to the countries your app runs in.

Before you turn on enforcement, test your updated allowlist against recent traffic.

For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

event_model_payload.headline: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
event_model_payload.summary: Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient. LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

event_model_payload.headline: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
event_model_payload.summary:
By Shreya S Ramanujam, Yongce Li, Afshine Amidi, Sina Ghiassian, Benjamin Klein.

Introduction

Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen:

If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode.

A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything.

“In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.”

Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual. At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not.

Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize:

  1. High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants.
  2. Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis.

Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail (“Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?”) rises from 0.77 to 0.86, and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~69%). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses.

So, what exactly does factuality mean?

Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1:

Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.”

It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show.

Let’s take another example:

Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.”

Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual.

But what about this?

Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.”

Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing exposés. So then, is this a factual synopsis?

Not quite! While technically true, it paints a misleading picture of the show. A new viewer might reasonably expect it to revolve around Lady Whistledown, rather than Daphne navigating the marriage market. This, too, is a type of non-factuality we want to catch.

Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all:

Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.”

Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag.

So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations?

Current Service and Its Limitations

Our current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations:

  1. High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well.
  2. Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction.

Optimizing the Holistic Pipeline

To understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights:

Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls?

Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy:

  • Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning.
  • Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps.

This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need.

The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening.

Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model:

Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new information

With confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise, not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts?

Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specialized

Instead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about:

  • Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true?
  • Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show?

Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors.

Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hid

At this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses?

Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router:

Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model:

  • Makes an assumption.
  • Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote).
  • Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict.

We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which:

  1. Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it.
  2. Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false.

Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality Service

Our findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated.

We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases:

  • FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check.
  • PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted.

Results

Based on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines:

Evaluation: Datasets and Metrics

We evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show.

We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below:

Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales.

On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times.

Evaluation Results

The best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold.

Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants.

Our takeaways from this experiment are:

  • Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts.
  • Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset.
  • Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment.
  • Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline.
  • Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline.

Alignment with Human Rationale

So far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons?

To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap.

We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator.

Conclusion + Future Work

Overall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service:

  • On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation.
  • On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning.

The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting. Some future directions to consider would be:

  • Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm.
  • Use the rationale from factuality checking to correct the faulty synopsis.

Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: Skipper, Airbnb’s embedded workflow engine, is now open source
event_model_payload.summary:
Durable workflows, running inside your service with no separate orchestration cluster.

By: Ricardo Gamba, Andriy Sergiyenko

Skipper, an embedded workflow engine used in production by teams all across Airbnb, is now available to the open source community. Skipper lets you express multi-step business processes as Java or Kotlin classes, persist their progress, and recover from crashes and transient failures. It runs inside your service and reuses its existing dependencies.

Skipper is available under the Apache 2.0 license. The code is on GitHub, alongside documentation and runnable examples. Our earlier engineering deep dive explains how we built it. Here, we’ll focus on the architecture of Skipper and where it fits in the ecosystem of options for development around workflows.

Why we developed Skipper

A process that spans multiple services, waits for human input, or involves a mix of synchronous and asynchronous steps, needs persistent storage for recording its progress. When a server restarts, it must know what has already happened, what (if anything) should be retried, and what is still awaiting processing. Implementing this separately for each process would mean repeatedly solving the same problems around partial failure, timers, and recovery, with associated testing and debugging; using a proven library is likely to improve quality and reduce toil.

Existing workflow engines meet these challenges. A common approach relies on a central orchestration service, whether self-hosted or fully managed, to handle durable execution. This setup provides a unified platform for multiple teams, streamlining central operations and monitoring.

For Airbnb, we wanted a new approach, one in which each service owned its workflows within its existing deployment and database. For critical services, that meant avoiding an additional shared orchestration dependency. It also let workflow execution stay in-process, without a separate coordinator between steps.

That requirement shaped Skipper’s architecture, as shown in the figure.

With Skipper, the service’s replicas also run the workflow runtime and scheduler. In a typical production deployment, they share a database that holds workflow state and scheduled work. The scheduler polls for runnable tasks and uses leases to coordinate ownership. If a replica fails, another can recover the work; takeover timing depends on scheduling and lease settings.

This reduces the number of separately deployed systems. It also puts responsibility for workflow execution, database capacity, and recovery with the service’s team. The duty of assuming those responsibilities is part of the tradeoff.

We believe that Skipper will appeal to teams that have a robust operational environment and need a workflow engine that adapts to their existing ways of working.

A workflow is a class

Skipper has two main abstractions. A workflow describes the orchestration: decisions, ordering, and waits. Actions perform work with potential side effects, such as calling an API or updating a database. Skipper records action results so they can be reused during recovery.

Consider a hypothetical listing-publication process. Some listings require a human review before publication; afterward, the host receives a notification:

class PublishListing : Workflow() {
  private val listing = actions()

  @StateField var reviewApproved: Boolean? = null

  @WorkflowMethod
  suspend fun publish(request: PublicationRequest): Boolean {
    if (request.requiresReview) {
      val reviewed = waitUntil(
        { reviewApproved != null },
        Duration.ofDays(1)
      )
      if (!reviewed || reviewApproved != true) return false
    }

    listing.publish(request.listingId, request.requestId)
    listing.notifyHost(request.listingId, request.requestId)
    return true
  }

  @SignalMethod
  fun recordReview(approved: Boolean) {
    reviewApproved = approved
  }
}

waitUntil hibernates the workflow without holding a thread. The recordReview signal lets an API handler or queue consumer supply the review decision. A redeploy during the wait does not discard the persisted workflow. If approval never arrives, the timer allows the workflow to complete and deliver a negative result.

The action implementations and request type are omitted here. Each action must make its own side effects idempotent, for example, by deduplicating publication and notification separately using the stable request ID. Skipper does not make calls to downstream systems transactionally.

Java workflows use the same model, with methods that can return CompletableFuture. The examples include Java, Kotlin, Spring Boot, and Dropwizard projects. For tests, WorkflowTest provides an isolated in-memory runtime with controllable time, so you can exercise waits, signals, retries, and completion while supplying fakes for downstream collaborators.

Recovery through checkpoints and replay

When Skipper resumes an interrupted workflow, it re-executes the workflow method from the top. Actions with durably persisted checkpoints return their saved results. Execution continues through the remaining work.

This requires deterministic workflow code: orchestration must remain compatible with replay. Clock reads, randomness, and I/O belong in actions or explicit checkpoints rather than directly in the workflow body.

By default, Skipper batches action checkpoints until execution completes or pauses for a wait or retry. This reduces database writes, but a crash before that batch is persisted can require several previously completed actions to execute again. Actions can request immediate checkpointing to narrow that window. Even then, a downstream effect and its checkpoint are not one atomic operation, so side effects remain at least once.

On the normal execution path, a workflow can run directly in the service process, backed by persisted state and scheduled recovery work. It does not need a round-trip to an external orchestration service between actions. Database access and downstream calls still contribute to latency; the benefit is removing the separate orchestration tier from that path.

Durability does not mean every business operation succeeds. Developers define which errors are retryable and choose retry policies. Permanent failures and exhausted retries are surfaced for handling; scheduler tasks that exhaust recovery attempts can require manual intervention. Skipper also supports Saga-style compensation when a process needs explicit recovery actions for previously completed steps.

Where Skipper fits

Skipper’s production use already spans multiple teams at Airbnb. It is a good fit for a Java or Kotlin service that owns a multi-step process, and wants durable execution within its existing deployment. It is especially useful when the alternative is maintaining custom retry jobs, state tables, and polling loops for each new process.

What’s in the release, and what’s next

The open-source release includes the core engine, MySQL and SQLite adapters, test utilities, and the admin UI. Signals, queries, retries, compensation, and workflow evolution primitives are part of the programming model. It also includes Skipper State Machine, a Kotlin DSL for processes that are easier to describe as states, events, and transitions. The documentation covers these capabilities and JVM compatibility.

Next, we plan to explore adding more storage plugins, such as Postgres, DynamoDB, etc., and improve tooling for workflow evolution and replay debugging. Open source project contributions around automated compatibility checks, migration assistance, and clearer replay visualization could also help developers work through problems common to replay-based engines.

If this type of work interests you, check out some of our open positions!

Acknowledgements

A huge thank you to everyone who contributed code, adopted Skipper, shared feedback, and helped get this release over the finish line. This work reflects contributions from teams across Airbnb.

Special thanks to:

Our engineering leadership sponsors Navjot Sidhu, Musaab At-Taras, Mini Atwal. Jon Parise for guiding the team through the open source process, and Gary Leung and Harshit Gupta for helping us shape Skipper with its first use-case.

event_model_payload.headline: Run cost-effective, always-on agents to monitor your environment: the engineering behind Watchers
event_model_payload.summary:
Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't. With the advent of modern AI, you might think the solution is to swarm your stack with agents that monitor every last detail, but that can quickly lead to astronomical bills.

And those are the gaps Watchers fill: catching what alerts miss while keeping costs in control. Generally Available as of ObservabilityCON 2026, Watchers are always-on agents in Grafana Assistant. You describe what to monitor (in natural language) and pick your data sources, and the watcher learns what "normal" looks like and tells you when you drift from that state.

Ultimately, this helps you surface problems without needing an alert, giving you wider coverage and more confidence in your system. But how do we keep Watchers cost-effective for our customers, especially in comparison to building your own agent that runn around the clock?

For example, let's say you deploy your own version of a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes, which means it runs 4,320 times a month. If each run were an agentic investigation, which cost us between $0.56 and $1.26 in a recent experiment, that one watcher you built would cost thousands of dollars a month.

Yet the Watchers running on our own Grafana Cloud stack cost a median of less than $5 a month. In this post, I'll show you the engineering behind that number, which mostly comes down to one question: where do you actually need an LLM's intelligence, and how much of it?

The TL;DR on Watchers

Watchers keeps an eye on one things you care about, such as a service, a dependency, or a fix you shipped after an incident. Think of it as the dashboard check you'd otherwise do by hand, done around the clock. It stays quiet until something needs attention, then it sends you its assessment and the evidence behind it. For critical findings, it can also launch an Investigation in Assistant to find the cause.

Here's the gist of how it helps you identify potential issues in a cost-effective manner, which I'll cover in greater detail in the remaining sections in this post:

  • The design: A capable agent calibrates each watcher once, so every run after that is plain code plus one call to a small, fast model.

  • The cost: Less than $10 a month per watcher for 41 of our 43 internal Watchers. Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026, and then will bill as part of Assistant token usage.

  • The results: Coverage beyond your alerts, so you catch what you didn’t know to watch for and better trust your system. Our own watcher found more than 10 customer-affecting production bugs in the past few months.

  • The integrations: Watchers read most of your telemetry, plus any HTTP API, and send findings to Slack, Microsoft Teams, webhooks, or Grafana Alerting.

Put the intelligence only where it's needed

Keeping an eye on a service comes down to three jobs: 

  1. Working out what to watch and what normal looks like

  2. Comparing the same signals with normal again and again

  3. Deciding whether anything is worth interrupting someone for

Only the first and last jobs need intelligence, and they need it in very different amounts. 

Let's go back to our example from the intro about a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes. Determining what to watch takes exploration and judgment, but once you've made a decision, you don't need to revisit it constantly. After all, the answer barely changes between 9 and 9:10 a.m. And deciding whether something matters enough to interrupt someone takes judgment on every run, but it's a narrow question once the legwork is done. The middle job is fetching data and doing arithmetic, which code does well and LLMs don't. 

So a watcher splits the work three ways:

Job

Who does it

When

Decide what to watch and what normal looks like

A calibration agent, with a capable model and tools

Once, and again when you recalibrate

Fetch the data and compare it with the baseline

Plain code: queries, statistics, and log pattern tracking

Every run

Decide whether it matters, and explain why

A small, fast model, in a single call with no tools

Every run

And here's what that workflow looks like:

Calibration: do the hard thinking once

Calibration is the secret sauce. Think of it as pre-processing: when you create a watcher, a background agent does the setup work an experienced engineer would normally do and writes down what it learns. The expensive reasoning happens once, and every run inherits a narrow, well-prepared task that an LLM is good at.

The calibration agent:

  • Settles the scope. It maps where your telemetry lives and asks you up front when it hits a question that only you can answer. For example: "This service runs in 32 production clusters and one ops cluster. Should each cluster be judged on its own?"

  • Starts from what your team knows. It mines your alert rules and dashboards first, since they encode failure modes, thresholds, and severities your team already agreed on.

  • Measures normal over time. It checks each signal at several points over the past week and reads daily and weekly traffic cycles, so a quiet Sunday night doesn't look like an outage.

  • Validates and writes it all down. Every check is tested against live data before it's saved, along with a calibration context: a compact decision guide covering the service, your decisions, deploy behavior, normal ranges, and known noise.

A calibration takes a few minutes at most. Call for call, it's the most expensive thing a watcher does, but it happens once, not every 10 minutes.

Run plain code, then make one model call

A calibrated watcher doesn't explore anything at run time. It executes its saved checks and turns the results into a compact digest, without a model:

  • Metrics: Code compares each value with the same time yesterday and with a statistical baseline, then applies the calibrated thresholds, so the model gets verdicts it can't miscompute.

  • Logs: Loki's patterns API already groups log lines into patterns at ingestion. The watcher keeps an inventory of them across runs, so it can spot new patterns, notice when a known one doubles in rate, and fetch examples only for what's new.

  • Deploys: A check that reports rollouts lets the model tell "this started right after a deploy" from coincidence.

Healthy checks collapse to one line each, and the digest goes to exactly one model call, with no tools. The model returns a structured decision: an assessment (OK, warning, or critical), a short report, the issues it's tracking and their evidence, and whether to notify anyone or launch an investigation.

For example, let's say you roll out a deployment and five minutes later you get an error rate that's slightly up and a log pattern nobody has seen before. Is that noise, or is it worth waking someone up for? This is a task that LLMs are genuinely good at. Weighing evidence like that and explaining the call plays to an LLM's strengths while crunching thousands of data points doesn't. Because the question is this narrow, a small, fast model is enough.

We don't take that on faith, either. Our evals replay real production decisions against candidate models, and the model most watchers use today didn't miss a single critical case, at about half the cost per decision of the model it replaced.

What it costs

Here's what that adds up to for the 43 Watchers running on our internal stack, at our list price of $2 per million tokens:

Types of Watchers

Cost to run per month

Median Watcher

Less than $5

41 of 43 Watchers

Less than $10

Most expensive Watcher (43 checks, every 15 minutes)

A little over $20

Even the most expensive one spends less than one cent per run. Cost follows the two things you control: how often a watcher runs (every five minutes to every three hours) and how much it watches. Calibration comes on top, and investigations a watcher launches are billed as investigations. Each watcher's Overview tab estimates its monthly token usage, so you see the cost before your bill does.

Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026. After that, they will draw on your plan’s monthly system-initiated allowance (shared with other automated work) and bill on Assistant token usage. See Grafana Assistant pricing for more info.

Note: Watchers will work exactly as they do today when billing goes live, and we expect the cost of running one to remain in line with what we’ve shared here.

What our own watcher found

A cost-effective watcher is only worth it if it catches things. Over the past few months, the watcher our team runs on Grafana Assistant itself found more than 10 production bugs that affected customers, including:

  • A crashlooping Microsoft Teams integration

  • Broken investigation reports

  • Missing webhook credentials in a newly enabled region

  • Slack OAuth failures

  • Even bugs in Watchers themselves, like alerts that never reached Alertmanager

Many of these surfaced as a new error pattern in the logs. A new pattern alone is often noise, but one that lines up with rising errors and a fresh deploy usually isn't. That's exactly the kind of call a watcher makes well.

It isn't always right about the cause, and it doesn't need to be. During one rollout, it flagged real failures from an exhausted MySQL database but blamed the wrong cause, and engineers found an expensive query plan that likely contributed. The watcher notices; people, or an Assistant Investigation, dig in.

Plug it into your stack

A watcher can sit on top of most of your stack:

  • Data sources: Prometheus (including Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus), CloudWatch metrics, Loki, Tempo, Pyroscope, Synthetic Monitoring, Grafana-managed alerts, and BigQuery for business signals. With the Infinity data source, it can also read any HTTP API that returns JSON or XML. One of ours watches the status pages of the LLM providers that Assistant depends on.

  • Destinations: Slack, Microsoft Teams, signed webhooks, and Grafana Alerting, so findings flow through your notification policies and contact points, including Grafana Cloud IRM. A critical finding can also launch an Assistant Investigation or trigger an Assistant Automation.

Watchers don't replace alert rules; they cover what you can't spell out in advance. To find the right mix, ask Assistant to review a service, and it recommends an alert, a watcher, or both for each failure mode.

To try it, go to AI > Watchers in Grafana Cloud and create a watcher for a service your team checks by hand after every release. Describe what normal looks like, pick your data sources, and let calibration do the rest. To learn more, refer to the Watchers documentation.

event_model_payload.headline: An early look at the Grafana UI refresh: Building a clearer, more consistent user experience
event_model_payload.summary:
Whether you’re investigating an incident or just exploring your data, a clear, consistent UI helps you move between workflows and find what matters faster. As Grafana has grown to support more use cases, we’ve seen opportunities to improve on that experience. That’s why, as part of the Grafana 13.3 release, we introduced the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7.

We’re approaching this work in phases, with the refreshed UI currently in public preview in both Grafana Cloud and self-managed versions of Grafana, and your feedback will play a major role in shaping what comes next. 

In this post, we’ll give you a closer look at why we decided to make this change now, why we think visual aesthetics matter in a UI, and the impact this will have on the Grafana user experience. You can also check out some of the visual updates in the video below.

Starting with why

“Purposes are deduced from behavior, not from rhetoric or stated goals.” – Donella Meadows

At Grafana Labs, our culture empowers individuals and teams to identify user needs, build solutions quickly, ship iteratively, and work in the open. This has allowed us to cover a large range of use cases with Grafana. But moving fast can come with challenges, including design debt, which leads to inconsistent and sometimes conflicting visual cues, workflows, and GUIs. We were aware of these challenges, but our focus remained steadfast on providing new functionality and supporting as many use cases as possible.

Meanwhile, over the last year, the product design team has worked with our engineers to build new interaction patterns to support AI solutions like Grafana Assistant and Assistant Workspace. Building these patterns opened the door to curiosity, and we started experimenting with new visual forms, colors, shapes, and effects that laid the groundwork for the refresh.

Through this work, our approach to UI style and aesthetics evolved, and so did our purpose: alongside supporting new workflows and use cases, we wanted to bring greater consistency to interactions and design patterns across Grafana. This refresh is the first step toward that goal.

Visual styling and usability

“The aesthetic quality of a product is integral to its usefulness.” – Dieter Rams

So why invest in visual styling? To stay relevant? To facilitate sales conversations? Because it looks cool?

All of those reasons are valid, but at Grafana Labs, product designers are utilitarians first. We believe digital products should exist with a clear purpose and function in mind. We think each color, font style, and line should establish a clear information hierarchy and help users quickly understand what's on the page, ultimately making our product easier to use.

As more workflows shift to terminals and agentic chat interfaces, we believe investing in visual style now is foundational to Grafana’s future usability. When fewer user journeys rely on a traditional UI, those that do must emphasize clarity and consistency.

What’s new: a closer look 

This first phase of the refresh focuses on making the Grafana UI clearer and more consistent across workflows and components, while giving you time to adapt to the changes. Here are some of the highlights:

  • New default light and dark themes: These themes use completely new color palettes with improved accessibility compliance by design.

  • Increased consistency across components: We have started to reduce the amount of available UI components and their variants. This means users only need to learn an interaction or a pattern once, and can then leverage it across the entire platform.

  • New font styles, borders, and shadows: By overhauling our visual primitives to work in a proportional and scalable way, we create layers of hierarchy and visual information. As part of our audits, we noticed that many areas of the UI competed for users’ attention. We’re moving to a state where you can immediately understand what’s most important on a page, so you can complete tasks faster and more efficiently. You’ll notice these changes across the building blocks of Grafana, including cards, panels, and drawers.

We’re rolling out the visual refresh gradually so Grafana contributors and users have time to adapt without disrupting critical workflows. Importantly, this is a visual refresh, not a redesign. Existing navigation stays the same, and there are no breaking changes for plugins. 

To try out the new UI in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle. You can switch back to the previous styling at any time.

For a full list of changes in the public preview, please visit our documentation.

Curiosity, monitoring, and feedback

"There are three key practices needed in order to build and maintain a circle of competence: curiosity and a desire to learn, monitoring, and feedback." – Shane Parrish & Rhiannon Beaubien

Curiosity is a key attribute of product designers at Grafana Labs and we knew that unifying the look and feel across Grafana meant making choices that could elicit strong reactions. This is why learning, gathering feedback, and monitoring the response have been central to our process.

We could have spent a year working on what we think is a perfect new visual styling, running hundreds of internal iterations, but instead we started with early internal dogfooding of the refreshed UI. This led to honest discussions and opinions from Grafanistas across the company, helping us iterate the visual refresh rapidly into a version we could not have achieved without working openly. 

Now, with the refresh in public preview, your feedback is central to how we’ll continue to refine our visual styling. Through our community Slack and a temporary in-app survey, you can tell us directly what’s working, what needs improvement, and what we might have missed. We monitor and discuss this feedback in the open, helping to amplify your voice and share it across the organization. Your responses will be integral to shaping future iterations of the refresh.

We can’t wait to hear what you think, and to continue our evolution toward a bolder visual experience for all Grafana users.

event_model_payload.headline: Announcing Rust 1.100.0
event_model_payload.summary:
The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.100.0 with:

$ rustup update stable

If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0.

If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across!

What's in 1.100.0 stable

  • Never type
  • Allocator API
  • DropGuard API
  • Conjuring zero-sized types
  • Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo
  • Reducing Cargo cache collisions
  • Cargo min-publish-age
  • Stabilized APIs

Never type

After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable! This also completes the project goal for this work.

The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return, break, and std::process::exit, also have the type !.

Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if:

fn mrrrow(option: Option<u32>) {
    let value = match option {
        // `x` has type `u32`
        Some(x) => x,
        // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`,
        // allowing the `match` to pass type checking.
        None => return,
    };
    // ...
}

While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions (-> !), this release allows naming the never type anywhere:

fn infallible_unwrap<T>(res: Result<T, !>) -> T {
    // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before
    let Ok(v) = res;
    v
}

Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using !. This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization).

Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible, we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable.

We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.

Allocator API

This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api, enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box. These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait.

This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!

DropGuard: run a closure on every exit path

The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return, ?, or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket.

Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard: a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped.

DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable.

DropGuard also implements a dismiss associated function[1] which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure:

use std::mem::DropGuard;
use std::num::ParseIntError;

/// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`.
/// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged.
fn parse_all(nums: &mut Vec<u32>, strings: &[&str]) -> Result<(), ParseIntError> {
    let len = nums.len();
    let mut nums = DropGuard::new(nums, move |nums| {
        nums.truncate(len);    // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure
    });

    for s in strings {
        nums.push(s.parse()?); // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back
    }

    DropGuard::dismiss(nums);  // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard
    Ok(())
}

Conjuring zero-sized types

As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this.

This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst.

Instead of transmuting (), MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init(), or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing.

Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition.

Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo

Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it.

Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g.

warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber`
  --> Cargo.toml:23:1
   |
23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber`

A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built.

This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml, completing this project goal. See also the other lints that have been introduced.

Reducing Cargo cache collisions

Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir. At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like --features, can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir. These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees.

The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory.

This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal, unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking.

We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases.

Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns

Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns.

You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml:

[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"

When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back:

$ cargo update
    Updating crates.io index
     Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age
      Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago)
      Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago)

When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update:

$ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE=allow cargo update clap --precise 4.6.9
    Updating crates.io index
    Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days)

The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it.

A few things to keep in mind:

  • This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back.

  • cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed.

  • Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would.

Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal, including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases.

Stabilized APIs

  • impl PartialEq> for Vec
  • impl PartialEq> for &[T]
  • impl PartialEq> for &mut [T]
  • std::alloc::Allocator
  • std::alloc::Global
  • std::alloc::System
  • impl Allocator for Global
  • impl Allocator for System
  • impl Allocator for &A
  • impl Allocator for Box
  • impl Allocator for &mut A
  • impl Allocator for Arc
  • impl Allocator for Rc
  • Box::new_in
  • Box::from_raw_in
  • Box::from_non_null_in
  • Box::into_raw_with_allocator
  • Box::into_non_null_with_allocator
  • Box::allocator
  • Vec::new_in
  • Vec::with_capacity_in
  • Vec::from_raw_parts_in
  • Vec::from_parts_in
  • Vec::into_raw_parts_with_allocator
  • Vec::into_parts_with_allocator
  • Vec::allocator
  • Child::main_thread_handle
  • impl Default for std::sync::Once
  • bool::toggle
  • Box::take
  • Box::map
  • Rc::map
  • Arc::map
  • impl AsRef for !
  • impl AsMut for !
  • core::mem::DropGuard
  • core::mem::conjure_zst
  • UnsafeCell::replace
  • UnsafeCell::as_ref_unchecked
  • UnsafeCell::as_mut_unchecked
  • str::trim_prefix
  • str::trim_suffix
  • [T]::trim_prefix
  • [T]::trim_suffix
  • Path::trim_prefix
  • Vec::from_fn
  • os::windows::process::CommandExt::show_window

Other changes

Check out everything that changed in Rust, Cargo, and Clippy.

Contributors to 1.100.0

Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!
